title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.2 One application versus repeated applications
text:
7.2 One application versus repeated applications
The spectral radius of a square matrix is \(\rho(A)=\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(A)}|\lambda|\), where \(\sigma(A)\) is the set of complex eigenvalues. For an eigenpair \(Av=\lambda v\) with \(v\ne0\), we have \(|\lambda|\,\|v\|=\|Av\|\leq\|A\|\,\|v\|\). Taking the maximum gives \(\rho(A)\leq\|A\|\) for any induced norm on the complex space. For real matrices the usual \(1,2,\infty\) formulas give the same operator norms over either field.
For Hermitian \(A\), an orthonormal eigenbasis diagonalizes \(A\) and \(A^*A\) with respective entries \(\lambda_i\) and \(|\lambda_i|^2\). Thus \(\|A\|_2=\rho(A)\). The same proof applies to every normal matrix (\(A^*A=AA^*\)), by unitary diagonalization.
Revisit \(B\). Its triangular form gives eigenvalues \(0,4\), so \(\rho(B)=4<5=\|B\|_2\). Its most stretched input \((0,1)^T\) changes direction. Indeed \(B^2=4B\), so \(\|B^k\|_2=5\cdot4^{k-1}\) for \(k\geq1\). The one-step maximum is \(5\), yet the long-run per-step growth factor is \(4\). More generally, for a stationary iteration with error recurrence \(e_{k+1}=Te_k\), the error tends to zero for every initial error exactly when \(\rho(T)<1\). A norm bound \(\|T\|<1\) guarantees contraction at every step. Session 8 studies this distinction.
crumbs: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning

title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.3 Conditioning a linear solve
text:
7.3 Conditioning a linear solve
Assume from here that \(A\) is square and invertible, \(Ax=b\), and all matrix norms are induced by the chosen vector norm unless marked otherwise. Relative measures below assume \(b\ne0\), which also gives \(x\ne0\).

What changes when the data change?
Hold \(A\) fixed and replace \(b\) by \(b+\delta b\). Subtracting the original equations from \(A(x+\delta x)=b+\delta b\) gives \(A\delta x=\delta b\). The absolute sensitivity is governed by \(\delta x=A^{-1}\delta b\). To compare relative changes, insert the scale of the original data,
\[
\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|}
\leq \|A^{-1}\|\frac{\|b\|}{\|x\|}
      \frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}
\leq \underbrace{\|A^{-1}\|\,\|A\|}_{\kappa(A)}
      \frac{\|\delta b\|}{\|b\|}.
\]
The last step uses \(\|b\|=\|Ax\|\leq\|A\|\,\|x\|\). The condition number \(\kappa(A)\) is dimensionless because the units of forward and inverse amplification cancel. Scaling \(A\) by any nonzero scalar leaves it unchanged. Also \(1=\|I\|\leq\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|\).
For this particular \(b\), the sharp worst-direction factor is \(\|A^{-1}\|\,\|b\|/\|x\|\). Maximizing over \(x\) as well yields \(\kappa(A)\). A large value describes possible amplification. The actual outcome depends on both the original solution direction and the direction of the perturbation. No solver entered the derivation.


Stretching factors and inversion
As a unit vector ranges over all directions, its squared image length ranges from \(\lambda_{\min}(A^*A)\) to \(\lambda_{\max}(A^*A)\). Write \(\sigma_{\min}\) and \(\sigma_{\max}\) for the corresponding positive square roots. Substituting \(w=Av\) in the definition of the inverse norm gives
\[
\|A^{-1}\|_2=\max_{v\ne0}\frac{\|v\|_2}{\|Av\|_2}
=\frac{1}{\sigma_{\min}},\qquad
\kappa_2(A)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}.
\]
Thus conditioning measures the aspect ratio of the image ellipsoid. For Hermitian positive-definite \(A\), all eigenvalues are positive and \(A^*A=A^2\), so \(\kappa_2(A)=\lambda_{\max}(A)/\lambda_{\min}(A)\). Inversion multiplies each eigenvector by the reciprocal eigenvalue. For a general invertible matrix the singular-value formula applies, even when eigenvectors fail to span the space.
Worked example. Set \(A_\varepsilon=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) with \(0<\varepsilon\leq1\). The unit circle maps to an ellipse with horizontal semiaxis \(1\) and vertical semiaxis \(\varepsilon\). Inversion stretches a vertical data perturbation by \(1/\varepsilon\) and preserves a horizontal one. For \(\varepsilon=10^{-4}\) the corresponding amplification factors are \(10^4\) and \(1\), and \(\kappa_2=10^4\). By comparison, \(10^{-4}I\) amplifies every direction by \(10^4\) under inversion but has condition number \(1\). Absolute amplification and relative sensitivity answer different questions.


If the matrix changes too
Suppose \((A+\delta A)(x+\delta x)=b+\delta b\). Expansion gives the exact identity \(A\delta x=\delta b-\delta A\,x-\delta A\,\delta x\). The extra terms express a change in the operator itself. Put \(d_A=\|\delta A\|/\|A\|\) and \(d_b=\|\delta b\|/\|b\|\). Apply \(A^{-1}\), take norms, and move the term containing \(\|\delta x\|\) to the left. When \(\kappa(A)d_A<1\), the result is
\[
\frac{\|\delta x\|}{\|x\|}
\leq \frac{\kappa(A)(d_A+d_b)}{1-\kappa(A)d_A}.
\]
The condition ensures invertibility of \(A+\delta A\) because \(\|A^{-1}\delta A\|<1\) and \(I+A^{-1}\delta A\) has a convergent geometric-series inverse. To first order in small perturbations the numerator gives the bound. For fixed \(A\) the denominator is exactly one.
crumbs: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning

title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.4 The error equation
text:
7.4 The error equation
Given a candidate \(\widehat{x}\), form the residual \(r=b-A\widehat{x}\) from known quantities. The forward error \(e=x-\widehat{x}\) involves the unknown exact solution. Linearity connects them:
\[
Ae=Ax-A\widehat{x}=b-A\widehat{x}=r,
\qquad \boxed{e=A^{-1}r}.
\]
This identity says that recovering the missing correction is itself a solve with the original matrix. It does not require forming an inverse. Taking norms gives \(\|e\|\leq\|A^{-1}\|\,\|r\|\). For \(b\ne0\), insert \(\|b\|/\|b\|\) and use \(\|b\|/\|x\|\leq\|A\|\):
\[
\boxed{\frac{\|x-\widehat{x}\|}{\|x\|}
\leq\kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\widehat{x}\|}{\|b\|}.}
\]
The second factor measures the defect on the scale of the equations. The first translates that defect into a worst-case relative uncertainty in solution space. For example, a verified \(\kappa(A)\leq20\) and a relative residual at most \(10^{-8}\) certify relative error at most \(2\cdot10^{-7}\). An estimated condition number gives a diagnostic estimate unless it is known to bound the true value from above.

One residual, two directions
Take \(A_\varepsilon\) as above, \(x=(1,0)^T\), \(b=(1,0)^T\), and \(\widehat{x}=(1,1)^T\). Then
\[
A_\varepsilon\widehat{x}=(1,\varepsilon)^T,\qquad
r=(0,-\varepsilon)^T,\qquad e=(0,-1)^T.
\]
Both reference norms are \(1\). The relative residual is \(\varepsilon\), the relative error is \(1\), and the upper bound is \((1/\varepsilon)\varepsilon=1\). Equality holds at every scale. An entire spurious vertical component survives in the computed solution while contributing only \(\varepsilon\) to the equations. Taking \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) makes the residual arbitrarily small while keeping every matrix invertible.
Keep the matrix and \(b\) fixed but choose \(\widehat{x}=(1-\varepsilon,0)^T\). The equally small horizontal residual \((\varepsilon,0)^T\) now corresponds to relative error \(\varepsilon\). Conversely, for the well-conditioned system \(A=I\), \(b=(1,0)^T\), every residual equals its error vector. The first approximation \((1,1)^T\) then has relative residual \(1\), immediately exposing the error.


Experiment in two dimensions
Predict the slope of each curve as \(\varepsilon\) decreases. The experiment prescribes a candidate so that it isolates what a residual can certify independently of how the candidate was obtained.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

eps_values = 10.0 ** (-np.arange(0, 13, dtype=float))
x = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
x_hat = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
measurements = []

for eps in eps_values:
    A = np.diag([1.0, eps])
    b = A @ x
    relative_residual = np.linalg.norm(b - A @ x_hat) / np.linalg.norm(b)
    relative_error = np.linalg.norm(x - x_hat) / np.linalg.norm(x)
    condition = np.linalg.cond(A, 2)
    measurements.append((condition, relative_residual, relative_error,
                         condition * relative_residual))

condition, residual, error, bound = np.array(measurements).T
for observed, predicted in zip((condition, residual, error, bound),
                               (1 / eps_values, eps_values, 1.0, 1.0)):
    np.testing.assert_allclose(observed, predicted, rtol=1e-13, atol=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 3.4), constrained_layout=True)
ax.loglog(eps_values, condition, "^-", label="Condition number")
ax.loglog(eps_values, residual, "v--", label="Relative residual")
ax.loglog(eps_values, error, "-", color="black", label="Relative error")
ax.loglog(eps_values, bound, "o", mfc="none", color="black", label="Bound")
ax.invert_xaxis()
ax.set(xlabel=r"Vertical stretching factor $\varepsilon$", ylabel="Magnitude")
ax.grid(True, which="major", alpha=0.25)
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.show()







Figure 7.1: As the vertical stretching factor decreases, the relative residual shrinks while the relative error remains one. Open circles mark the upper bound, which is attained at every point.





In exact arithmetic the four quantities are \(1/\varepsilon,\varepsilon,1,1\). At \(10^{-8}\) this gives \(10^8,10^{-8},1,1\). The code computes all four from the arrays and checks agreement to relative tolerance \(10^{-13}\). The range down to \(10^{-12}\) stays far above underflow. The vertical residual subtracts a nonzero entry from zero, so it avoids the cancellation that can complicate real residual evaluations.

title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.5 Backward error and stability
text:
7.5 Backward error and stability
Ask how the data would have to change to make the computed answer exact. With \(A\) fixed, \(A\widehat{x}=b-r\), so the unique admissible change is \(\delta b=-r\). The relative right-hand-side backward error is therefore \(\eta_b=\|r\|/\|b\|\). For the vertical error above, \(\widehat{x}\) is an exact answer for data only \(\varepsilon\) away in relative terms.
A different model allows simultaneous, unstructured changes to both inputs. In the Euclidean and induced spectral norms let \(\eta_{A,b}\) be the smallest \(t\) for which \((A+\delta A)\widehat{x}=b+\delta b\), with \(\|\delta A\|_2\leq t\|A\|_2\) and \(\|\delta b\|_2\leq t\|b\|_2\). Then
\[
\eta_{A,b}=\frac{\|r\|_2}{\|A\|_2\|\widehat{x}\|_2+\|b\|_2}.
\]
Indeed \(r=\delta A\widehat{x}-\delta b\) gives the lower bound by the triangle inequality. For nonzero \(r,\widehat{x}\), set \(q=r/\|r\|_2\), \(v=\widehat{x}/\|\widehat{x}\|_2\) and take \(\delta A=t\|A\|_2qv^*\), \(\delta b=-t\|b\|_2q\). The two contributions point along \(q\) and attain the bound at the stated \(t\). Zero residual gives zero backward error, and \(\widehat{x}=0\) requires \(\delta b=-b\). Restrictions such as symmetry, sparsity, or componentwise tolerances define other models. To bound forward error from \(\eta_{A,b}\), use the simultaneous perturbation estimate with \(d_A,d_b\leq\eta_{A,b}\) and check its denominator.
Backward stability means that an algorithm, over its stated class of inputs, returns exact solutions for admissibly perturbed data with backward error bounded on the scale of \(C u\), where \(u\) is unit roundoff and \(C\) is a suitably modest factor under the stated assumptions. A single observed backward error assesses one result. An algorithmic stability claim requires a bound across inputs. On an ill-conditioned system, even an error on the scale of roundoff can be amplified by the inverse.
Worked example — same problem, different algorithms. Solve the scalar system \(1x=1\) in binary64 arithmetic with rounding to nearest, ties to even. Direct division gives \(1\). Another procedure computes \(((b+M)-M)/A\) with \(M=2^{53}\). This is the same formula in exact arithmetic. In binary64, the consecutive representable numbers at and just above \(M\) are \(M\) and \(M+2\). The midpoint \(M+1\) rounds to \(M\), so the procedure returns \(0\). Here \(\kappa=1\), and both the relative residual and relative forward error of the second answer are \(1\). The damaging operation was introduced by the algorithm. Session 4 used the same diagnostic discipline for QR by checking both the reconstruction residual \(\|A-\widehat Q\widehat R\|\) and the orthogonality defect \(\|I-\widehat Q^*\widehat Q\|\).
crumbs: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning

title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.6 Central Synthesis — Conditioning, Backward Error, and Forward Error
text:
7.6 Central Synthesis — Conditioning, Backward Error, and Forward Error
Start with the candidate produced by the algorithm. Substitution into the equations gives a defect. Specify which inputs may change, then translate the defect into a backward error. A sensitivity estimate for that same data model converts the backward error into a statement about forward accuracy. In the fixed-\(A\) model the entire argument fits in one line:
\[
A\widehat{x}=b-r
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x-\widehat{x}=A^{-1}r
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\|x-\widehat{x}\|}{\|x\|}\leq\kappa(A)\eta_b.
\]
Reading a solver report. The following quantities assume consistent norms and nonzero reference data where needed.








Diagnostic
Quantity
Available without \(x\)?




Absolute residual
\(\|b-A\widehat{x}\|\)
Yes, in the units of \(b\)


Relative residual
\(\|r\|/\|b\|\)
Yes, relative to data scale


Absolute forward error
\(\|x-\widehat{x}\|\)
Usually requires a reference solution


Relative forward error
\(\|x-\widehat{x}\|/\|x\|\)
Usually requires a reference solution


Condition number
\(\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|\)
Yes, often estimated using solves


Backward error
\(\eta_b\) or \(\eta_{A,b}\)
Yes, after specifying the model



A small upper bound certifies accuracy. A large upper bound leaves accuracy undecided, as the two residual directions for \(A_\varepsilon\) illustrate. Good conditioning helps only when the algorithm delivers small backward error. In practice the computed residual also contains rounding from the matrix-vector product and subtraction. If \(A\widehat{x}\) is very close to \(b\), that rounding can dominate the defect. Recomputing the residual in higher precision, as in mixed-precision iterative refinement, makes the diagnostic more informative.

Connections to the lecture and seminar

Direct methods (Session 7). For a backward-stable QR solve, or an LU solve with suitably controlled growth, a small backward error and large condition number can coexist. Pivoting and the choice of factorization concern the algorithm. Sensitivity of the original solve is common to all of them.
Stationary iterations (Session 8). The iteration matrix governs how errors propagate between steps. The system matrix governs how the current residual translates into solution error. A residual stopping tolerance needs the latter relationship.
Eigensolvers (Sessions 9 and 11). For a unit candidate \(\widehat v\) and approximate eigenvalue \(\widehat\lambda\), the eigenpair residual \(s=A\widehat v-\widehat\lambda\widehat v\) is computable. For Hermitian \(A\), expanding in an orthonormal eigenbasis gives \(\|s\|_2^2=\sum_i |\lambda_i-\widehat\lambda|^2|c_i|^2\), where \(c_i\) are the coefficients of \(\widehat v\). If several eigenvalues cluster near \(\widehat\lambda\), many mixtures give small residuals. Accuracy of an individual eigenvector requires spectral separation.
Chebyshev filtering (Sessions 9–11). In exact arithmetic a polynomial \(p(A)\) weights each eigenvector component by \(p(\lambda_i)\). Separation between wanted and unwanted filter values drives subspace improvement. In finite precision, polynomial evaluation introduces errors, and unequal amplification can make block columns nearly dependent. QR restores a usable basis to the extent that its directions are still resolved. Check basis orthogonality and Ritz residuals alongside the predicted filter response.

Course reading. The Review I route follows §§1.3, 1.3.3, and 1.4.4 of the book. Kanschat and Scheichl, Numerical Linear Algebra, Appendix B.1 gives the operator-norm and spectral-radius framework, with Chapters 3–4 supplying eigenvalue and iteration contexts. Scheichl and Zech, Numerik 0, §§2.1–2.2 and 3.1–3.3 develop conditioning, stability, matrix norms, and perturbation bounds. Bastian, Numerik 0, §§3, 5, and 6 connects finite arithmetic to linear-system sensitivity.

section: 7.7 Independent exercises
text:
7.7 Independent exercises

Three views of one matrix (3 min). For \(C=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), compute the induced \(1,\infty,2\) norms and \(\rho(C)\). Exhibit a Euclidean unit input attaining the spectral norm.
A first step that grows (3 min). For \(T=\begin{pmatrix}0&6\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\), find \(\rho(T)\) and \(\|T\|_2\). Starting from \((0,1)^T\), calculate the first two errors in \(e_{k+1}=Te_k\). Explain their behavior.
Two data errors (4 min). Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(4,1/2)\), \(x=(1,0)^T\), and \(b=Ax\). Compute \(\kappa_2(A)\). Perturb \(b\) first by \((0.04,0)^T\), then by \((0,0.04)^T\). Find the relative data and solution changes. Which direction attains the global bound?
Reconstruct the certificate (5 min). Given \(Ax=b\) and a candidate \(y\), derive the absolute and relative forward-error bounds from the definition of the induced norm. State every nonzero or invertibility assumption. Recover the relative right-hand-side perturbation estimate by choosing \(y\) appropriately.
Audit an accuracy claim (6 min). A report gives a relative residual of \(10^{-9}\) and an estimated \(\kappa_2\) of \(10^9\). It claims nine accurate digits. Assess the claim, then construct two invertible diagonal-system examples with those exact diagnostics, one with relative error \(1\) and one with relative error \(10^{-9}\). You may use the same matrix for both.
Two solvers and two data models (6 min). A matrix has verified \(\kappa_2(A)=3\). On the same data, solvers P and Q produce relative residuals \(10^{-14}\) and \(0.2\), respectively. Give upper and lower bounds on their relative forward errors. Which stability claims about the algorithms follow? For Q, suppose additionally that \(\|A\|_2\|\widehat x\|_2=2\|b\|_2\). Calculate the simultaneous backward error and explain why it differs from \(0.2\).

title: 7  Session 6 — Matrix Norms and Conditioning
section: 7.8 Worked solutions
text:
7.8 Worked solutions
1. Three views. The absolute column sums are \(1,2\) and row sums are \(3,0\), giving \(\|C\|_1=2\) and \(\|C\|_\infty=3\). A unit input \((s,t)^T\) produces length \(|s-2t|\leq\sqrt5\) by Cauchy–Schwarz. Equality holds at \((1,-2)^T/\sqrt5\), so \(\|C\|_2=\sqrt5\). Triangularity gives eigenvalues \(1,0\) and spectral radius \(1\).
2. A first step that grows. Both eigenvalues are zero. Acting on \((s,t)^T\) gives \((6t,0)^T\), so \(\|T\|_2=6\). Starting on the vertical axis gives \(e_1=(6,0)^T\) and \(e_2=0\). The maximally stretched direction maps into the kernel. Indeed \(T^2=0\) for all initial vectors, consistent with \(\rho(T)=0\).
3. Two data errors. The singular values are \(4,1/2\), so \(\kappa_2=8\). Since \(b=(4,0)^T\), both relative perturbations are \(0.04/4=0.01\). Multiplication by \(A^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,2)\) gives corrections \((0.01,0)^T\) and \((0,0.08)^T\). The original solution has unit norm, so the relative changes are \(0.01\) and \(0.08\). The vertical perturbation attains \(8\cdot0.01\).
4. Reconstruct the certificate. Let \(A\) be square and invertible and take a vector norm with its induced matrix norm. Set \(e=x-y\) and \(r=b-Ay\). Then \(Ae=r\), hence \(e=A^{-1}r\). The defining supremum bounds \(\|e\|\) by \(\|A^{-1}\|\,\|r\|\) (including \(r=0\)). For \(b\ne0\) we have \(x\ne0\) and \(\|b\|/\|x\|\leq\|A\|\). Dividing the absolute bound by \(\|x\|\) and inserting this ratio gives \(\|e\|/\|x\|\leq\kappa(A)\|r\|/\|b\|\). If \(Ay=b+\delta b\), then \(r=-\delta b\) and \(e=-(y-x)\). Taking norms gives the desired relative perturbation estimate.
5. Audit an accuracy claim. Even if the condition estimate is exact, the upper bound is \(1\). An estimated condition number introduces additional uncertainty. Choose \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-9})\) and \(x=b=(1,0)^T\). With \(y=(1,1)^T\), \(r=(0,-10^{-9})^T\) and \(e=(0,-1)^T\). With \(y=(1-10^{-9},0)^T\), \(r=e=(10^{-9},0)^T\). Both candidates have the reported diagnostics in exact arithmetic. Their relative errors are \(1\) and \(10^{-9}\) respectively. The report omits the direction information that distinguishes them.
6. Two solvers. Write \(h=\|r\|/\|b\|\) and \(f=\|e\|/\|x\|\). From \(r=Ae\) and \(x=A^{-1}b\) we get \(h\leq\|A\|\,\|A^{-1}\|f\). Combine this with \(f\leq\kappa(A)h\) to obtain \(h/3\leq f\leq3h\). P has \(10^{-14}/3\leq f\leq3\cdot10^{-14}\). Q has \(1/15\leq f\leq0.6\). The lower bound establishes an actual loss of accuracy for Q. Conditioning is identical in both runs. P delivered small backward error on this instance, which alone cannot establish backward stability over a class of inputs. Q’s result contradicts any claimed fixed-\(A\) stability guarantee requiring a relative backward error smaller than \(0.2\) on these data. For the simultaneous model the denominator is \(3\|b\|_2\), giving \(\eta_{A,b}=0.2/3=1/15\). Allowing perturbations in the operator as well as the data makes a smaller common budget sufficient.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
text:
8.1 Elimination changes the equations
Given \(Ax=b\), how can we turn the equations into a form we can solve one unknown at a time? Session 1 supplies the algebraic idea of composing linear maps. Session 6 supplies a separate question about the answer we compute: how much uncertainty does a small residual leave in the solution? A direct solver brings these questions together. Its transformations determine the work, the intermediate numbers and, ultimately, how much accuracy survives.
One-hour route. Spend 12 minutes on elimination, substitution and LU, 9 on pivoting and the experiment results, 8 on Cholesky, and 8 on comparing and assessing solvers. Reserve 23 minutes for the exercises. The experiment runs during rendering. Studying its implementation is optional.
Throughout, \(A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}\) with \(\mathbb F=\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), and \(A^*\) denotes the conjugate transpose. Derivations use exact arithmetic unless rounding is mentioned.
In \(Ax=b\), applying an invertible map \(E\) to the equation space gives \(EAx=Eb\). Every solution satisfies the transformed equations, and multiplication by \(E^{-1}\) recovers the originals. In particular, the unknown \(x\) keeps its original coordinates. Each elementary row operation has an explicit inverse: swap the same rows again, scale by the reciprocal of a nonzero scale factor, or undo a row addition by subtracting the same multiple. Carry the right-hand side through every operation.
Starting with \(A^{(1)}=A\), suppose the first \(k-1\) columns already have zeros below their diagonals. The pivot \(a^{(k)}_{kk}\) is the coefficient used to eliminate the remaining entries below it in column \(k\). For a nonzero pivot and each \(i>k\), set \[
m_{ik}=\frac{a^{(k)}_{ik}}{a^{(k)}_{kk}},
\qquad R_i\gets R_i-m_{ik}R_k .
\] The new column entry is zero by construction. The pivot row has zeros in the preceding columns, so those columns stay triangular. Gaussian elimination stops at upper-triangular form and uses substitution. Gauss–Jordan elimination continues by normalizing pivots and clearing entries above them to obtain reduced row echelon form.
Running example. Start with the augmented matrix below. Subtract twice row 1 from row 2 and add row 1 to row 3: \[
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r}2&1&1&3\\4&5&0&14\\-2&2&5&-3\end{array}\right]
\longrightarrow
\left[\begin{array}{rrr|r}2&1&1&3\\0&3&-2&8\\0&3&6&0\end{array}\right].
\] The first two multipliers were \(2\) and \(-1\). Now subtract row 2 from row 3. The multiplier is \(1\), using the current entries \(3/3\). The final system is \[
Ux=y,\qquad U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&3&-2\\0&0&8\end{pmatrix},
\qquad y=\begin{pmatrix}3\\8\\-8\end{pmatrix}.
\] The three diagonal entries \(2,3,8\) are the pivots, including the last coefficient used in the solve.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.2 Triangular systems have a natural order
text:
8.2 Triangular systems have a natural order
The last equation of \(Ux=y\) determines \(x_n\). At row \(i\), all terms to the right of \(u_{ii}x_i\) are already known. Isolating that term gives backward substitution. A lower-triangular system \(Ly=b\) has the reverse dependency and gives forward substitution: \[
\begin{aligned}
x_i &= \frac{y_i-\sum_{j=i+1}^n u_{ij}x_j}{u_{ii}},
   &&i=n,n-1,\ldots,1,\\
y_i &= \frac{b_i-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\ell_{ij}y_j}{\ell_{ii}},
   &&i=1,2,\ldots,n.
\end{aligned}
\] An empty sum is zero. For a unit lower-triangular matrix every \(\ell_{ii}=1\), so the divisions disappear. A square triangular matrix has a unique solution for every right-hand side exactly when every diagonal entry is nonzero: its determinant is their product. With a zero on the diagonal, consistency determines whether there are infinitely many solutions or none.
In the example the last equation gives \(x_3=-1\), the second gives \(x_2=(8+2x_3)/3=2\), and the first gives \(x_1=(3-x_2-x_3)/2=1\). Across all rows there are \(n(n-1)/2\) off-diagonal products to subtract, hence \(O(n^2)\) work. Substitution computes the action of an inverse on the one vector we need. Forming the whole inverse would solve for all its columns and introduce extra work and rounding.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.3 LU remembers the elimination
text:
8.3 LU remembers the elimination
Let \(e_k\) be the \(k\)th coordinate vector and \(m_k\) the column containing \(m_{ik}\) for \(i>k\) and zeros elsewhere. Since \(e_k^T A^{(k)}\) extracts row \(k\), one stage is \[
A^{(k+1)}=E_k A^{(k)},\qquad
E_k=I-m_k e_k^T,\qquad E_k^{-1}=I+m_k e_k^T.
\] The inverse follows from \(e_k^T m_k=0\). After the last stage, \[
U=E_{n-1}\cdots E_1 A,\qquad
A=LU,\qquad L=E_1^{-1}\cdots E_{n-1}^{-1}.
\] The inverse factors occur in reverse order from the elimination factors. In this product every cross term with indices \(j<k\) contains \(e_j^T m_k=0\). Thus \(L=I+\sum_k m_k e_k^T\): write each multiplier, with its original sign, below the diagonal in the column where it was used.
Verification and reuse. In the running example, \[
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&1&1\end{pmatrix}}_{L}
\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&3&-2\\0&0&8\end{pmatrix}}_{U}
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\4&5&0\\-2&2&5\end{pmatrix}=A.
\] For instance, row 3 of the product is minus row 1 of \(U\) plus rows 2 and 3. Solve \(Ly=b\) from the top: \(y_1=3\), \(y_2=14-2(3)=8\), and \(y_3=-3+3-8=-8\). This recovers exactly the transformed right-hand side. Backward substitution then gives the previously obtained \(x=(1,2,-1)^T\). For a new load vector \(b\), only these two substitutions change. The same factors solve a whole block \(AX=B\) by solving \(LY=B\) and \(UX=Y\) column by column or in a block.
When does this work without exchanges? For nonsingular \(A\), unpivoted elimination succeeds exactly when every leading principal minor \(d_k=\det A_{1:k,1:k}\) is nonzero. To see why, set \(d_0=1\). Once the first \(k-1\) stages succeed, row additions restricted to the leading \(k\) rows triangularize the leading \(k\)-by-\(k\) block. Thus \(d_k=d_{k-1}u_{kk}\). Induction gives the criterion and the pivot formula \(u_{kk}=d_k/d_{k-1}\). Nonsingularity alone guarantees only \(d_n\ne0\).
For a real dense matrix, updating a trailing \(j\)-by-\(j\) block takes about \(2j^2\) flops when a multiplication and a subtraction count separately. Summing over \(j=1,\ldots,n-1\) gives \(2n^3/3+O(n^2)\); multiplier divisions affect lower-order terms. Each further right-hand side costs about \(2n^2\) flops for both substitutions together.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.4 Pivot choice and element growth
text:
8.4 Pivot choice and element growth
A zero pivot on a perfectly conditioned system. Take \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b=(2,3)^T.
\] Unpivoted elimination asks for division by zero. Yet \(A^*A=I\), so both singular values are one and \(\kappa_2(A)=1\). With the row swap \(P=A\), we obtain \(PA=I=LU\) with \(L=U=I\). The transformed right-hand side \(Pb=(3,2)^T\) is already the solution. It was the ordering of the equations that failed.
Partial pivoting. At stage \(k\), select a row \(p\ge k\) maximizing \(|a^{(k)}_{pk}|\) and exchange it with row \(k\). If the maximum is zero, the active column is zero and the remaining square system is singular in exact arithmetic. Otherwise the multipliers have magnitude at most one. Each exchange is multiplication on the left by a permutation matrix. Their chronological action on the original equations gives a net permutation \(P\). Think of replaying elimination with those rows placed in their final order from the start: the record of multipliers for each equation must move with that equation. In particular, a late exchange swaps the two rows of the already filled columns of \(L\). The result is \[
PA=LU,\qquad Ly=Pb,\qquad Ux=y.
\] We use this convention throughout. A source writing \(A=\widetilde P LU\) uses \(\widetilde P=P^{-1}=P^T\). One swap is its own inverse, but a sequence of swaps need not be. Complete pivoting searches the whole active submatrix and may swap columns as well. A column permutation reorders unknowns and must be undone when reporting the solution.
A small nonzero pivot. Consider \[
A_\varepsilon=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad 0<\varepsilon\ll1 .
\] Without a swap, \(m_{21}=1/\varepsilon\) and \(u_{22}=1-1/\varepsilon\). The updated right-hand side \(b_2-b_1/\varepsilon\) may also be large. Back substitution reconstructs \(x_1=(b_1-\widehat x_2)/\varepsilon\): even a tiny absolute error in \(\widehat x_2\) is divided by \(\varepsilon\). When \(b_1\) and \(\widehat x_2\) are nearly equal, cancellation exposes the error already in these operands. With a swap, \(m_{21}=\varepsilon\), \(u_{22}=1-\varepsilon\), and the final division for \(x_1\) uses the pivot \(1\).
The growth factor compares the largest absolute entry seen in the coefficient matrices during elimination with the largest in the original matrix. Exclude stored multipliers and the augmented right-hand side. For this family unpivoted growth is of order \(1/\varepsilon\), while partial pivoting gives growth factor one. Large entries increase the scale of local rounding errors, which may survive even when the entries later cancel. Partial pivoting controls each multiplier, but repeated updates can still cause large growth on exceptional matrices. Its generally good practical accuracy depends in part on the growth actually encountered.

Experiment: hold conditioning nearly fixed and change the pivot
Take \(x=(1,7/4)^T\) and \(\varepsilon=3\cdot 2^{-k}\). For the exponents below, \(b=(\varepsilon+7/4,11/4)^T\) is exactly representable in binary64, as are \(A_\varepsilon\) and \(x\). Thus we know the exact solution of the stored data. As \(\varepsilon\to0\), the limiting symmetric matrix has eigenvalues \((1\pm\sqrt5)/2\). Its singular values are their absolute values, so \(\kappa_2\) tends to \((3+\sqrt5)/2\approx2.618\). Predict which solver’s error can increase while this condition number stays nearly fixed.

import numpy as np

def solve_two_by_two(A, b, pivot):
    """One elimination step and back substitution in binary64."""
    U = np.array(A, dtype=np.float64, copy=True)
    y = np.array(b, dtype=np.float64, copy=True)
    if U.shape != (2, 2) or y.shape != (2,):
        raise ValueError("Expected a 2-by-2 matrix and a length-2 vector")
    if pivot and abs(U[1, 0]) > abs(U[0, 0]):
        U = U[[1, 0], :]
        y = y[[1, 0]]
    if U[0, 0] == 0:
        raise ValueError("Zero first pivot")
    multiplier = U[1, 0] / U[0, 0]
    U[1, 1] -= multiplier * U[0, 1]
    y[1] -= multiplier * y[0]
    if U[1, 1] == 0:
        raise ValueError("Zero second pivot")
    x2 = y[1] / U[1, 1]
    x1 = (y[0] - U[0, 1] * x2) / U[0, 0]
    return np.array([x1, x2])

exact = np.array([1.0, 1.75])
print(" k  cond2  method       rel.res.  rel.error")
for k in (10, 25, 40, 50):
    eps = 3.0 * 2.0**(-k)
    A = np.array([[eps, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0]])
    b = A @ exact
    answers = [
        ("no swap", solve_two_by_two(A, b, False)),
        ("partial", solve_two_by_two(A, b, True)),
        ("library", np.linalg.solve(A, b)),
    ]
    for method, computed in answers:
        residual = np.linalg.norm(b - A @ computed) / np.linalg.norm(b)
        error = np.linalg.norm(computed - exact) / np.linalg.norm(exact)
        print(f"{k:2}  {np.linalg.cond(A):5.3f}  {method:8}"
              f"  {residual:9.2e}  {error:9.2e}")

 k  cond2  method       rel.res.  rel.error
10  2.628  no swap    2.31e-14   3.76e-14
10  2.628  partial    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
10  2.628  library    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
25  2.618  no swap    7.62e-10   1.23e-09
25  2.618  partial    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
25  2.618  library    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
40  2.618  no swap    2.50e-05   4.04e-05
40  2.618  partial    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
40  2.618  library    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
50  2.618  no swap    2.56e-02   4.13e-02
50  2.618  partial    0.00e+00   0.00e+00
50  2.618  library    0.00e+00   0.00e+00


Read across methods at fixed \(k\) first. They receive identical data; the library solve provides a practical reference, while the known \(x\) provides the forward-error measurement. At \(k=50\) the unpivoted first component loses about \(0.083\) in absolute value. The condition number is still about \(2.62\). A displayed zero residual is a zero in the arithmetic used for the check. Re-evaluating a residual at higher precision can distinguish small errors hidden by that rounding.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.5 Cholesky uses positive definiteness
text:
8.5 Cholesky uses positive definiteness
Session 5 characterized a Hermitian positive-definite (HPD) matrix by \(A=A^*\) and \(z^*Az>0\) for all \(z\ne0\), equivalently by Hermitian symmetry and strictly positive eigenvalues. The real case is symmetric positive definite (SPD).
Cholesky theorem. Every HPD matrix admits a unique factorization \(A=LL^*\) with \(L\) lower triangular and strictly positive real diagonal. For real SPD matrices, \(A=LL^T\). Conversely, any such product is Hermitian and \(z^*LL^*z=\|L^*z\|_2^2>0\) for \(z\ne0\), since \(L^*\) is invertible.
Why no pivot search is necessary. Partition the first column from the rest: \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&w^*\\w&B\end{pmatrix},
\qquad S=B-ww^*/a .
\] Testing on \(e_1\) gives \(a>0\). For any \(z\ne0\), test the quadratic form on \(v=\binom{-w^*z/a}{z}\), interpreted as a stacked scalar and column. Direct multiplication gives \(v^*Av=z^*Sz>0\). Thus the trailing matrix \(S\) after eliminating column one is again HPD. Cholesky takes \(\sqrt a\) as its first diagonal entry, \(w/\sqrt a\) below it, and factors \(S\) recursively. This is symmetric Gaussian elimination: the trailing update preserves Hermitian symmetry, so only one triangle needs to be updated. General LU would maintain two factors without using this relationship.
How to compute the entries. Expand \(a_{ij}=\sum_{s\le j}\ell_{is}\overline{\ell_{js}}\) for \(i\ge j\), and process columns in increasing order: \[
\begin{aligned}
\ell_{jj}&=\sqrt{a_{jj}-\sum_{s<j}|\ell_{js}|^2},\\
\ell_{ij}&=\frac{a_{ij}-\sum_{s<j}\ell_{is}\overline{\ell_{js}}}
                  {\ell_{jj}},\qquad i>j.
\end{aligned}
\] Each radicand is the leading entry of an HPD trailing matrix, hence real and positive. Taking its positive square root fixes the only sign or phase ambiguity. The column formulas then determine every subsequent entry uniquely.
Worked example. Solve with \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2&0\\2&5&-2\\0&-2&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad b=(4,4,-2)^T.
\] The first column of \(L\) is \((2,1,0)^T\). In column two, \(\ell_{22}=\sqrt{5-1}=2\) and \(\ell_{32}=(-2-0)/2=-1\). Finally \(\ell_{33}=\sqrt{2-0^2-(-1)^2}=1\). Multiplication verifies both the factorization and positive definiteness: \[
\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\1&2&0\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&-1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}4&2&0\\2&5&-2\\0&-2&2\end{pmatrix}.
\] Forward substitution in \(Ly=b\) gives \(y_1=2\), \(y_2=(4-2)/2=1\), \(y_3=-2+1=-1\). In \(L^*x=y\), the last row gives \(x_3=-1\), then \(2x_2-x_3=1\) gives \(x_2=0\), and \(2x_1+x_2=2\) gives \(x_1=1\).
Where the hypotheses matter. A positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix has \(z^*Az\ge0\); if singular, it cannot have a Cholesky factor with strictly positive diagonal (try \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\)). An indefinite Hermitian matrix has directions of both signs. For \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) both diagonal entries are positive, yet the second radicand is \(1-2^2=-3\). A non-Hermitian matrix cannot equal \(LL^*\) because every such product is Hermitian. In floating point a very small positive radicand can be lost in subtraction. An implementation checks for breakdown; a failure near the boundary of positive definiteness needs interpretation in light of input accuracy and rounding.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.6 Choosing and assessing a solver
text:
8.6 Choosing and assessing a solver
Classical leading work below assumes a dense, real, nonsingular square matrix. QR uses Householder reflectors stored implicitly. Each method takes \(O(n^2)\) additional work per right-hand side.









Method
When to use it
Factorization work
Reliability




LU, no swaps
Leading minors nonzero and pivot behavior understood
\(2n^3/3\)
Small relative pivots can give large growth.


LU, partial pivoting
General square solve
\(2n^3/3\)
Bounded multipliers; accuracy still depends on growth.


Cholesky
Hermitian positive definite
\(n^3/3\)
Positive exact pivots; backward stable on successful completion under standard rounding assumptions.


Householder QR
General square solve; also useful for least squares
\(4n^3/3\)
Unitary transformations preserve the 2-norm; normwise backward stable.



Cholesky roughly halves the leading LU factorization cost by updating one triangle. Session 4’s QR solve applies the reflectors to form \(Q^*b\), then solves \(Rx=Q^*b\). In all four methods the factors act directly on any new right-hand side. Explicitly constructing \(A^{-1}\) adds work even if many right-hand sides are expected.
Residual, backward error and forward error. Given a computed \(\widehat x\), set \(r=b-A\widehat x\). The residual answers how far the computed vector misses the equations. Since \(A\widehat x=b-r\), it is also an explicit backward perturbation to the right-hand side. With perturbations allowed in both \(A\) and \(b\), a common normwise backward-error measure is \[
\eta=\frac{\|r\|_2}{\|A\|_2\|\widehat x\|_2+\|b\|_2}.
\] It is the smallest common relative bound on \(\|\Delta A\|_2/\|A\|_2\) and \(\|\Delta b\|_2/\|b\|_2\) needed for \((A+\Delta A)\widehat x=b+\Delta b\), assuming \(b\ne0\). A backward-stable solve delivers a solution to data perturbed on the scale of rounding, up to dimension-dependent factors. A measured small backward error describes this particular result; a stability analysis concerns the algorithm over its class of inputs.
For nonsingular \(A\) and \(b\ne0\), Session 6 gives \[
x-\widehat x=A^{-1}r,\qquad
\frac{\|x-\widehat x\|_2}{\|x\|_2}
\le \kappa_2(A)\frac{\|r\|_2}{\|b\|_2}.
\] A small relative residual and moderate condition number certify small forward error. A large condition number weakens that certificate: an error pointing along a small-singular-value direction can have a very small image under \(A\). Even a backward-stable solver can then lose forward accuracy.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.7 Where the factors reappear
text:
8.7 Where the factors reappear
Sparse systems and Session 8. Discretizing a differential operator often couples each unknown only to a few neighbors. During elimination two neighbors of the eliminated unknown can become coupled to one another. A newly nonzero factor entry in a previously zero position is fill-in. Its extent depends on ordering and can dominate storage and work. Dense costs can therefore be prohibitive, and the cost of a sparse factorization depends on more than the initial number of nonzeros. A direct method follows a finite elimination and substitution schedule in exact arithmetic. An iterative method produces successive approximations and stops using an accuracy criterion. A factorization of a simpler approximation to \(A\) can also supply an inexpensive solve inside an iterative method as a preconditioner.
Eigenvalue methods and the seminar. At a fixed shift \(\sigma\) outside the spectrum, inverse iteration repeatedly solves \((A-\sigma I)y=x\) with changing \(x\). One pivoted LU of the shifted matrix can serve every step. An eigencomponent with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is scaled by \(1/(\lambda-\sigma)\). In Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration the corresponding weight is \(p(\lambda)\): a polynomial recurrence applies \(A\) repeatedly to vectors or blocks, avoiding a shifted factorization and its possible fill-in. QR orthonormalization still has a role after filtering. Sessions 9–11 return to these choices.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.8 Central Synthesis — From Elimination to Reliable Numerical Solvers
text:
8.8 Central Synthesis — From Elimination to Reliable Numerical Solvers








Question
What the factorization tells us
What to check




Mathematical equivalence
Each invertible row operation acts on both sides. Elimination ends with triangular equations having the same solution.
Track the right-hand side and the row order.


Computational efficiency
\(LU\) records all elimination steps; substitutions reuse them. HPD structure makes the second Cholesky factor the adjoint of the first.
Match the structure and number of right-hand sides to the factorization.


Numerical stability
Pivot choices determine multipliers and affect element growth. An algebraically valid elimination can produce poor factors after rounding.
Inspect a scaled residual or backward error, then use conditioning to assess forward accuracy.



The two pivot examples separate two diagnoses. The exchange matrix forces a row swap even in exact arithmetic. The small-pivot family permits both algorithms in exact arithmetic, yet choosing the smaller pivot can lose accuracy. In either case \(\kappa_2(A)\) is a property of the input shared by both algorithms. Conversely, selecting a stable solver leaves the sensitivity of an ill-conditioned problem in place.
Course reading. The revision plan and seminar connection are in §§1.3–1.4 of the course notes book. For elimination, pivoting and Cholesky, see Scheichl and Zech, Num0 notes, §§3.4–3.7, and Bastian, num0, §§7–10. For the orthogonal alternative, see Kanschat and Scheichl, Numerical Linear Algebra, Chapter 2.

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.9 Exercises
text:
8.9 Exercises

Recover a triangular system (3 min). Eliminate below the first pivot of \(A=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\6&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with \(b=(1,11)^T\). Record the multiplier, \(L\) and \(U\). Solve via \(Ly=b\) and \(Ux=y\).
Undo two stages (3 min). Suppose \(E_1=I-2e_2e_1^T+e_3e_1^T\), \(E_2=I-3e_3e_2^T\), and \(E_2E_1A=U\). Derive \(L\) in \(A=LU\). Show by multiplication what goes wrong if you reverse the two inverse factors.
Choose a Cholesky solve (4 min). For \(C=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}9&3\\3&5\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) construct a Cholesky factor, certify positive definiteness and solve \(Cx=(6,-2)^T\). Classify \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\) and \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\0&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) with respect to the same algorithm.
Diagnose a pivot (3 min). Let \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Determine its first unpivoted pivot, determinant and \(\kappa_2\). Repeat for \(tJ\), \(t>0\). For the experiment’s \(A_\varepsilon\), identify which intermediate quantity grows and why swapping helps. Which of these observations concerns the problem’s sensitivity?
A late row exchange (6 min). Take \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}4&4&0\\2&2&1\\1&3&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad b=(4,4,3)^T .
\] Decide whether unpivoted elimination succeeds. Construct \(P,L,U\) using partial pivoting, verify \(PA=LU\) by multiplication, and solve the two triangular systems. Check the residual. Distinguish an exact zero residual from a small residual evaluated in floating point.
A good residual for a poor answer (4 min). Take \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-8})\), \(b=(1,0)^T\) and \(\widehat x=(1,1)^T\). Compute the relative residual, relative forward error and \(\kappa_2(D)\). Give a right-hand-side perturbation making \(\widehat x\) exact. Can these data alone establish that a particular solver is unstable?

title: 8  Session 7 — Direct Numerical Methods
section: 8.10 Worked solutions
text:
8.10 Worked solutions
1. The multiplier is \(6/2=3\). Subtracting three times the first equation from the second gives \(4x_2=8\). Thus \[
L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
U=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&4\end{pmatrix}.
\] Forward substitution gives \(y=(1,11-3)^T=(1,8)^T\). Back substitution gives \(x_2=2\) and \(x_1=(1+2)/2=3/2\).
2. Multiplying \(E_2E_1A=U\) first by \(E_2^{-1}\) and then by \(E_1^{-1}\) gives \[
L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&0&1\end{pmatrix}
  \begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&3&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&3&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] In reversed order row 3 of the product becomes \(3(2,1,0)+(-1,0,1)=(5,3,1)\). The spurious \(6\) in column one records an operation on a row already modified at the wrong stage.
3. The first column is \((3,1)^T\) and the remaining diagonal is \(\sqrt{5-1}=2\). With \(L=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}3&0\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), multiplication gives \(LL^T=C\). Invertibility of \(L\) implies \(z^TCz=\|L^Tz\|_2^2>0\) for every nonzero real \(z\). Forward substitution gives \(y=(2,-2)^T\) and backward substitution gives \(x=(1,-1)^T\). The all-ones matrix has quadratic form \((z_1+z_2)^2\) on real vectors and is singular positive semidefinite. The diagonal matrix is indefinite. The final matrix is nonsymmetric. None admits a real Cholesky factor with strictly positive diagonal.
4. The first pivot is zero in both cases. The determinants are \(-1\) and \(-t^2\), respectively. Since \((tJ)^T(tJ)=t^2 I\), both singular values are \(t\), giving \(\kappa_2=1\) for every \(t>0\), including \(t=1\). In \(A_\varepsilon\) the multiplier \(1/\varepsilon\) and updated entry \(1-1/\varepsilon\) grow in magnitude. Exchanging the rows gives a multiplier \(\varepsilon\) and updated entry \(1-\varepsilon\). The singular-value ratio measures relative worst-case sensitivity. The intermediate quantities describe a particular elimination order.
5. The first pivot is \(4\), with multipliers \(1/2,1/4\). The remaining rows become \((0,0,1)\) and \((0,2,2)\), so the second unpivoted pivot vanishes. Swap rows two and three, including their stored first-column multipliers. The final multiplier is zero. Then \[
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1/4&1&0\\1/2&0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
U=\begin{pmatrix}4&4&0\\0&2&2\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] The rows of \(LU\) are \((4,4,0)\), \((1,1,0)+(0,2,2)=(1,3,2)\) and \((2,2,0)+(0,0,1)=(2,2,1)\), exactly those of \(PA\). Here \(Pb=(4,3,4)^T\). Forward substitution gives \(y=(4,3-1,4-2)^T=(4,2,2)^T\). From the bottom, \(x_3=2\), \(x_2=(2-4)/2=-1\), \(x_1=(4+4)/4=2\). Direct multiplication gives \(Ax=(4,4,3)^T\) and \(r=0\). With nonsingular \(A\), an exact zero proves \(\widehat x=x\). For a numerical residual one must allow for rounding in its evaluation and use conditioning to turn a relative residual into a forward-error bound.
6. The exact solution is \((1,0)^T\) and \(r=(0,-10^{-8})^T\). The relative residual is \(10^{-8}\), the relative forward error is \(1\), and \(\kappa_2(D)=10^8\). The residual bound is attained. Perturbing \(b\) by \(-r=(0,10^{-8})^T\) makes \(\widehat x\) exact. This example shows how the poorly scaled direction weakens the residual certificate. Judging the stability of an algorithm would also require its precision, the backward-error scale expected at that precision, and information about the procedure that produced the result.

End-of-session mastery checklist
Before Session 8, Basic Iterative Methods, check that you can independently:

Prove that simultaneous elementary operations on \(A\) and \(b\) preserve the solution set.
Eliminate by hand, identify pivots and multipliers, and derive \(A=LU\) by undoing the stages.
Explain what each factor stores, perform both substitutions and reuse factors for new loads.
Construct \(PA=LU\), including a late exchange, and apply the same permutation to \(b\).
Distinguish pivot breakdown, singularity, poor conditioning and numerical instability with examples.
State and justify the HPD hypothesis, compute a Cholesky factor and explain the saving in work.
Choose among pivoted LU, Cholesky and Householder QR using structure, cost and accuracy.
Interpret a computed residual using backward error and conditioning.
Explain how triangular solves enter iterative and shifted eigenvalue methods, and identify the main operation in a polynomial filter.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
text:
9.1 From a linear system to a fixed point
A factorization gives us a way to solve \(Ax=b\). An iteration poses a different design question. Can we compute an inexpensive correction from the data we have, and prove that applying it repeatedly removes an error we cannot observe?
Study route (75 minutes). Allow 12 minutes for splittings and fixed points, 10 for the two hand calculations, 15 for the convergence theorem and its guarantees, and 10 for stopping, the figure, and synthesis. Use the remaining 28 minutes for the exercises. Reading the Python implementation line by line is optional.
In Session 7, elimination reduced a system to triangular solves. Given suitable pivots, LU solves a nonsingular system in finitely many operations in exact arithmetic. Dense factorization costs order \(n^3\) operations and order \(n^2\) storage. Sparse elimination can introduce entries where the original matrix had zeros (fill-in). On a large grid, storing the factors can be a greater obstacle than storing the original equations. A sparse matrix-vector product needs work proportional to the number of stored nonzeros. A sparse triangular solve can also visit each stored coefficient once, although its rows depend on one another. The question is how many such inexpensive sweeps we need for a given accuracy.
A fixed point of a map \(F\) satisfies \(x^*=F(x^*)\). Starting with \(x^{(0)}\), evaluate \(x^{(k+1)}=F(x^{(k)})\). For continuous \(F\), any limit of the whole sequence is a fixed point, since passing to the limit gives \(x^*=F(x^*)\). Existence alone gives no assurance that the sequence approaches it.
We study stationary linear iterations. The update is affine, \(F(x)=Bx+c\), and stationary means that the same \(B\) and \(c\) are used at every sweep. The fixed-point equation is \((I-B)x=c\). It has a unique solution exactly when \(I-B\) is invertible.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
text:
Build the update by choosing an easy solve
Let \(A\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, \(b\in\mathbb{F}^n\), and \(\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}\) or \(\mathbb{C}\). Split \(A=M-N\) with \(M\) invertible. Since \(Ax=b\) is equivalent to \(Mx=Nx+b\), evaluate the right-hand side at the current approximation and solve for the next one:
\[
Mx^{(k+1)}=Nx^{(k)}+b,\qquad
x^{(k+1)}=Bx^{(k)}+c,\quad B=M^{-1}N,\quad c=M^{-1}b.
\]
The identity \(I-B=M^{-1}A\) verifies consistency and uniqueness at once. Multiplying the fixed-point equation by \(M\) recovers precisely the original system. Subtracting \(Mx^{(k)}\) from both sides of the sweep gives another useful reading:
\[
r^{(k)}=b-Ax^{(k)},\qquad Md^{(k)}=r^{(k)},\qquad
x^{(k+1)}=x^{(k)}+d^{(k)}.
\]
Thus \(M^{-1}r^{(k)}\) approximates the exact correction \(A^{-1}r^{(k)}\). Taking \(M=A\) would give that correction in one step, at the price of solving the original problem. A more economical \(M\) changes the propagation matrix \(B=I-M^{-1}A\). In code, solve with \(M\) using its structure. Forming its inverse can destroy sparsity and adds unnecessary work.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.2 Two choices of splitting, one system
text:
9.2 Two choices of splitting, one system
Write \(A=D+L+U\), retaining the actual signs of entries in the diagonal, strictly lower, and strictly upper parts. Assume \(a_{ii}\ne0\) for each \(i\). This makes both \(D\) and \(D+L\) invertible. A nonsingular \(A\) can have a zero diagonal entry, so this assumption needs its own check.

Jacobi uses a snapshot
Take \(M=D\), \(N=-(L+U)\). Reading \(Dx^{(k+1)}=b-(L+U)x^{(k)}\) by rows gives
\[
B_J=-D^{-1}(L+U),\qquad c_J=D^{-1}b,\qquad
x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.
\]
Every row reads the same old vector. Keep separate input and output arrays during the sweep. Rows can then be distributed across processors and the outputs become the common input for the next sweep.


Gauss–Seidel reuses a corrected component
Visit rows in order \(1,\ldots,n\). By row \(i\), the first \(i-1\) components have already been updated. Moving their terms to the left gives \((D+L)x^{(k+1)}=b-Ux^{(k)}\), hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{GS}&=-(D+L)^{-1}U, \qquad c_{GS}=(D+L)^{-1}b,\\
x_i^{(k+1)}&=\frac{1}{a_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k+1)}-\sum_{j>i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
This is forward substitution with \(M=D+L\). One array suffices. An entry below the diagonal creates a dependency on the newly computed component. A different ordering can change the sweep and its convergence behavior.


Worked example — when does the second unknown first change?
Use the same start \(x^{(0)}=(0,0)^T\) for both methods, with
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
x^*=\begin{pmatrix}2/3\\1/3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Write the old coordinates as \((u,v)\) and the new ones as \((u',v')\). Both methods compute \(u'=(1+v)/2\). Jacobi takes \(v'=u/2\) and Gauss–Seidel takes \(v'=u'/2=(1+v)/4\). Reading off the coefficients and constant terms gives
\[
B_J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix},\quad c_J=\binom{1/2}{0},\qquad
B_{GS}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/2\\0&1/4\end{pmatrix},\quad c_{GS}=\binom{1/2}{1/4}.
\]



Sweep \(k\)
Jacobi \((u,v)\)
Gauss–Seidel \((u,v)\)




0
\((0,0)\)
\((0,0)\)


1
\((1/2,0)\)
\((1/2,1/4)\)


2
\((1/2,1/4)\)
\((5/8,5/16)\)


3
\((5/8,1/4)\)
\((21/32,21/64)\)



In the first Jacobi sweep the second row still sees \(u=0\). In the first Gauss–Seidel sweep it sees \(u'=1/2\), and its equation is already satisfied at the end of the sweep. The next first-row update can disturb that equation again. To decide whether these corrections solve both equations in the limit, track an entire error vector across a sweep.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.3 The error obeys a homogeneous equation
text:
9.3 The error obeys a homogeneous equation
Use the signed error \(e^{(k)}=x^{(k)}-x^*\) throughout this session. This reverses the exact-minus-approximate convention of Session 6 and preserves all norm estimates. The solver stores \(x^{(k)}\). The vector \(x^*\) is fixed and generally unknown. We can reason about their difference because both obey the same affine rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{(k+1)}&=Bx^{(k)}+c,\\
x^*&=Bx^*+c,\\
e^{(k+1)}&=B(x^{(k)}-x^*)=Be^{(k)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The translation \(c\) cancels. Centered at the solution, every sweep is the same linear transformation. Applying it \(k\) times yields
\[
\boxed{e^{(k)}=B^ke^{(0)}}.
\]
Since the starting guess is arbitrary, \(e^{(0)}\) ranges over the entire space. Convergence for every start therefore requires all directions to decay. For the running example, \(B_J\) swaps the coordinates and halves them, so every Euclidean error norm halves at every sweep. Meanwhile \(B_{GS}(u,v)^T=v(1/2,1/4)^T\). One sweep sends every error onto the line spanned by \((2,1)^T\), where every subsequent sweep multiplies it by \(1/4\). This advantage is specific to the system and splitting.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.4 When do all matrix powers decay?
text:
9.4 When do all matrix powers decay?
Convergence theorem. For any fixed finite square matrix \(B\) over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\) and fixed vector \(c\), the following are equivalent in exact arithmetic:

The map \(x\mapsto Bx+c\) has a unique fixed point, and the iterates approach it for every initial vector.
\(B^k\to0\) as \(k\to\infty\).
\(\rho(B)=\max_{\lambda\in\sigma(B)}|\lambda|<1\), taking eigenvalues over \(\mathbb C\).

Proof. Under the first condition, choose initial errors equal to the coordinate vectors in turn. The error formula shows that every column of \(B^k\) tends to zero. In finite dimensions this implies convergence to zero in any matrix norm. Conversely, if \(B^k\to0\), the eigenvector identity \(B^kv=\lambda^k v\) forces \(|\lambda|<1\) for every eigenvalue. For real matrices the column argument also gives decay on complex vectors by linearity.
To finish, assume \(\rho(B)<1\). For diagonalizable \(B=V\Lambda V^{-1}\), cancellation of adjacent factors yields \(B^k=V\Lambda^kV^{-1}\). Each diagonal entry \(\lambda_i^k\) vanishes. For a defective matrix, take its complex Jordan form. A block \(J=\lambda I+H\) of size \(s\) has \(H^s=0\). For \(k\ge s\) its binomial expansion is
\[
J^k=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}H^j.
\]
For \(0<|\lambda|<1\), exponential decay dominates every fixed polynomial factor in \(k\). A block with \(\lambda=0\) vanishes after \(s\) powers. Thus all blocks tend to zero, and conjugating back gives \(B^k\to0\). Finally \(1\) is absent from the spectrum, so \(x^*=(I-B)^{-1}c\) exists uniquely and \(x^{(k)}-x^*=B^ke^{(0)}\to0\). This completes the proof.
How fast? For diagonalizable \(B\), \(\|B^k\|_2\le\kappa_2(V)\rho(B)^k\). For normal \(B\), a unitary eigenbasis gives \(\|B^k\|_2=\rho(B)^k\). In general the asymptotic worst-case exponential factor is \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\|B^k\|^{1/k}=\rho(B)\), by the same block argument and the eigenvector lower bound. An initial error can miss a slowly decaying eigendirection. Consecutive error ratios can also vary.
A sufficient norm test. In any chosen induced norm, \(q=\|B\|<1\) gives \(\|e^{(k)}\|\le q^k\|e^{(0)}\|\) by submultiplicativity. This test can be inconclusive. For example,
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&4\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
\]
has \(\|B\|_2=4\) and sends \((0,1)^T\) to \((4,0)^T\) in the first step. Yet \(B^2=0\) and \(\rho(B)=0\). This nonnormal example exhibits transient amplification before complete decay. The decisive condition concerns the powers of the iteration matrix. The eigenvalues of the original \(A\) do not in general give those of \(B\).

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.5 Two guarantees that avoid computing eigenvalues
text:
9.5 Two guarantees that avoid computing eigenvalues
Strict row diagonal dominance. If \(|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|\) for every row, Jacobi and forward Gauss–Seidel both converge from every start. For Jacobi the maximum absolute row sum of \(B_J\) is directly less than one. For Gauss–Seidel let \(\ell_i=\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|\) and \(u_i=\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|\). At a coordinate \(i\) attaining the maximum new error, the homogeneous row update gives
\[
(|a_{ii}|-\ell_i)\|e^{(k+1)}\|_\infty\le u_i\|e^{(k)}\|_\infty.
\]
The largest of the ratios \(u_i/(|a_{ii}|-\ell_i)\) is strictly below one. Thus the entire sweep contracts. These tests are sufficient. The spectral-radius criterion is exact.
Hermitian positive definiteness. If \(A=A^*\) and \(z^*Az>0\) for all \(z\ne0\), Gauss–Seidel converges. To see why, measure error in the energy norm \(\|e\|_A^2=e^*Ae\). A row update changes one coordinate by \(t\). Along coordinate vector \(s_i\), the energy becomes
\[
\|e+t s_i\|_A^2=\|e\|_A^2+2\operatorname{Re}(\overline{t}(Ae)_i)+a_{ii}|t|^2.
\]
Its unique minimizer is \(t=-(Ae)_i/a_{ii}\), exactly the current row correction. Every nonzero correction strictly decreases energy. If a full sweep makes no correction, every row of \(Ae\) was zero and \(e=0\). By continuity on the compact energy unit sphere, the maximum energy-norm ratio for a full sweep is strictly less than one. Jacobi evaluates all corrections at the old point, so this successive minimization argument does not apply.
Divergence in a uniquely solvable SPD system. Let \(w=(1,1,1)^T\), \(A=(I+3ww^T)/4\), and \(b=Aw\). The diagonal is one and every off-diagonal entry is \(3/4\). Along \(w\), \(A\) has eigenvalue \(5/2\); on \(w^\perp\) it has eigenvalue \(1/4\). Hence \(A\) is SPD and \(x^*=w\) is unique. Here \(B_J=I-A\) has eigenvalue \(-3/2\) along \(w\) and \(3/4\) on \(w^\perp\). From zero the initial error is \(-w\), so it alternates sign and grows by \(3/2\) per sweep. An initial error orthogonal to \(w\) decays by \(3/4\) instead. This system shows both the limit of the SPD guarantee for Jacobi and the importance of the words every initial guess.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.6 What can we measure without the solution?
text:
9.6 What can we measure without the solution?
Since \(b=Ax^*\), our sign convention gives
\[
r^{(k)}=b-Ax^{(k)}=-Ae^{(k)},\qquad e^{(k)}=-A^{-1}r^{(k)}.
\]
The residual measures how much the right-hand side must change to make the current approximation exact (the required change is \(-r^{(k)}\)). The error measures distance to the solution. In any compatible vector norm and its induced matrix norm, for \(b\ne0\),
\[
\frac{\|e^{(k)}\|}{\|x^*\|}\le
\underbrace{\|A^{-1}\|\|A\|}_{\kappa(A)}
\frac{\|r^{(k)}\|}{\|b\|}.
\]
Here we used \(\|b\|\le\|A\|\|x^*\|\). An ill-conditioned matrix can map a large error to a small residual. Assess the requested accuracy in light of this factor.







Diagnostic
How to use it




Absolute and relative residual
Recompute \(b-Ax^{(k)}\). Stop when its norm is at most \(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}+\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\|b\|\). The absolute term also handles \(b=0\).


Size of the last change
A small correction can signal slow progress or rounding. A verified contraction factor can turn it into an error bound.


Iteration budget and finite values
Report exhaustion, stagnation, or nonfinite values separately from meeting the residual tolerance.



For a contraction with known \(q=\|B\|<1\), successive changes shrink at least geometrically since \(x^{(k+1)}-x^{(k)}=B(x^{(k)}-x^{(k-1)})\). Sum the tail from the current iterate to the limit to obtain, for \(k\ge1\),
\[
\|x^*-x^{(k)}\|
\le\frac{q}{1-q}\|x^{(k)}-x^{(k-1)}\|.
\]
A factor \(q\) close to one makes this certificate weak. In floating point, a computed sweep can be written as \(\widehat e^{(k+1)}=B\widehat e^{(k)}+\delta^{(k)}\), with \(\delta^{(k)}\) the local arithmetic error. Earlier perturbations propagate through powers of \(B\) and each sweep introduces a new one. Even for \(q<1\), uniformly bounded perturbations of size \(\epsilon\) contribute up to \(\epsilon/(1-q)\) to the error. Recomputing the residual also incurs rounding. Exact-arithmetic convergence establishes neither attainable accuracy nor backward stability of an implementation.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.7 Computational experiment — predict the slopes
text:
9.7 Computational experiment — predict the slopes
For the hand example, the characteristic polynomials are \(t^2-1/4\) for Jacobi and \(t(t-1/4)\) for Gauss–Seidel. Predict the two error slopes before reading the figure. The code computes the spectral radii independently and implements each sweep directly. Dense arrays keep the small experiment inspectable. The exact solution is used only for measurement.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def jacobi(A, b, x):
    return x + (b - A @ x) / np.diag(A)

def gauss_seidel(A, b, x):
    y = x.copy()
    for i in range(len(b)):
        lower = A[i, :i] @ y[:i]
        upper = A[i, i+1:] @ x[i+1:]
        y[i] = (b[i] - lower - upper) / A[i, i]
    return y

def history(A, b, exact, x0, sweep, max_steps, rtol=1e-11):
    if np.any(np.diag(A) == 0):
        raise ValueError("A diagonal entry is zero")
    x = np.array(x0, dtype=float)
    rows = []
    threshold = 1e-14 + rtol * np.linalg.norm(b)
    for k in range(max_steps + 1):
        residual = np.linalg.norm(b - A @ x)
        error = np.linalg.norm(x - exact)
        if not np.isfinite([residual, error]).all():
            raise FloatingPointError("Nonfinite history entry")
        rows.append((error, residual))
        if residual <= threshold:
            return np.array(rows), "residual tolerance"
        if k < max_steps:
            y = sweep(A, b, x)
            if np.array_equal(y, x):
                return np.array(rows), "stagnation"
            x = y
    return np.array(rows), "iteration limit"


A = np.array([[2., -1.], [-1., 2.]])
b = np.array([1., 0.])
exact = np.array([2/3, 1/3])
start = np.zeros(2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharey=True, layout="constrained")
methods = [
    ("Jacobi", jacobi, np.diag(np.diag(A)), "-", "C0"),
    ("Gauss–Seidel", gauss_seidel, np.tril(A), "--", "C1"),
]
for name, sweep, M, style, color in methods:
    B = np.linalg.solve(M, M - A)
    rho = max(abs(np.linalg.eigvals(B)))
    values, status = history(A, b, exact, start, sweep, 80)
    assert status == "residual tolerance"
    # Check the sweep on a vector with both coordinates nonzero.
    z = np.array([0.75, -0.25])
    assert np.allclose(sweep(A, b, z), B @ z + np.linalg.solve(M, b))
    label = f"{name} ({rho:.2f})"
    for ax, column in zip(axes, values.T):
        ax.semilogy(column, style, color=color, label=label)

for ax, title in zip(axes, ["Error norm", "Residual norm"]):
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="Sweep k")
    ax.grid(True, which="major", alpha=0.25)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Euclidean norm")
axes[1].legend(title="Method (spectral radius)", fontsize=8)
plt.show()







Figure 9.1: Euclidean error and residual for the two sweeps from zero. Each curve ends at the first accepted residual.





The Jacobi curve loses a factor of two per sweep. The Gauss–Seidel curve loses a factor of four per sweep from the first updated vector onward. In this particular run even the first Gauss–Seidel error lies on the same line as the initial error. For Jacobi, the residual alternates between coordinate axes; for Gauss–Seidel its second coordinate is zero after each sweep. Both residual histories therefore have a direct interpretation in terms of the equations still violated. The straight lines here arise from the special matrices and starting vector. The nilpotent example above explains why a single sweep of another convergent method can increase the error.
Optional divergence check. Run eight sweeps on the SPD counterexample. The reported ratio is a measurement of the growing mode selected by the initial error.

w = np.ones(3)
C = (np.eye(3) + 3 * np.outer(w, w)) / 4
values, status = history(C, C @ w, w, np.zeros(3), jacobi, 8)
ratios = values[1:, 0] / values[:-1, 0]
assert np.allclose(ratios, 1.5)
print(f"{status} after 8 sweeps; error factor {ratios[-1]:.2f}")

iteration limit after 8 sweeps; error factor 1.50

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.8 From sparse solves to spectral filtering
text:
9.8 From sparse solves to spectral filtering
For large systems, the splitting gives two reusable operations: apply \(A\) and solve approximately for a correction. A few sweeps can also serve as part of a preconditioner. In multigrid, suitable relaxation methods such as weighted Jacobi can damp oscillatory error on a grid, leaving smoother components for a coarser grid. Total cost depends on both the work per sweep and the number of sweeps.
Krylov methods build approximations from a growing subspace. Starting with \(r_0=b-Ax^{(0)}\), a typical unpreconditioned approximation lies in \(x^{(0)}+\mathcal K_m(A,r_0)\), where
\[
\mathcal K_m(A,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Ar_0,\ldots,A^{m-1}r_0\}.
\]
Here the choice of approximation can adapt as the space grows. In our stationary methods the error polynomial in \(B\) is already prescribed: \(p_k(t)=t^k\).
Session 9 reuses the calculation \(B^kv=\lambda^kv\) in a different role. Power iteration repeatedly applies an operator and normalizes, so directions with larger eigenvalue magnitudes can grow relative to other directions. Subspace iteration carries several directions together. In Session 10 a filter \(p_m(A)\) multiplies an eigencomponent by \(p_m(\lambda)\). Its purpose is to separate wanted and unwanted spectral components. A convergent stationary solver must drive every initial error component to zero. This difference in objectives determines which spectral comparison matters.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.9 Central Synthesis — Iterative Solvers as Spectral Error Dynamics
text:
9.9 Central Synthesis — Iterative Solvers as Spectral Error Dynamics








Question
Calculation
What it establishes




Where is the fixed point?
\(A=M-N\) gives \(Mx=Nx+b\).
The fixed points solve the original system. Invertibility of \(A\) gives uniqueness.


What does one sweep do?
Solve \(Md=r^{(k)}\), then add \(d\).
The choice of easy solve determines \(B=I-M^{-1}A\).


What happens after many sweeps?
Subtract the fixed-point identity. Then \(e^{(k+1)}=Be^{(k)}\) and \(e^{(k)}=B^ke^{(0)}\).
Every start succeeds exactly when \(B^k\to0\), equivalently \(\rho(B)<1\).


How accurate is the result in hand?
Recompute \(r=b-A\widehat x\) and relate it to \(e=-A^{-1}r\).
Conditioning governs the forward-error certificate. Rounding and the stopping rule affect the delivered answer.



For the SPD counterexample, both splittings target exactly the same unique point, yet Jacobi can move away from it at every step. For the running example both converge, yet the two methods require different numbers of sweeps to satisfy the same tolerance. Solvability, convergence of a chosen algorithm, and accuracy of a computed answer each require their own argument.
Course reading. Kanschat and Scheichl, Numerical Linear Algebra, §4.2 and Appendix B.1, connect stationary iterations with the spectral radius. Bastian, num0, §§13–14, develops splittings, convergence conditions, and stopping. Scheichl and Zech, Num0 notes, §6.3, gives the relaxation viewpoint. The notation here reserves \(M\) for the easy solve and \(B\) for error propagation.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.10 Exercises
text:
9.10 Exercises

Reconstruct a splitting (3 min). For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\), \(b=(2,3)^T\), take \(M=4I\). Find \(N,B,c\) and the fixed point. Which coordinate of a generic initial error decays more slowly?
Recover the theorem (5 min). Starting with an affine iteration and a fixed point, prove the power formula by induction. Explain why testing every initial error tests the columns of \(B^k\), why a unit-modulus eigenvalue prevents convergence from every start, and why defective blocks with eigenvalues inside the unit circle still decay.
Read a stopping report (4 min). Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,10^{-6})\), \(b=(1,0)^T\) and \(\widehat x=(1,1)^T\). Compute relative residual, relative error and the conditioning bound in the Euclidean norm. Separately, for \(F(x)=0.999x+0.001\) starting at zero, what does a first change of \(0.001\) certify about the error at the new iterate?
Which initial errors succeed? (5 min) Take \(B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\0&1/2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(c=0\). Find the unique fixed point and all starts that converge to it. Contrast applying \(B^k\) to a generic start here with applying powers to select a dominant eigendirection.
Mastery problem — predict and audit two sweeps (11 min). Take \(A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\), \(b=(6,1)^T\), and start at zero. Derive the two component rules, both iteration matrices and their constant vectors. Compute their spectra, predict convergence, and perform two sweeps of each. Compute the second residual for each. Use the powers of the iteration matrices to explain which features of the observed behavior should persist.

title: 9  Session 8 — Basic Iterative Methods
section: 9.11 Worked solutions
text:
9.11 Worked solutions
1. Reconstruct a splitting. From \(N=M-A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) we obtain \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1/2,1/4)\) and \(c=(1/2,3/4)^T\). Solving \((I-B)x=c\) gives \((1,1)^T\), which also satisfies \(Ax=b\). After \(k\) sweeps the first signed error is \(2^{-k}e_1^{(0)}\) and the second is \(4^{-k}e_2^{(0)}\). The first coordinate dominates eventually if its initial error is nonzero.
2. Recover the theorem. Subtraction gives \(e^{(k+1)}=Be^{(k)}\). At \(k=0\), \(B^0e^{(0)}=e^{(0)}\). If the formula holds at \(k\), multiplication by \(B\) establishes it at \(k+1\). Taking the initial errors to be coordinate vectors tests every column; decay of all columns implies \(B^k\to0\) in finite dimensions. For a unit-modulus eigenvalue, \(\|B^kv\|=|\lambda|^k\|v\|=\|v\|\) on a complex eigenvector. Decay on every real start would imply decay on its real and imaginary parts and hence on \(v\) as well. Inside the unit disk a Jordan block contributes terms of the form \(\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}\) for finitely many \(j\). These vanish by exponential decay for \(\lambda\ne0\) and nilpotence for \(\lambda=0\). Thus every block decays. Also \(1\) is excluded, so \((I-B)x=c\) has one solution.
3. Read a stopping report. Here \(x^*=(1,0)^T\), \(e=(0,1)^T\), and \(r=(0,-10^{-6})^T\). The relative residual is \(10^{-6}\) and the relative error is \(1\). The condition number is \(10^6\), so its upper bound on the relative error is \(1\), attained in this direction. In the scalar problem the fixed point is \(1\) and \(x^{(1)}=0.001\). The a posteriori estimate gives \(0.999/(1-0.999)\) times \(0.001\), hence \(0.999\). This equals the actual error magnitude. The small change certifies little progress toward a substantially accurate solution.
4. Which initial errors succeed? The diagonal entries are the eigenvalues \(-2\) and \(1/2\). Since \(1\) is absent, the unique fixed point is zero. Eigenvectors are \((1,0)^T\) for \(-2\) and \((2,5)^T\) for \(1/2\). Writing the start as \(\alpha(1,0)^T+\beta(2,5)^T\), its two coefficients become \((-2)^k\alpha\) and \(2^{-k}\beta\). Precisely the line \(\alpha=0\) converges to zero. For generic starts the growth spoils the solve, while normalization would make the direction, up to sign, approach the dominant eigenline. The same powers explain both phenomena.
5. Mastery problem. Write \((u,v)\) for the old coordinates. In both methods \(u'=(6-2v)/4\). Jacobi uses \(v'=(1+u)/2\); Gauss–Seidel uses \(v'=(1+u')/2=5/4-v/4\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_J&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1/2\\1/2&0\end{pmatrix}, & c_J&=(3/2,1/2)^T,\\
B_{GS}&=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1/2\\0&-1/4\end{pmatrix}, & c_{GS}&=(3/2,5/4)^T.
\end{aligned}
\]
Jacobi has characteristic polynomial \(t^2+1/4\) and eigenvalues \(\pm i/2\). The triangular Gauss–Seidel matrix has eigenvalues \(0,-1/4\). Both radii are below one. Substituting successively and multiplying by \(A\) for the last column gives



Method
\(x^{(1)}\)
\(x^{(2)}\)
\(b-Ax^{(2)}\)




Jacobi
\((3/2,1/2)^T\)
\((5/4,5/4)^T\)
\((-3/2,-1/4)^T\)


Gauss–Seidel
\((3/2,5/4)^T\)
\((7/8,15/16)^T\)
\((5/8,0)^T\)



The exact solution is \((1,1)^T\). Jacobi rotates the error through a quarter turn and halves its Euclidean length; \(B_J^2=-I/4\). After two sweeps its signed error is \((1/4,1/4)^T\). For Gauss–Seidel the range of \(B_{GS}\) is the line spanned by \((2,1)^T\), on which \(B_{GS}\) multiplies by \(-1/4\). Its first error \((1/2,1/4)^T\) becomes \((-1/8,-1/16)^T\). Its second-row residual vanishes at the end of every sweep by construction.
