14.12 Session 8 — Consolidation, exercises, and proof reconstruction
The goal of this final session is to consolidate the theory.
At this stage, you should be able to recognize a common structural pattern:
\[
\boxed{ \begin{gathered}
  \text{A transformation acts on vectors}\\
  T:V\to W\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{It induces a transformation on measurements}\\
  T^\vee:W^*\to V^*\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Its kernel and image determine}\\
  \text{which measurements vanish or factor through it}.
\end{gathered} }
\]
The following exercises test definitions, proofs, computations, structural understanding, and applications.
Try solving them before consulting the worked solutions.

Exercise 1 — Construct a dual basis
Let
\[
v_1=(1,1),\qquad v_2=(1,-1)
\]
be a basis of \(\mathbb R^2\).
Find the dual basis \((\varepsilon^1,\varepsilon^2)\).
Verify its defining properties.
Then express the functional
\[
f(x,y)=3x+y
\]
as a linear combination of the dual basis functionals.


Exercise 2 — Change of coordinates for covectors
Let \(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be an invertible basis matrix.
Prove that the coordinate column of a vector transforms by \(B^{-1}\), while the coefficient column of a functional transforms by \(B^T\), when moving from standard to \(B\)-basis coordinates.
Explain why the scalar evaluation of the functional must remain unchanged.


Exercise 3 — Calculate a dual map
Let
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&2&0\\
  0&1&1
\end{pmatrix} :\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2.
\]
Define the output functional
\[
g(y_1,y_2)=3y_1-2y_2.
\]
Compute \(A^\vee(g)\) directly by composition.
Then verify the answer using \(A^T\).


Exercise 4 — Find an annihilator
Let
\[
S= \operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\} \subseteq\mathbb R^3.
\]
Find a basis of \(S^0\).
Verify the dimension formula
\[
\dim S^0=\dim V-\dim S.
\]


Exercise 5 — Verify the fundamental duality identities
For the matrix \(A\) from Exercise 3, calculate
\[
\ker A,\qquad \operatorname{im}A,
\]
and the kernel and image of its dual map.
Verify explicitly that
\[
\operatorname{im}A^\vee=(\ker A)^0
\]
and
\[
\ker A^\vee=(\operatorname{im}A)^0.
\]


Exercise 6 — Dual of a quotient
Let
\[
S=\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,1)\} \subseteq\mathbb R^3.
\]
Find a basis of \(S^0\).
Construct the corresponding functionals on the quotient \(\mathbb R^3/S\).
Explain why they are well-defined.


Exercise 7 — Dual exact sequences
Consider the short exact sequence
\[
0\to S\xrightarrow{i}V\xrightarrow{q}V/S\to0.
\]
Prove that the dual sequence
\[
0\to(V/S)^* \xrightarrow{q^\vee}V^* \xrightarrow{i^\vee}S^* \to0
\]
is exact when \(V\) is finite-dimensional.
Identify the kernel and image of each nontrivial map.


Exercise 8 — The double-dual map
Define
\[
J_V(v)(f)=f(v).
\]
Prove that \(J_V:V\to V^{**}\) is a linear isomorphism for finite-dimensional \(V\).
Then prove that for every linear map \(T:V\to W\),
\[
J_W\circ T=T^{\vee\vee}\circ J_V.
\]
Explain why this is called a natural identification.


Exercise 9 — Graph duality
Let
\[
D= \begin{pmatrix}
  -1&1&0\\
  0&-1&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Consider the edge functional
\[
g(d_1,d_2)=2d_1-d_2.
\]
Calculate \(D^\vee(g)\).
Show that it annihilates the constant-vector subspace.
Then explain the relationship to the theorem
\[
\operatorname{im}D^\vee=(\ker D)^0.
\]


Exercise 10 — Left eigenvectors and spectral projections
Let
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its right eigenvectors can be chosen as
\[
v_1=(1,0),\qquad v_2=(1,1).
\]
Construct their dual basis.
Prove that the corresponding functionals are eigenfunctionals of \(A^\vee\).
Construct the two spectral projectors \(P_1,P_2\), verify
\[
P_1+P_2=I,
\]
and show that
\[
A=2P_1+3P_2.
\]
Finally, determine \(p(A)\) for
\[
p(t)=t-2
\]
using the spectral projectors rather than ordinary matrix arithmetic.

14.13 Worked solutions

Solution 1 — Dual basis
The basis matrix is
\[
B= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&1\\
  1&-1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its inverse is
\[
B^{-1} = \frac12 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&1\\
  1&-1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The rows of \(B^{-1}\) give the dual basis:
\[
\boxed{ \varepsilon^1(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{2}, \qquad \varepsilon^2(x,y)=\frac{x-y}{2}. }
\]
Evaluating at the basis vectors gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
  &v_1&v_2\\
  \hline \varepsilon^1&1&0\\
  \varepsilon^2&0&1
\end{array}
\]
as required.
For
\[
f(x,y)=3x+y,
\]
the dual basis coefficients are
\[
f(v_1)=4,\qquad f(v_2)=2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{f=4\varepsilon^1+2\varepsilon^2.}
\]
Indeed,
\[
4\frac{x+y}{2}+2\frac{x-y}{2}=3x+y.
\]


Solution 2 — Coordinate transformations
Let \(x_{\mathrm{std}}\) denote the standard coordinate column and \(x_B\) its coordinates in the basis matrix \(B\).
Then
\[
x_{\mathrm{std}}=Bx_B,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{x_B=B^{-1}x_{\mathrm{std}}.}
\]
For a functional with standard coefficient column \(c_{\mathrm{std}}\),
\[
f(x)=c_{\mathrm{std}}^Tx_{\mathrm{std}}.
\]
Substituting,
\[
f(x)=c_{\mathrm{std}}^TBx_B =(B^Tc_{\mathrm{std}})^Tx_B.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{c_B=B^Tc_{\mathrm{std}}.}
\]
The two transformation rules ensure that the scalar \(f(x)\) is independent of the coordinate system.


Solution 3 — Dual map
We have
\[
Ax= \begin{pmatrix}
  x_1+2x_2\\
  x_2+x_3
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  A^\vee(g)(x) &=g(Ax)\\
  &=3(x_1+2x_2)-2(x_2+x_3)\\
  &=3x_1+4x_2-2x_3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{ A^\vee(g)(x_1,x_2,x_3) =3x_1+4x_2-2x_3. }
\]
Using the coefficient column \(c=(3,-2)^T\),
\[
A^Tc= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  2&1\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  -2
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
  3\\
  4\\
  -2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The two computations agree.


Solution 4 — Annihilator
Since the two generators of \(S\) are independent,
\[
\dim S=2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\dim S^0=3-2=1.
\]
Write
\[
f(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz.
\]
The conditions for \(f\in S^0\) are
\[
a+b=0,\qquad b+c=0.
\]
Thus
\[
a=c=-b.
\]
Choosing \(a=1\), we obtain
\[
\boxed{ S^0=\operatorname{span}\{f\}, \qquad f(x,y,z)=x-y+z. }
\]
The annihilator has dimension one, as predicted.


Solution 5 — Fundamental duality identities
For
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&2&0\\
  0&1&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
the kernel equations are
\[
x_1+2x_2=0,\qquad x_2+x_3=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\ker A=\operatorname{span}\{(-2,1,-1)\}.}
\]
The two rows of \(A\) are independent, so \(A\) has rank two.
Its image equals \(\mathbb R^2\):
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{im}A=\mathbb R^2.}
\]
Since \(A^\vee\) is represented by \(A^T\), its image is represented by
\[
\boxed{ \operatorname{im}A^\vee = \operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(0,1,1)\} }
\]
in standard coefficient coordinates.
Both coefficient vectors annihilate the kernel vector \((-2,1,-1)\):
\[
(1,2,0)\cdot(-2,1,-1)=0,
\]
\[
(0,1,1)\cdot(-2,1,-1)=0.
\]
The annihilator of a one-dimensional subspace of \(\mathbb R^3\) has dimension two.
Thus
\[
\operatorname{im}A^\vee=(\ker A)^0.
\]
Finally, since \(A^T:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^3\) is injective,
\[
\ker A^\vee=\{0\}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{im}A=\mathbb R^2\), its annihilator is also zero:
\[
(\operatorname{im}A)^0=\{0\}.
\]
Hence the second identity holds.


Solution 6 — Quotient duality
A functional on \(\mathbb R^3\) has the form
\[
f(x,y,z)=ax+by+cz.
\]
To annihilate \(S\), we require
\[
a+b+c=0.
\]
A convenient basis is
\[
f_1(x,y,z)=x-y,
\]
\[
f_2(x,y,z)=y-z.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{S^0=\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2\}.}
\]
They induce functionals on the quotient:
\[
\overline f_1((x,y,z)+S)=x-y,
\]
\[
\overline f_2((x,y,z)+S)=y-z.
\]
Adding \(t(1,1,1)\) to a representative leaves both expressions unchanged.
Therefore they are well-defined.
They are independent and span the two-dimensional dual space \((\mathbb R^3/S)^*\).


Solution 7 — Dual exact sequence
The sequence is
\[
0\to(V/S)^* \xrightarrow{q^\vee}V^* \xrightarrow{i^\vee}S^* \to0.
\]
Since \(q\) is surjective, \(q^\vee\) is injective:
\[
\ker q^\vee=\{0\}.
\]
Its image is
\[
\operatorname{im}q^\vee=S^0.
\]
The map \(i^\vee\) restricts a functional on \(V\) to \(S\).
Therefore,
\[
\ker i^\vee=S^0.
\]
Hence
\[
\operatorname{im}q^\vee=\ker i^\vee.
\]
Finally, \(i^\vee\) is surjective because every linear functional on \(S\) extends to a linear functional on \(V\).
Thus the sequence is exact.


Solution 8 — Double dual
Define
\[
J_V(v)(f)=f(v).
\]
The map is linear because
\[
J_V(\alpha v+\beta w)(f) =\alpha f(v)+\beta f(w).
\]
If \(J_V(v)=0\), then every functional vanishes on \(v\).
By nondegeneracy of evaluation, \(v=0\). Thus \(J_V\) is injective.
Since
\[
\dim V=\dim V^{**},
\]
it is also surjective.
Therefore \(J_V\) is an isomorphism.
For naturality, let \(T:V\to W\). For every \(g\in W^*\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  (T^{\vee\vee}(J_V(v)))(g) &=J_V(v)(T^\vee g)\\
  &=(T^\vee g)(v)\\
  &=g(Tv)\\
  &=J_W(Tv)(g).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{ T^{\vee\vee}\circ J_V=J_W\circ T. }
\]
The identification is natural because it commutes with every linear map without depending on a choice of basis or inner product.


Solution 9 — Graph duality
The coefficient column of the edge functional is
\[
c=\begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
D^Tc = \begin{pmatrix}
  -1&0\\
  1&-1\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
  -2\\
  3\\
  -1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{ D^\vee(g)(p_1,p_2,p_3) =-2p_1+3p_2-p_3. }
\]
On a constant vector \(p=t(1,1,1)\),
\[
D^\vee(g)(p)=(-2+3-1)t=0.
\]
Therefore the pulled-back functional annihilates \(\ker D\).
For any edge functional \(g\), the equality \(g(Dp)=g(0)=0\) for \(p\in\ker D\) gives
\[
\operatorname{im}D^\vee\subseteq(\ker D)^0.
\]
The two rows of \(D\) are independent, so \(\operatorname{im}D^\vee\) has dimension two. The annihilator of the one-dimensional space \(\ker D\) also has dimension two. Thus the inclusion is an equality.


Solution 10 — Spectral projectors
The right eigenvectors are
\[
v_1=(1,0),\qquad v_2=(1,1).
\]
Their dual basis is
\[
\ell^1(x,y)=x-y, \qquad \ell^2(x,y)=y.
\]
These are left eigenfunctionals:
\[
A^\vee\ell^1=2\ell^1, \qquad A^\vee\ell^2=3\ell^2.
\]
The spectral projectors are
\[
P_1(x,y)=\ell^1(x,y)v_1=(x-y,0),
\]
and
\[
P_2(x,y)=\ell^2(x,y)v_2=(y,y).
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ P_1= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&-1\\
  0&0
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad P_2= \begin{pmatrix}
  0&1\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
Adding,
\[
P_1+P_2=I.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
2P_1+3P_2 = \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&3
\end{pmatrix} =A.
\]
For \(p(t)=t-2\),
\[
p(2)=0,\qquad p(3)=1.
\]
Thus
\[
p(A)=p(2)P_1+p(3)P_2=P_2.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ p(A)= \begin{pmatrix}
  0&1\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
Notice that \(P_1,P_2\) are projections but not orthogonal projections under the standard Euclidean inner product.
This is a concrete example of spectral decomposition using a right eigenbasis and its dual left eigenbasis.

14.15 Final conceptual synthesis
We can now summarize Module B through one central idea:
Duality studies a mathematical object through the linear measurements that can be performed on it.
The original space \(V\) contains vectors.
The dual space \(V^*\) contains scalar-valued linear observations of those vectors.
A transformation \(T:V\to W\) maps vectors forward, while its dual \(T^\vee:W^*\to V^*\) pulls observations backward.
Annihilators describe measurements that vanish on prescribed subspaces, and quotient duality describes measurements that remain meaningful after certain vector differences have been identified.
Linear map
\[
T:V\to W
\]
Dual map
\[
T^\vee:W^*\to V^*
\]
Kernel–image duality
\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{im}T^\vee&=(\ker T)^0,\\
  \ker T^\vee&=(\operatorname{im}T)^0
\end{aligned} }
\]
Quotients and exact sequences
\[
(V/S)^*\cong S^0
\]

Module B mastery checklist
Before beginning Module C, aim to complete the following without referring to the study material.

Explain duality in at least two applications: graph operators, variational problems, or solvability conditions.

section: 14.16 Transition to Module C — Inner-product geometry
text:
14.16 Transition to Module C — Inner-product geometry
Module B has developed duality without requiring inner products.
Module C will add inner-product structure and investigate what new possibilities it creates.
The central question will be:
If covectors are linear measurements, how can an inner product represent each covector by a uniquely determined vector?
The Riesz representation theorem answers this question.
For a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(V\), every \(f\in V^*\) has a unique representing vector \(a_f\in V\) such that
\[
\boxed{ f(v)=\langle v,a_f\rangle \qquad\forall v\in V. }
\]
This creates an isomorphism between the space of vectors and the space of linear measurements.
It transforms the algebraic relationships of Module B into geometric ones.
For example,
\[
\operatorname{im}T^\vee=(\ker T)^0
\]
becomes, under the Riesz identifications,
\[
\boxed{ \operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp, }
\]
where \(T^*\) is now the inner-product adjoint.
Similarly, annihilators correspond to orthogonal complements, and the dual map corresponds to the adjoint.
That is the bridge to orthogonal projections, self-adjoint matrices, positive definiteness, least squares, and spectral theory.
One particularly important connection deserves emphasis:
In Module B, we constructed spectral coefficients using dual eigenfunctionals,
\[
x=\sum_i\ell^i(x)v_i.
\]
For a Hermitian matrix with an orthonormal eigenbasis, Riesz representation allows those functionals to be written as inner products:
\[
\ell^i(x)=v_i^Hx.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ x=\sum_i(v_i^Hx)v_i. }
\]
This is the familiar orthonormal spectral expansion.
It is also the foundation for Rayleigh–Ritz approximation, orthogonal spectral projections, and the Hermitian eigenvalue algorithms relevant to your HASC seminar.
The central achievement of Module B is understanding that algebraic duality comes first: inner-product geometry provides a particularly powerful way to represent it, but does not create it.

title: 15  Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
text:
15.1 Introduction — From algebraic structure to geometry
Riesz Representation, Adjoint Operators, Orthogonal Projections, Self-Adjointness, Positive Definiteness, and Least Squares
Advanced undergraduate · 8 study sessions · Approximately 16–22 hours
In Module A, we studied linear transformations through their kernels, images, quotients, and direct-sum decompositions.
In Module B, we introduced the dual space \(V^*\), whose elements are linear measurements of vectors. We learned that a map
\[
T:V\longrightarrow W
\]
induces a dual map
\[
T^\vee:W^*\longrightarrow V^*, \qquad T^\vee(f)=f\circ T.
\]
We also established the fundamental algebraic duality identities
\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{im}T^\vee&=(\ker T)^0,\\
  \ker T^\vee&=(\operatorname{im}T)^0.
\end{aligned} }
\]
These results require only vector-space structure.
Module C asks what additional mathematical structure becomes available when we equip vector spaces with inner products.
The answer is substantial. Inner products allow us to introduce lengths, angles, orthogonality, distances, and geometric projections.
More surprisingly, they allow us to represent linear functionals by vectors. This is the content of the Riesz representation theorem.
That identification turns algebraic dual maps into adjoint operators and annihilators into orthogonal complements.
From there we obtain self-adjoint matrices, positive definiteness, least-squares approximation, and the geometry underlying numerical eigenvalue methods.
The central conceptual progression is:
Algebraic duality
\(V^*,\qquad T^\vee,\qquad S^0\) — Module B
Introduce an inner product and Riesz representation
Inner-product geometry
\(V\cong V^*,\qquad T^*,\qquad S^\perp\) — Module C
Develop self-adjointness and orthogonal approximation
Numerical and variational methods
Least squares · SVD · Galerkin methods · Rayleigh–Ritz · Eigenvalue algorithms

15.3 Study roadmap

1

Exercises, worked solutions, a MATLAB laboratory, and a mastery checklist follow.

Conventions
We will work primarily with finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces. This lets us concentrate on the mathematics without repeatedly introducing complex conjugation.
In the real case, inner products are symmetric and bilinear.
For complex spaces, we use the convention
\[
\langle x,y\rangle=y^Hx,
\]
which is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second. Under this convention, a complex linear functional is represented as
\[
f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle.
\]
The same adjoint identity will hold:
\[
\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,T^*y\rangle.
\]
In standard orthonormal coordinates, the adjoint matrix is the conjugate transpose \(A^H\), rather than the ordinary transpose \(A^T\).
We will return to the complex case when it adds something conceptually important.

title: 15  Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
section: 15.4 Session 1 — Inner products: introducing geometry into vector spaces
text:
15.4 Session 1 — Inner products: introducing geometry into vector spaces

Why introduce an inner product?
A vector space has addition and scalar multiplication.
Those operations are sufficient for discussing linear independence, bases, kernels, images, and quotient spaces.
But a vector-space structure alone does not tell us:

How long a vector is.
Whether two vectors are perpendicular.
How far apart two vectors are.
Which vector in a subspace best approximates a given vector.

An inner product provides this additional geometric structure.


Definition of an inner product
Let \(V\) be a real vector space.
An inner product on \(V\) is a function
\[
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb R
\]
satisfying the following properties for all \(x,y,z\in V\) and \(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb R\):
Bilinearity
\[
\langle\alpha x+\beta y,z\rangle = \alpha\langle x,z\rangle+\beta\langle y,z\rangle,
\]
with linearity in the other argument as well.
Symmetry
\[
\boxed{\langle x,y\rangle=\langle y,x\rangle.}
\]
Positive definiteness
\[
\boxed{ \langle x,x\rangle\ge0, \qquad \langle x,x\rangle=0\iff x=0. }
\]
The ordinary Euclidean inner product on \(\mathbb R^n\) is
\[
\boxed{\langle x,y\rangle=x^Ty.}
\]
But it is not the only possible inner product.
That fact will become central later.


From inner products to lengths and angles
An inner product defines a norm:
\[
\boxed{\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}.}
\]
It also defines a distance:
\[
d(x,y)=\|x-y\|.
\]
Two vectors are called orthogonal if
\[
\boxed{x\perp y\iff\langle x,y\rangle=0.}
\]
For nonzero real vectors, we can define the angle \(\theta\in[0,\pi]\) between them by
\[
\cos\theta = \frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\|x\|\|y\|}.
\]
Why is the right-hand side always between \(-1\) and \(1\)?
Because of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.


The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
Theorem. For all \(x,y\) in an inner-product space,
\[
\boxed{ |\langle x,y\rangle| \le\|x\|\|y\|. }
\]

Proof
If \(y=0\), the statement is immediate.
Suppose \(y\ne0\).
For any \(t\in\mathbb R\),
\[
0\le\|x-ty\|^2.
\]
Expanding,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \|x-ty\|^2 &=\langle x-ty,x-ty\rangle\\
  &=\|x\|^2-2t\langle x,y\rangle+t^2\|y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Choose
\[
t=\frac{\langle x,y\rangle}{\|y\|^2}.
\]
Substituting gives
\[
0\le \|x\|^2- \frac{\langle x,y\rangle^2}{\|y\|^2}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\langle x,y\rangle^2 \le\|x\|^2\|y\|^2.
\]
Taking square roots proves the result.
Equality holds precisely when \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly dependent.


Why this theorem matters
Cauchy–Schwarz establishes much of the basic geometry of inner-product spaces.
For example, it gives the triangle inequality:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \|x+y\|^2 &=\|x\|^2+2\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2\\
  &\le(\|x\|+\|y\|)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\|x+y\|\le\|x\|+\|y\|.}
\]
Thus the norm induced by an inner product really is a norm.
It also implies that, for fixed \(a\),
\[
f(x)=\langle x,a\rangle
\]
is a continuous linear functional.
This observation will be essential in the Riesz representation theorem.



Orthogonality and the Pythagorean theorem
If \(x\perp y\), then
\[
\langle x,y\rangle=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \|x+y\|^2 &=\langle x+y,x+y\rangle\\
  &=\|x\|^2+2\langle x,y\rangle+\|y\|^2\\
  &=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ x\perp y \Longrightarrow \|x+y\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2. }
\]
Unlike many elementary geometric presentations, this result does not require a diagram of a triangle.
It follows directly from the algebraic properties of the inner product.
This is how Euclidean geometry generalizes to arbitrary inner-product spaces, including spaces of functions.


Positive definite matrices define inner products
Now consider a real symmetric matrix
\[
G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}
\]
satisfying
\[
x^TGx>0 \qquad\text{for every }x\ne0.
\]
Such a matrix is called symmetric positive definite, or SPD.
Define
\[
\boxed{\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^TGy.}
\]
Let’s verify that this is an inner product.
Bilinearity follows from matrix multiplication.
Symmetry follows because
\[
x^TGy=y^TG^Tx=y^TGx.
\]
Positive definiteness follows from the assumption
\[
x^TGx>0
\]
for nonzero \(x\).
Therefore every SPD matrix defines an inner product.
Conversely, every inner product on \(\mathbb R^n\), once a basis is fixed, can be represented using an SPD matrix.
This is an important result:
An SPD matrix can encode the geometry of a vector space.


Different inner products give different geometries
Consider
\[
G= \begin{pmatrix}
  4&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
\langle x,y\rangle_G =4x_1y_1+x_2y_2.
\]
The induced norm is
\[
\|x\|_G=\sqrt{4x_1^2+x_2^2}.
\]
The vectors of unit norm satisfy
\[
4x_1^2+x_2^2=1.
\]
That is the ellipse shown in Figure 15.1.

Figure 15.1: The Euclidean unit circle (blue) and the weighted unit ellipse (orange) share their vertical intercepts. On the horizontal axis their positive intercepts are 1 and 1/2.





The same coordinate plane can carry different inner-product geometries. The weighted norm assigns a larger cost to displacement in the first coordinate direction.
The two coordinate axes remain orthogonal in this example, but this need not hold for an arbitrary SPD matrix.
For example, if
\[
G= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  1&2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
then
\[
\langle e_1,e_2\rangle_G=1.
\]
Thus the standard coordinate axes are not orthogonal in the \(G\)-inner product.
Orthogonality depends on the chosen geometry.


Gram matrices of nonorthonormal bases
There is another reason SPD matrices arise naturally.
Let \(V\) be an inner-product space with basis
\[
\mathcal B=(v_1,\ldots,v_n).
\]
Define its Gram matrix
\[
\boxed{G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle.}
\]
Suppose
\[
x=\sum_i a_iv_i,\qquad y=\sum_j b_jv_j.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle x,y\rangle &=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\\
  &=a^TGb.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the matrix of the inner product in a possibly nonorthonormal basis is its Gram matrix.
The Gram matrix is symmetric.
It is positive definite because, for \(a\ne0\),
\[
a^TGa = \left\|\sum_i a_iv_i\right\|^2>0.
\]
The strict inequality follows from linear independence of the basis.
If the basis vectors are columns of an invertible matrix \(B\) in ordinary Euclidean coordinates, then
\[
\boxed{G=B^TB.}
\]

Example
Let
\[
v_1=(1,0),\qquad v_2=(1,1).
\]
Then
\[
G= \begin{pmatrix}
  \langle v_1,v_1\rangle&\langle v_1,v_2\rangle\\
  \langle v_2,v_1\rangle&\langle v_2,v_2\rangle
\end{pmatrix} = \boxed{ \begin{pmatrix}
  1&1\\
  1&2
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
The matrix is SPD.
The two basis vectors are not orthogonal, which is reflected in the nonzero off-diagonal entries.


Connection to numerical methods
Gram matrices occur whenever we represent geometric or functional-analytic information in a finite-dimensional basis.
Examples include least-squares normal equations, finite-element mass matrices, weighted projections, and generalized eigenvalue problems.
This leads to an important distinction:
An inner product is an abstract geometric structure. A Gram matrix is its representation in a chosen basis.
The matrix changes when the basis changes, even if the underlying inner product remains the same.



Checkpoint 1
Given the basis
\[
v_1=(1,1),\qquad v_2=(1,-1),
\]
calculate its Gram matrix under the standard Euclidean inner product.
Then explain why orthonormal bases have Gram matrix \(I\), and why a basis need not be orthonormal to have an invertible Gram matrix.

title: 15  Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
section: 15.5 Session 2 — The Riesz representation theorem
text:
15.5 Session 2 — The Riesz representation theorem
We now reach the conceptual bridge between Modules B and C.
Module B taught us that a covector is a linear functional
\[
f:V\to\mathbb R.
\]
We also emphasized that a covector is not inherently an ordinary vector.
But once an inner product is available, we can associate vectors with functionals.
The Riesz representation theorem says that this correspondence is complete and unique.

Every vector defines a linear functional
Fix \(a\in V\).
Define
\[
f_a:V\to\mathbb R
\]
by
\[
\boxed{f_a(x)=\langle x,a\rangle.}
\]
Linearity of the inner product implies that \(f_a\) is a linear functional.
Therefore,
\[
f_a\in V^*.
\]
This defines a map
\[
\boxed{ R_V:V\to V^*, \qquad R_V(a)=f_a. }
\]
For real spaces, \(R_V\) is linear.
The question is whether every linear functional arises this way.


Finite-dimensional Riesz representation theorem
Theorem. Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
For every linear functional
\[
f:V\to\mathbb R,
\]
there exists a unique vector \(a_f\in V\) such that
\[
\boxed{ f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle \qquad\forall x\in V. }
\]
The vector \(a_f\) is called the Riesz representative of \(f\).
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{R_V:V\to V^*\text{ is an isomorphism}.}
\]
This is a fundamental identification between vectors and linear measurements.
It depends on the chosen inner product.


Proof using an orthonormal basis
Choose an orthonormal basis
\[
(e_1,\ldots,e_n)
\]
of \(V\).
Recall that orthonormality means
\[
\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}.
\]
Take an arbitrary functional \(f\in V^*\).
Define
\[
\boxed{ a_f=\sum_{i=1}^n f(e_i)e_i. }
\]
We claim that
\[
f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle.
\]
Write
\[
x=\sum_{i=1}^n x_ie_i.
\]
Then
\[
f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_if(e_i).
\]
On the other hand,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle x,a_f\rangle &= \left\langle \sum_i x_ie_i, \sum_j f(e_j)e_j \right\rangle\\
  &= \sum_{i,j}x_if(e_j)\langle e_i,e_j\rangle\\
  &=\sum_i x_if(e_i)\\
  &=f(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus a representing vector exists.

Uniqueness
Suppose both \(a,b\in V\) represent the same functional:
\[
\langle x,a\rangle=\langle x,b\rangle \qquad\forall x\in V.
\]
Subtracting,
\[
\langle x,a-b\rangle=0 \qquad\forall x\in V.
\]
Choose \(x=a-b\).
Then
\[
\|a-b\|^2=0.
\]
Positive definiteness implies \(a=b\).
Therefore the representing vector is unique.
This completes the proof.



Geometric interpretation
Suppose \(f\ne0\).
Its kernel is a hyperplane:
\[
\ker f=\{x:f(x)=0\}.
\]
Using Riesz representation,
\[
f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle.
\]
Therefore,
\[
x\in\ker f \iff \langle x,a_f\rangle=0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{ \ker f=\{x:x\perp a_f\}. }
\]
The Riesz representative \(a_f\) is normal to the kernel hyperplane.
The length \(\|a_f\|\) describes the scale of the measurement.
Indeed, by Cauchy–Schwarz,
\[
|f(x)| = |\langle x,a_f\rangle| \le\|x\|\|a_f\|.
\]
Equality is attained for a suitable nonzero multiple of \(a_f\).
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ \sup_{\|x\|\le1}|f(x)|=\|a_f\|. }
\]
This is often written
\[
\boxed{\|f\|_{V^*}=\|a_f\|_V.}
\]
So Riesz representation preserves the natural norms of functionals and their representing vectors.
It is not merely an algebraic isomorphism; in the real Hilbert-space setting, it is an isometric isomorphism.


Connection to dual bases
Recall Module B.
Let \(\mathcal B=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)\) be a possibly nonorthonormal basis of \(V\), with dual basis
\[
(\varepsilon^1,\ldots,\varepsilon^n).
\]
Each dual-basis functional has a Riesz representative \(a_i\in V\):
\[
\varepsilon^i(x)=\langle x,a_i\rangle.
\]
In particular,
\[
\boxed{ \langle v_j,a_i\rangle=\delta_{ij}. }
\]
Thus the Riesz representatives of the dual basis form a basis biorthogonal to the original basis.
If the original basis is orthonormal, then \(a_i=v_i\).
If it is not orthonormal, the Riesz representatives generally differ from the original basis vectors.
This reveals an important structural relationship:
The dual basis is an algebraic construction determined by coordinate extraction. Its Riesz representatives depend additionally on the inner product.


Riesz representation in a weighted inner product
Consider
\[
V=\mathbb R^n
\]
with inner product
\[
\langle x,y\rangle_G=x^TGy,
\]
where \(G\) is SPD.
Suppose the functional \(f\) is represented in standard coordinates by
\[
f(x)=c^Tx.
\]
We want its Riesz representative \(a_f\) relative to the \(G\)-inner product.
By definition,
\[
f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle_G.
\]
Therefore,
\[
c^Tx=x^TGa_f \qquad\forall x.
\]
This implies
\[
Ga_f=c.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{ a_f=G^{-1}c. }
\]
The formula is simple but conceptually important.
The same covector \(f\) has different representing vectors under different inner products.

Example
Let
\[
f(x_1,x_2)=2x_1+x_2.
\]
Under the Euclidean inner product,
\[
a_f=\begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Under
\[
G= \begin{pmatrix}
  4&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix},
\]
the representative becomes
\[
a_f = G^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  1
\end{pmatrix} = \boxed{ \begin{pmatrix}
  1/2\\
  1
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
The functional has not changed.
What has changed is the geometry used to represent it.
This is one of the most useful ways to understand the Riesz theorem: it converts covectors into vectors, but the conversion depends on geometric structure.



Gradients are Riesz representatives
This idea also clarifies the concept of a gradient.
Let
\[
F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R
\]
be differentiable.
At a point \(x\), the derivative is a linear functional
\[
DF(x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.
\]
It assigns to a direction \(h\) the first-order change in \(F\):
\[
F(x+h)=F(x)+DF(x)[h]+o(\|h\|).
\]
Under the Euclidean inner product, the gradient is defined by
\[
\boxed{ DF(x)[h]=\langle h,\nabla F(x)\rangle. }
\]
Thus \(\nabla F(x)\) is the Riesz representative of the derivative functional.
The derivative and the gradient are not fundamentally the same kind of object:
\[
DF(x)\in V^*, \qquad \nabla F(x)\in V.
\]
The inner product identifies them.

Example
Let
\[
F(x_1,x_2)=x_1^2+3x_2^2.
\]
Then
\[
DF(x)[h] = 2x_1h_1+6x_2h_2.
\]
The Euclidean gradient is
\[
\nabla F(x)= \begin{pmatrix}
  2x_1\\
  6x_2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If we change the inner product to one defined by \(G\), the gradient becomes
\[
\boxed{ \nabla_G F(x)=G^{-1}\nabla F(x). }
\]
This is not an arbitrary modification of the gradient.
It follows directly from the Riesz representation theorem.


Computational significance
This relationship appears in optimization, preconditioned gradient methods, and numerical algorithms for variational problems.
Changing the inner product changes which vector represents the same derivative functional.
That can change the geometry of optimization steps and sometimes improve numerical behavior.



The infinite-dimensional Riesz theorem: a preview
The finite-dimensional theorem is a special case of a more general result.
A Hilbert space is a complete inner-product space.
For a real Hilbert space \(H\), every continuous linear functional
\[
f:H\to\mathbb R
\]
has a unique representing vector \(a_f\in H\) satisfying
\[
\boxed{ f(x)=\langle x,a_f\rangle_H \qquad\forall x\in H. }
\]
Moreover,
\[
\|f\|=\|a_f\|.
\]
The word continuous is essential in infinite dimensions.
Unlike the finite-dimensional situation, not every algebraic linear functional on an infinite-dimensional normed space is necessarily continuous.

Example in a function space
Take
\[
H=L^2(0,1),
\]
with inner product
\[
\langle u,v\rangle = \int_0^1u(x)v(x)\,dx.
\]
Define
\[
F(u)=\int_0^1x\,u(x)\,dx.
\]
This is a continuous linear functional.
Its Riesz representative is the function
\[
a_F(x)=x,
\]
because
\[
F(u)=\langle u,a_F\rangle.
\]
So a linear measurement of functions can itself be represented by a function belonging to the same Hilbert space.
This is one of the foundational ideas of functional analysis.


Why completeness matters
A deeper geometric proof of Riesz representation uses the orthogonal decomposition
\[
H=\ker f\oplus^\perp(\ker f)^\perp.
\]
Because a nonzero continuous functional has a closed kernel, Hilbert-space completeness ensures the existence of the required orthogonal projection.
The orthogonal complement of the kernel is one-dimensional, so the functional measures precisely one distinguished direction, with a suitable scale factor.
We will develop this geometry in Session 4.



Checkpoint 2
Explain why the same functional can have different Riesz representatives under different inner products.
Then derive the formula
\[
a_f=G^{-1}c
\]
for a weighted inner product.
Finally, explain why the derivative \(DF(x)\) is intrinsically a functional, whereas its gradient depends on the chosen inner product.

title: 15  Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
section: 15.6 Session 3 — Adjoint operators and the geometry of linear maps
text:
15.6 Session 3 — Adjoint operators and the geometry of linear maps
We are now ready to answer the question that originally motivated our discussion of Riesz representation:
Why does every linear transformation between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces have an adjoint, and what does that adjoint mean?

Defining the adjoint
Let \(V,W\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, and let
\[
T:V\to W
\]
be linear.
The adjoint of \(T\) is the unique linear map
\[
T^*:W\to V
\]
such that
\[
\boxed{ \langle Tx,y\rangle_W = \langle x,T^*y\rangle_V }
\]
for every \(x\in V\) and \(y\in W\).
Notice that the direction is reversed:
\[
T:V\to W, \qquad T^*:W\to V.
\]
But \(T^*\) is not generally an inverse of \(T\).
Rather, it tells us how to transfer an inner-product measurement of an output back into the input space.


Deriving the adjoint from Riesz representation
Fix \(y\in W\).
Define
\[
f_y:V\to\mathbb R
\]
by
\[
f_y(x)=\langle Tx,y\rangle_W.
\]
This is a linear functional on \(V\).
By the Riesz representation theorem, there is a unique vector \(z_y\in V\) such that
\[
f_y(x)=\langle x,z_y\rangle_V
\]
for every \(x\in V\).
Therefore,
\[
\langle Tx,y\rangle_W=\langle x,z_y\rangle_V.
\]
Define
\[
\boxed{T^*y=z_y.}
\]
We obtain
\[
\langle Tx,y\rangle_W = \langle x,T^*y\rangle_V.
\]
This proves existence.
Uniqueness follows because the Riesz representative of each \(f_y\) is unique.
To prove that \(T^*\) is linear, observe that for any \(y_1,y_2\in W\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle x,T^*(\alpha y_1+\beta y_2)\rangle &=\langle Tx,\alpha y_1+\beta y_2\rangle\\
  &=\alpha\langle Tx,y_1\rangle+\beta\langle Tx,y_2\rangle\\
  &=\langle x,\alpha T^*y_1+\beta T^*y_2\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Uniqueness of the representing vector implies
\[
T^*(\alpha y_1+\beta y_2) = \alpha T^*y_1+\beta T^*y_2.
\]
Thus \(T^*\) is linear.
The adjoint is the result of applying Riesz representation to the functionals obtained by composing output measurements with \(T\).


The adjoint and the algebraic dual map
Module B introduced
\[
T^\vee:W^*\to V^*, \qquad T^\vee(g)=g\circ T.
\]
Module C has introduced the Riesz identifications
\[
R_V:V\to V^*, \qquad R_W:W\to W^*.
\]
The adjoint is related to these maps by
\[
\boxed{ R_V\circ T^* = T^\vee\circ R_W. }
\]
Indeed, for \(y\in W\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  (T^\vee(R_Wy))(x) &=(R_Wy)(Tx)\\
  &=\langle Tx,y\rangle_W\\
  &=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_V\\
  &=(R_V(T^*y))(x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the two functionals agree.
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{ T^*=R_V^{-1}\circ T^\vee\circ R_W. }
\]
The two paths in Figure 15.2 express this identity.






flowchart LR
  W["W"] -->|"adjoint of T"| V["V"]
  V -->|"Riesz map on V"| VD["V∗"]
  W -->|"Riesz map on W"| WD["W∗"]
  WD -->|"dual of T"| VD




Figure 15.2: Both routes turn an output vector into the same linear functional on the input space.





The Riesz maps connect vector spaces to their duals. The adjoint represents the algebraic dual map using those identifications.
In real finite-dimensional spaces, both Riesz maps are linear isomorphisms.
In complex spaces, the Riesz identification is conjugate-linear under our convention, but the adjoint remains a complex-linear transformation.
The main conceptual relationship is the same.


Matrix representation in orthonormal coordinates
Suppose
\[
T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m
\]
is represented by \(A\).
With standard Euclidean inner products,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle Ax,y\rangle &=(Ax)^Ty\\
  &=x^TA^Ty\\
  &=\langle x,A^Ty\rangle.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{[T^*]=A^T.}
\]
For complex matrices,
\[
\boxed{[T^*]=A^H=\overline A^{\,T}.}
\]
The distinction between the algebraic dual and the adjoint now becomes explicit.








Construction
Underlying structure
Matrix in the appropriate standard coordinates




Algebraic dual \(T^\vee\)
Vector spaces
\(A^T\)


Inner-product adjoint \(T^*\)
Inner-product spaces
\(A^T\) over \(\mathbb R\), \(A^H\) over \(\mathbb C\)



They coincide in real Euclidean coordinates, but not because they are conceptually identical.


Geometric meaning: pulling measurements backward
Suppose \(x\in V\) is an input, and \(Tx\in W\) is its output.
We want to measure the output in the direction \(y\in W\).
The measurement is
\[
\langle Tx,y\rangle_W.
\]
The adjoint identity tells us that the same scalar can be obtained before applying \(T\):
\[
\boxed{ \underbrace{\langle Tx,y\rangle_W}_{\text{output measurement}} = \underbrace{\langle x,T^*y\rangle_V}_{\text{input measurement}}. }
\]
Thus \(T^*y\) is the input-space direction representing the output measurement associated with \(y\).
Another interpretation involves hyperplanes.
The output condition
\[
\langle w,y\rangle_W=0
\]
describes a hyperplane perpendicular to \(y\).
Its preimage under \(T\) is characterized by
\[
\langle Tx,y\rangle_W=0.
\]
By the adjoint identity,
\[
\langle x,T^*y\rangle_V=0.
\]
Thus, when \(T^*y\ne0\), the preimage is the input hyperplane perpendicular to \(T^*y\). If \(T^*y=0\), the preimage is all of \(V\).
The adjoint pulls normal directions of output hyperplanes backward into the input space.
This geometric idea is useful in optimization, automatic differentiation, inverse problems, and sensitivity analysis.


Adjoints under nonstandard inner products
Suppose \(V=\mathbb R^n\) and \(W=\mathbb R^m\), with inner products
\[
\langle x,z\rangle_V=x^TG_Vz,
\]
\[
\langle y,w\rangle_W=y^TG_Ww,
\]
where \(G_V,G_W\) are SPD.
Let \(T\) be represented by \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\).
We seek the matrix \(A^\dagger_G\) of its adjoint.
The defining equation is
\[
\langle Ax,y\rangle_W = \langle x,A^\dagger_Gy\rangle_V.
\]
Expanding,
\[
x^TA^TG_Wy=x^TG_VA^\dagger_Gy.
\]
Because this holds for all \(x,y\),
\[
A^TG_W=G_VA^\dagger_G.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ A^\dagger_G=G_V^{-1}A^TG_W. }
\]
Here \(A^\dagger_G\) denotes the weighted adjoint solely within this formula; many numerical linear algebra texts reserve \(A^\dagger\) for the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. To avoid confusion, we will otherwise write \(A^{*_{G_V,G_W}}\).
Thus,
\[
\boxed{ A^{*_{G_V,G_W}} = G_V^{-1}A^TG_W. }
\]
For complex inner products with Hermitian positive definite Gram matrices, replace \(A^T\) by \(A^H\).
This is a central formula for numerical methods using weighted inner products.

Example
Let
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&2\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}
\]
and use the same weighted inner product in the domain and codomain:
\[
G= \begin{pmatrix}
  4&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then
\[
A^{*_{G}} = G^{-1}A^TG = \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  8&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The adjoint is not the ordinary transpose
\[
A^T= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  2&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The reason is that the geometric identification between vectors and functionals is different.


Structural lesson
The algebraic dual map is determined by \(T\). The adjoint depends on both \(T\) and the inner products chosen on its domain and codomain.
This distinction is essential when analyzing finite-element mass matrices, generalized eigenvalue problems, and weighted optimization methods.



Algebraic properties of adjoints
Let \(T:V\to W\), \(S:W\to Z\) be linear maps between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
The adjoint satisfies
\[
\boxed{(S\circ T)^*=T^*\circ S^*.}
\]

Proof
For \(x\in V,z\in Z\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle STx,z\rangle_Z &=\langle Tx,S^*z\rangle_W\\
  &=\langle x,T^*S^*z\rangle_V.
\end{aligned}
\]
By uniqueness of the adjoint,
\[
(ST)^*=T^*S^*.
\]
Other important identities include
\[
\boxed{(T^*)^*=T,}
\]
and, for real scalars,
\[
\boxed{(\alpha T+\beta S)^*=\alpha T^*+\beta S^*.}
\]
For complex scalars, conjugation appears:
\[
(\alpha T+\beta S)^* = \overline\alpha T^*+\overline\beta S^*.
\]
An invertible operator also satisfies
\[
\boxed{(T^{-1})^*=(T^*)^{-1}.}
\]
All these identities follow from the defining inner-product relationship.



Fundamental orthogonality relationships
We now recover the geometric versions of the annihilator identities from Module B.
Theorem. For a linear map \(T:V\to W\) between finite-dimensional inner-product spaces,
\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
  \ker T&=(\operatorname{im}T^*)^\perp,\\
  \ker T^*&=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp.
\end{aligned} }
\]

Proof of the first identity
Take \(x\in V\).
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
  x\in\ker T &\iff Tx=0\\
  &\iff \langle Tx,y\rangle_W=0\quad\forall y\in W\\
  &\iff \langle x,T^*y\rangle_V=0\quad\forall y\in W\\
  &\iff x\perp\operatorname{im}T^*.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\ker T=(\operatorname{im}T^*)^\perp.
\]
Applying the same argument to \(T^*\), using \((T^*)^*=T\), gives the second identity.
Taking orthogonal complements and using finite dimensionality,
\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{im}T^*&=(\ker T)^\perp,\\
  \operatorname{im}T&=(\ker T^*)^\perp.
\end{aligned} }
\]
These are the four fundamental orthogonality identities.
They give the decompositions
\[
\boxed{ V=\ker T\oplus^\perp\operatorname{im}T^* }
\]
and
\[
\boxed{ W=\operatorname{im}T\oplus^\perp\ker T^*. }
\]
The superscript \(\perp\) indicates an orthogonal direct sum.


Comparison with Module B
Recall the algebraic identity
\[
\operatorname{im}T^\vee=(\ker T)^0.
\]
The Riesz representation theorem identifies the annihilator \((\ker T)^0\) with the orthogonal complement \((\ker T)^\perp\), and identifies \(T^\vee\) with \(T^*\).
Thus,
\[
\boxed{ \text{Annihilator duality} \quad\xrightarrow{\text{Riesz}}\quad \text{Orthogonality duality}. }
\]
This is one of the central conceptual achievements of Module C.


A finite-versus-infinite-dimensional qualification
For a bounded operator between Hilbert spaces, we always have
\[
\ker T=(\operatorname{im}T^*)^\perp
\]
and
\[
\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp.
\]
However, the images need not be closed in infinite dimensions.
Therefore the corresponding statements are
\[
\boxed{ \begin{aligned}
  (\ker T)^\perp&=\overline{\operatorname{im}T^*},\\
  (\ker T^*)^\perp&=\overline{\operatorname{im}T}.
\end{aligned} }
\]
The closure bars are essential.
We will return to this distinction when studying functional analysis.



Checkpoint 3
Starting only from the definition of an adjoint, prove
\[
\ker T^*=(\operatorname{im}T)^\perp.
\]
Then explain why the identity
\[
\operatorname{im}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp
\]
is closely related to the annihilator theorem from Module B.
Finally, derive the weighted-adjoint formula without memorizing it.

title: 15  Module C — Inner-Product Geometry
section: 15.7 Session 4 — Orthogonal projections and closest-point approximation
text:
15.7 Session 4 — Orthogonal projections and closest-point approximation
In Module A, we studied direct-sum decompositions
\[
V=K\oplus U
\]
and the corresponding algebraic projections.
These projections are generally not unique.
Inner-product geometry gives us a distinguished choice: the projection along the orthogonal complement.
More importantly, it explains why this choice solves an optimization problem.

Orthogonal complements
Let \(U\subseteq V\) be a subspace of an inner-product space.
Its orthogonal complement is
\[
\boxed{ U^\perp= \{x\in V:\langle x,u\rangle=0\quad\forall u\in U\}. }
\]
It is a subspace.
In finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, we have
\[
\boxed{ V=U\oplus^\perp U^\perp. }
\]
This means every vector \(x\in V\) has a unique decomposition
\[
\boxed{x=u+r}
\]
with
\[
u\in U,\qquad r\in U^\perp.
\]
The vector \(u\) is the orthogonal projection of \(x\) onto \(U\).


Constructing the orthogonal decomposition
Choose an orthonormal basis
\[
(q_1,\ldots,q_k)
\]
of \(U\).
Define
\[
u=\sum_{i=1}^k\langle x,q_i\rangle q_i.
\]
This vector belongs to \(U\).
Let
\[
r=x-u.
\]
For every basis vector \(q_j\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \langle r,q_j\rangle &=\langle x,q_j\rangle -\sum_i\langle x,q_i\rangle\langle q_i,q_j\rangle\\
  &=\langle x,q_j\rangle-\langle x,q_j\rangle\\
  &=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(r\) is orthogonal to every basis vector of \(U\), hence to every vector of \(U\).
So
\[
x=u+r, \qquad u\in U,\quad r\in U^\perp.
\]
Uniqueness follows because
\[
U\cap U^\perp=\{0\}.
\]
This proves the orthogonal decomposition theorem in finite dimensions.


Why orthogonal projection gives the closest point
Suppose
\[
x=u+r, \qquad u\in U,\quad r\perp U.
\]
Take any other \(z\in U\).
Then
\[
x-z=(u-z)+r.
\]
Since \(u-z\in U\) and \(r\perp U\),
\[
\langle u-z,r\rangle=0.
\]
By the Pythagorean theorem,
\[
\boxed{ \|x-z\|^2 = \|u-z\|^2+\|r\|^2. }
\]
The second term is fixed, while the first is nonnegative.
The minimum occurs exactly when \(z=u\).
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ u=\underset{z\in U}{\operatorname{argmin}}\|x-z\|. }
\]
Thus the orthogonal projection is the unique closest point to \(x\) in \(U\).
This is one of the most important applications of inner-product geometry.
