Figure 16.1 shows the rapid reduction of the unwanted-to-desired response ratio as the polynomial degree increases.
The values arise from
\[
\frac1{|T_d(-5/3)|}.
\]


Acting on a vector
Let
\[
x=q_1+q_2+q_3.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat p_3(A)x = q_1+\frac{27}{365}q_2-\frac{27}{365}q_3.
\]
The desired component is preserved.
The unwanted components are strongly attenuated.
After normalization, the resulting vector is much closer to the eigendirection \(q_1\).
This is the basic mechanism of Chebyshev-filtered iteration.



Applying the Chebyshev recurrence to a matrix
Define the rescaled matrix
\[
\boxed{ B=s(A)=\frac{2A-(a+b)I}{b-a}. }
\]
We want to compute
\[
T_d(B)X
\]
for a vector or block \(X\), without forming \(T_d(B)\) explicitly.
Set
\[
Y_0=X,
\]
\[
Y_1=BX.
\]
Then use the recurrence
\[
\boxed{ Y_{j+1}=2BY_j-Y_{j-1}. }
\]
After \(d\) steps,
\[
Y_d=T_d(B)X.
\]
If a normalized filter is required, divide by the appropriate normalization factor.
This requires repeated applications of \(A\) to vectors or blocks, along with vector additions and scalar multiplications.
For sparse matrices, each recurrence step can often be implemented using a sparse matrix-vector or matrix-block product.
The three-term recurrence avoids explicitly forming powers of \(A\), which would generally be computationally expensive and could destroy sparsity.


A rigorous subspace convergence estimate
We can now explain the convergence mechanism for filtered subspace iteration.
Suppose \(A\) is Hermitian and has the spectral decomposition
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  Q_1&Q_2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  \Lambda_1&0\\
  0&\Lambda_2
\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
  Q_1&Q_2
\end{pmatrix}^*.
\]
Here:

The columns of \(Q_1\in\mathbb C^{n\times k}\) span the desired invariant subspace.
The columns of \(Q_2\) span its orthogonal complement.
\(\Lambda_1\) contains the desired eigenvalues.
\(\Lambda_2\) contains the unwanted eigenvalues.

Let the starting block \(X\in\mathbb C^{n\times k}\) have full column rank.
Write its spectral coordinates as
\[
\boxed{ X=Q_1C+Q_2D, }
\]
where \(C\in\mathbb C^{k\times k}\) and \(D\in\mathbb C^{(n-k)\times k}\).
Assume \(C\) is invertible.
This is the algebraic condition that the trial subspace has full-dimensional overlap with the desired subspace.

Representing the trial subspace as a graph
Because \(C\) is invertible,
\[
X=(Q_1+Q_2DC^{-1})C.
\]
Multiplication on the right by an invertible matrix does not change the column space.
Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{im}X = \operatorname{im}(Q_1+Q_2M),
\]
where
\[
\boxed{M=DC^{-1}.}
\]
The matrix \(M\) describes how much the trial subspace tilts away from the desired invariant subspace.
In fact,
\[
\boxed{ \|M\|_2=\tan\theta_{\max}, }
\]
where \(\theta_{\max}\) is the largest principal angle between the two \(k\)-dimensional subspaces.


Apply a polynomial filter
Now compute
\[
Y=p(A)X.
\]
Using the spectral decomposition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
  Y &=Q_1p(\Lambda_1)C +Q_2p(\Lambda_2)D.
\end{aligned}
\]
Assume that \(p(\Lambda_1)\) is invertible, so that the filter does not annihilate a desired eigendirection.
The new graph matrix is
\[
\boxed{ M_{\mathrm{new}} = p(\Lambda_2)M\,p(\Lambda_1)^{-1}. }
\]
Therefore,
\[
\|M_{\mathrm{new}}\|_2 \le \|p(\Lambda_2)\|_2 \|M\|_2 \|p(\Lambda_1)^{-1}\|_2.
\]
Since these are diagonal spectral matrices,
\[
\|p(\Lambda_2)\|_2 = \max_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{unwanted}}}|p(\lambda)|,
\]
while
\[
\|p(\Lambda_1)^{-1}\|_2 = \frac1{ \min_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{wanted}}}|p(\lambda)| }.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{ \tan\theta_{\max}^{\mathrm{new}} \le \gamma_p\, \tan\theta_{\max}^{\mathrm{old}}, }
\]
where
\[
\boxed{ \gamma_p= \frac{ \max_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{unwanted}}}|p(\lambda)| }{ \min_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{wanted}}}|p(\lambda)| }. }
\]
This is the central exact-arithmetic estimate behind polynomial-filtered subspace iteration.
If
\[
\gamma_p<1,
\]
the trial subspace moves closer to the desired invariant subspace, as measured by its largest principal angle.


What makes Chebyshev filtering effective?
The purpose of Chebyshev filtering is to construct a polynomial with a small \(\gamma_p\), while keeping its evaluation computationally practical.
The mathematical problem is therefore a polynomial approximation and spectral separation problem.
The computational problem is to evaluate the filter accurately and efficiently.
This is precisely where spectral theory, numerical analysis, and hardware-aware implementation intersect.



Finite-precision and hardware-aware considerations
The estimate above assumes exact arithmetic.
Real computations introduce additional effects.
A computed matrix-vector product can be modeled schematically as
\[
\operatorname{fl}(Ax)=Ax+\delta,
\]
where \(\delta\) represents the error of the operation.
Similarly, a computed Chebyshev recurrence does not satisfy the exact polynomial recurrence.
If
\[
\widehat Y_{j+1} = 2B\widehat Y_j-\widehat Y_{j-1}+E_j,
\]
then the matrices \(E_j\) represent perturbations due to arithmetic, communication, compression, or approximate matrix products.
A convergence analysis must account for how these perturbations propagate through the recurrence.
The simple exact-arithmetic inequality
\[
\tan\theta_{\mathrm{new}} \le\gamma_p\tan\theta_{\mathrm{old}}
\]
then requires additional error terms.
Several numerical issues arise:
Spectral bounds. The unwanted interval \([a,b]\) must adequately contain the unwanted spectrum. An eigenvalue lying unexpectedly outside the interval may be amplified instead of suppressed.
Polynomial degree. Increasing the degree improves spectral separation in exact arithmetic, but also increases the number of matrix operations and opportunities for rounding error.
Scaling. Chebyshev polynomials can grow rapidly outside \([-1,1]\). Careful scaling may be needed to avoid overflow or loss of numerical range.
Orthogonalization. A filtered block still needs a numerically reliable basis. QR factorization or other orthogonalization procedures control loss of linear independence.
Low precision. Lower-precision arithmetic can reduce cost on some hardware, but the resulting perturbations may limit attainable subspace accuracy.
Residuals. A small recurrence change does not automatically imply a small eigenpair residual. Residual evaluation provides a separate measure of the quality of the computed Ritz pairs.
For your HASC seminar, these are the mathematical questions that connect the exact spectral theory to implementations using inexact products, reduced precision, and hardware-dependent performance characteristics.
The detailed error recurrences, stability conditions, and performance tradeoffs belong to Module E.


Checkpoint 7
Derive the mapping
\[
s(t)=\frac{2t-(a+b)}{b-a}
\]
and explain why it is appropriate for Chebyshev filtering.
Then reconstruct the filtered-subspace inequality
\[
\tan\theta_{\mathrm{new}} \le\gamma_p\tan\theta_{\mathrm{old}}.
\]
Finally, explain why the convergence factor must involve both the maximum unwanted filter response and the minimum desired filter response.

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.11 Session 8 — Spectral theory beyond matrices
text:
16.11 Session 8 — Spectral theory beyond matrices
We end the module by connecting finite-dimensional spectral theory to functional analysis, PDEs, and structural algebra.
These connections are important because they reveal which ideas are truly general and which depend on special assumptions such as finite dimensionality or self-adjointness.

Spectrum in infinite-dimensional spaces
For a finite-dimensional complex matrix, \(\lambda\) belongs to the spectrum precisely when
\[
A-\lambda I
\]
is not invertible.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, the same broad definition remains useful, but invertibility must be understood in the appropriate operator-theoretic sense.
For a bounded operator \(T:X\to X\) on a complex Banach space, the spectrum is
\[
\boxed{ \sigma(T)= \{\lambda\in\mathbb C: T-\lambda I \text{ has no bounded inverse defined on all of }X\}. }
\]
The spectrum may contain values that are not eigenvalues.
This is a major difference from finite-dimensional linear algebra.


A self-adjoint operator with no eigenvalues
Consider the Hilbert space
\[
H=L^2(0,1).
\]
Define the multiplication operator
\[
\boxed{ (Mf)(x)=xf(x). }
\]
This operator is bounded and self-adjoint.
Indeed,
\[
\langle Mf,g\rangle = \int_0^1 xf(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx = \langle f,Mg\rangle.
\]
Its spectrum is
\[
\boxed{\sigma(M)=[0,1].}
\]
But it has no eigenvalues.
To see why, suppose
\[
Mf=\lambda f.
\]
Then
\[
(x-\lambda)f(x)=0
\]
for almost every \(x\in(0,1)\).
Thus \(f\) can be nonzero only on the set \(\{x=\lambda\}\), which has measure zero.
Therefore \(f=0\) as an element of \(L^2(0,1)\).
So no nonzero eigenfunction exists.
This example shows that the finite-dimensional picture of spectral theory cannot always be extended by simply replacing matrices with infinite-dimensional operators.


Compact self-adjoint operators
An operator \(T:H\to H\) on a Hilbert space is compact if it maps bounded sets into relatively compact sets—that is, sets whose closures are compact.
Compact self-adjoint operators have spectral properties resembling those of finite-dimensional Hermitian matrices.
For such an operator:

Every nonzero spectral value is an eigenvalue.
Nonzero eigenvalues have finite multiplicity.
The nonzero spectrum can accumulate only at zero.
The Hilbert space admits an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors, including a basis for the kernel when necessary.

A typical example is
\[
T:\ell^2\to\ell^2, \qquad T(x_1,x_2,\ldots) = \left(x_1,\frac{x_2}{2},\frac{x_3}{3},\ldots\right).
\]
Its eigenvectors are the standard coordinate sequences, with eigenvalues
\[
1,\frac12,\frac13,\ldots.
\]
The eigenvalues approach zero.
Zero belongs to the spectrum but is not an eigenvalue, because the operator is injective.
This example is particularly useful for connecting spectral theory with numerical conditioning and compact inverse problems.


Differential operators and PDE eigenvalue problems
Consider the eigenvalue problem
\[
\boxed{ -u''(x)=\lambda u(x), \qquad 0<x<1, }
\]
with boundary conditions
\[
u(0)=u(1)=0.
\]
We seek nonzero solutions \(u\).
For positive \(\lambda\), write
\[
\lambda=\omega^2.
\]
The general solution is
\[
u(x)=A\sin(\omega x)+B\cos(\omega x).
\]
The condition \(u(0)=0\) gives \(B=0\).
The condition \(u(1)=0\) then requires
\[
\sin\omega=0.
\]
For a nonzero solution,
\[
\omega=n\pi,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ \lambda_n=n^2\pi^2. }
\]
The corresponding normalized eigenfunctions are
\[
\boxed{ q_n(x)=\sqrt2\sin(n\pi x). }
\]
They form an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(0,1)\).
Thus the differential operator
\[
L=-\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
\]
with Dirichlet boundary conditions has a spectral decomposition involving infinitely many eigenfunctions.
A careful operator-theoretic formulation regards \(L\) as an unbounded self-adjoint operator on \(L^2(0,1)\), with a suitable dense domain such as
\[
D(L)=H^2(0,1)\cap H_0^1(0,1).
\]
The eigenvalues grow without bound.
Its inverse, defined on \(L^2(0,1)\), is compact.
This is an important bridge between finite-dimensional spectral theory, compact operators, and PDEs.


Variational formulation of the PDE eigenproblem
Multiply
\[
-u''=\lambda u
\]
by a test function \(v\in H_0^1(0,1)\), and integrate by parts:
\[
\int_0^1u'(x)v'(x)\,dx = \lambda\int_0^1u(x)v(x)\,dx.
\]
Define
\[
a(u,v)=\int_0^1u'v'
\]
and
\[
m(u,v)=\int_0^1uv.
\]
Then the weak eigenvalue problem is
\[
\boxed{ a(u,v)=\lambda m(u,v) \qquad\forall v\in H_0^1(0,1). }
\]
Its finite-element discretization gives
\[
\boxed{Kc=\lambda Mc,}
\]
where \(K\) and \(M\) are stiffness and mass matrices.
This is exactly the generalized eigenvalue structure introduced in Module C.
The finite-dimensional spectral theory therefore arises as an approximation of the spectral theory of a differential operator.


The min–max principle in PDE approximation
For the Dirichlet Laplacian, the Rayleigh quotient is
\[
\boxed{ \rho(u)= \frac{\int_0^1|u'(x)|^2\,dx} {\int_0^1|u(x)|^2\,dx}. }
\]
The smallest eigenvalue can be characterized by
\[
\boxed{ \lambda_1= \min_{u\in H_0^1(0,1)\setminus\{0\}}\rho(u). }
\]
More generally, a min–max principle characterizes the higher eigenvalues using finite-dimensional trial subspaces of \(H_0^1(0,1)\).
Now restrict the variational problem to a conforming finite-element space
\[
V_h\subseteq H_0^1(0,1).
\]
Because the minimization is performed over a smaller set,
\[
\boxed{\lambda_{1,h}\ge\lambda_1.}
\]
The corresponding upper-bound property extends to higher eigenvalues under the standard min–max ordering, provided the trial space has sufficient dimension.
As the finite-element spaces approximate the full function space, the computed eigenvalues can converge to the true PDE eigenvalues.
This provides a conceptual reason for eigenvalue convergence in variational numerical methods.
It also explains why Rayleigh–Ritz is so important in both finite-dimensional numerical linear algebra and infinite-dimensional spectral approximation.


Spectral theory as algebra: a module viewpoint
We can now revisit an abstract question from the beginning of the curriculum.
Why are invariant subspaces so fundamental?
There is an elegant answer from abstract algebra.
Let \(V\) be a vector space over \(\mathbb F\), and let
\[
T:V\to V
\]
be a linear operator.
We can make \(V\) into a module over the polynomial ring \(\mathbb F[t]\).
Define the action of a polynomial
\[
p(t)=a_0+a_1t+\cdots+a_dt^d
\]
on \(v\in V\) by
\[
\boxed{ p(t)\cdot v=p(T)v. }
\]
In particular,
\[
t\cdot v=Tv.
\]
Now ask: what are the submodules of this \(\mathbb F[t]\)-module?
A subspace \(U\subseteq V\) is a submodule precisely when it is preserved by multiplication by \(t\), meaning
\[
T(U)\subseteq U.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ \text{Invariant subspaces of }T = \mathbb F[t]\text{-submodules of }V. }
\]
This is a genuinely useful universal perspective.
It connects linear operator theory with module theory.

Eigenspaces as algebraic kernels
The eigenspace
\[
E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)
\]
consists of vectors annihilated by the polynomial \(t-\lambda\):
\[
(t-\lambda)\cdot v=0.
\]
Generalized eigenspaces consist of vectors annihilated by higher powers:
\[
\ker(T-\lambda I)^k.
\]
Thus Jordan theory can be understood in terms of the polynomial-ring module structure.


Diagonalizability and decomposition
A diagonalizable operator is one for which the module decomposes into a direct sum of eigenspaces:
\[
V=\bigoplus_\lambda E_\lambda.
\]
Over a field where the minimal polynomial splits, diagonalizability is equivalent to the minimal polynomial having no repeated roots.
For a Jordan block
\[
J= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
the minimal polynomial is
\[
(t-2)^2.
\]
The repeated factor reflects the coupling that prevents diagonalization.
For a self-adjoint operator, the spectral theorem provides an especially strong decomposition: an orthogonal direct sum of eigenspaces.


Exact sequences return
If \(U\subseteq V\) is invariant, the sequence
\[
0\longrightarrow U \longrightarrow V \longrightarrow V/U \longrightarrow0
\]
is not only an exact sequence of vector spaces.
It is also an exact sequence of \(\mathbb F[t]\)-modules, because the operator induces a well-defined action on the quotient.
A vector-space complement of \(U\) need not be invariant.
Therefore, the sequence may split as vector spaces without splitting as \(\mathbb F[t]\)-modules.
This is a structural explanation of why invariant complements are more restrictive than ordinary complements.
It also explains why Jordan blocks represent genuinely nontrivial extensions of eigenspace behavior.


Why this viewpoint is valuable
This perspective unifies several ideas:

Linear operators become actions of polynomial rings.
Invariant subspaces become submodules.
Eigenspaces become kernels of polynomial actions.
Spectral decompositions become module decompositions.
Polynomial functional calculus becomes the ring action itself.

You do not need to study the full structure theorem for finitely generated modules over principal ideal domains before learning numerical eigenvalue methods.
But it is useful to recognize that the same mathematics has an abstract algebraic interpretation.
The Hilbert-space setting adds geometric requirements—orthogonality, completeness, and self-adjointness—that cannot be recovered from the module structure alone.



Checkpoint 8
Explain why the spectral theorem for finite-dimensional Hermitian matrices does not extend verbatim to all bounded self-adjoint operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
Then derive the generalized finite-element eigenproblem
\[
Kc=\lambda Mc
\]
from the weak PDE eigenvalue formulation.
Finally, prove that a subspace is invariant under \(T\) if and only if it is a submodule of \(V\) under the action \(p(t)\cdot v=p(T)v\).

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.12 Exercises — Module D
text:
16.12 Exercises — Module D
The exercises are organized to develop the same six perspectives used throughout the curriculum: rigorous theory, geometry, computation, structural connections, universal generalization, and applications.
For the proof-based exercises, try writing a complete argument before consulting the solutions.

Exercise 1 — Diagonalizability and field dependence
Consider
\[
R= \begin{pmatrix}
  0&-1\\
  1&0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
and
\[
J= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Determine the eigenvalues and eigenspaces of both matrices over \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathbb C\).
Which matrices are diagonalizable over each field?
Explain why the reasons for failure of real diagonalizability are different in these two examples.


Exercise 2 — An invariant subspace without an invariant complement
Let
\[
J= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&2
\end{pmatrix}, \qquad U=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}.
\]
Prove that \(U\) is invariant under \(J\).
Show that \(U\) has many complementary vector subspaces.
However, prove that none of its one-dimensional complements is invariant under \(J\).
Interpret the result using the distinction between ordinary vector-space direct sums and decompositions into invariant subspaces.


Exercise 3 — Spectral projectors
Consider
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1&0\\
  1&2&0\\
  0&0&9
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Construct the spectral projector onto the eigenspace associated with eigenvalue \(1\) in two ways:

Using the corresponding normalized eigenvector.
Using the Lagrange interpolation polynomial

\[
\ell_1(t)=\frac{(t-3)(t-9)}{(1-3)(1-9)}.
\]
Verify that the two formulas agree.
Then calculate \(p(A)\) for
\[
p(t)=\frac{9-t}{8}.
\]


Exercise 4 — Principal angles
Let
\[
U=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_2\} \subseteq\mathbb R^3
\]
and
\[
W=\operatorname{span} \left\{ \cos\phi\,e_1+\sin\phi\,e_3,\ e_2 \right\},
\]
where \(0\le\phi\le\pi/2\).
Calculate the two principal angles between \(U\) and \(W\).
Determine
\[
\|P_U-P_W\|_2.
\]
Explain why the answer is independent of the particular orthonormal bases chosen.


Exercise 5 — Rayleigh–Ritz and residuals
Let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(1,3,9)
\]
and
\[
Q= \begin{pmatrix}
  1/\sqrt2&0\\
  1/\sqrt2&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Construct the reduced matrix
\[
H=Q^TAQ.
\]
Find its Ritz values and Ritz vectors.
Calculate the residual norm of each Ritz pair.
Verify the eigenvalue inclusion bound
\[
\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\sigma(A)) \le\|r\|_2.
\]


Exercise 6 — Eigenvalue versus eigenvector accuracy
Consider
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)
\]
and
\[
x(\theta)= \begin{pmatrix}
  \cos\theta\\
  \sin\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Derive
\[
\rho_A(x)=1+3\sin^2\theta.
\]
Calculate the residual
\[
r=Ax-\rho_A(x)x
\]
and its norm.
Show that the Rayleigh quotient error relative to eigenvalue \(1\) is quadratic in \(\sin\theta\), while the residual norm is asymptotically linear in \(\sin\theta\) near \(\theta=0\).


Exercise 7 — SVD and minimum-norm least squares
Consider
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  3&0\\
  0&1\\
  0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Find an SVD of \(A\).
Determine its pseudoinverse \(A^+\).
For
\[
b=(6,2,5)^T,
\]
calculate the least-squares minimizer and the residual.
Find the best rank-one approximation of \(A\) in spectral norm, and give its error.


Exercise 8 — Power iteration
Let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(9,3,1), \qquad x_0=(1,1,1)^T.
\]
Find \(A^kx_0\).
Determine the ratios of the second and third spectral coefficients to the first after \(k\) iterations.
Explain the convergence rate.
What happens if the initial vector instead belongs to
\[
\operatorname{span}\{e_2,e_3\}?
\]


Exercise 9 — A Chebyshev filter
Let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(1,3,9).
\]
We want to retain the eigenspace associated with eigenvalue \(1\).
Take the unwanted spectral interval \([3,9]\).
Construct the affine map taking this interval onto \([-1,1]\).
Then construct the normalized degree-three Chebyshev filter satisfying \(p_3(1)=1\).
Calculate
\[
p_3(3),\qquad p_3(9).
\]
Apply the filter to
\[
x=(1,1,1)^T.
\]
Explain the result in spectral terms.


Exercise 10 — A residual-based subspace estimate
Let
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)
\]
and
\[
x(\theta)= \begin{pmatrix}
  \cos\theta\\
  \sin\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Let
\[
U=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}.
\]
Using the Rayleigh quotient \(\rho_A(x)\), show that
\[
\boxed{ \|(I-P_U)x\| \le \frac{\|Ax-\rho_A(x)x\|} {|4-\rho_A(x)|} }
\]
whenever \(\rho_A(x)\ne4\).
Determine the value of the left-hand side and discuss when the bound is informative.


Exercise 11 — Spectral theory of a differential operator
Consider
\[
-u''=\lambda u
\]
on \((0,1)\), with
\[
u(0)=u(1)=0.
\]
Derive the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.
Normalize the eigenfunctions in \(L^2(0,1)\).
Write down the Rayleigh quotient associated with the problem.
Explain why restricting the variational eigenproblem to a finite-dimensional conforming subspace produces approximations of the eigenvalues from above.


Exercise 12 — Universal structure
Let \(T:V\to V\) be linear and define an action of \(\mathbb F[t]\) on \(V\) by
\[
p(t)\cdot v=p(T)v.
\]
Prove that a vector subspace \(U\subseteq V\) is a submodule if and only if \(U\) is invariant under \(T\).
Explain why an invariant subspace permits a quotient operator on \(V/U\).
Finally, use the Jordan block from Exercise 2 to explain why a short exact sequence of operator modules need not split, even when the corresponding sequence of vector spaces does.

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.13 Worked solutions
text:
16.13 Worked solutions

Solution 1 — Diagonalizability
For
\[
R= \begin{pmatrix}
  0&-1\\
  1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
the characteristic polynomial is
\[
\lambda^2+1.
\]
Thus it has no real eigenvalues.
Over \(\mathbb C\), the eigenvalues are
\[
\lambda_1=i,\qquad\lambda_2=-i.
\]
Corresponding eigenvectors can be chosen as
\[
v_1=(1,-i)^T, \qquad v_2=(1,i)^T.
\]
They are linearly independent over \(\mathbb C\), so \(R\) is diagonalizable over \(\mathbb C\), but not over \(\mathbb R\).
For
\[
J= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1\\
  0&2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
the only eigenvalue is \(2\), with algebraic multiplicity two.
The eigenspace is
\[
E_2=\ker(J-2I)=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}.
\]
Thus \(J\) has only one independent eigenvector, even over \(\mathbb C\).
It is not diagonalizable over either field.
The rotation matrix lacks real eigenvalues because its characteristic polynomial does not split over \(\mathbb R\).
The Jordan block is defective because its eigenspace has insufficient dimension, even over a field containing all its eigenvalues.


Solution 2 — No invariant complement
We have
\[
Je_1=2e_1,
\]
so \(U=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\) is invariant.
Every line
\[
W=\operatorname{span}\{(a,b)^T\}
\]
with \(b\ne0\) is a complement of \(U\).
Suppose such a complement were invariant.
Because it is one-dimensional, its nonzero generator would have to be an eigenvector of \(J\):
\[
J(a,b)^T=\lambda(a,b)^T.
\]
But the only eigenvectors of \(J\) belong to \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\), which requires \(b=0\).
This contradicts the requirement \(b\ne0\).
Therefore \(U\) has vector-space complements but no invariant complement.
The short exact sequence involving \(U\), \(V\), and \(V/U\) splits as vector spaces, but not as modules under the action of \(J\).


Solution 3 — Spectral projectors
The normalized eigenvector for eigenvalue \(1\) is
\[
q_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0)^T.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{ P_1=q_1q_1^T = \frac12 \begin{pmatrix}
  1&-1&0\\
  -1&1&0\\
  0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
The Lagrange polynomial is
\[
\ell_1(t)=\frac{(t-3)(t-9)}{16}.
\]
It satisfies
\[
\ell_1(1)=1,\qquad \ell_1(3)=0,\qquad \ell_1(9)=0.
\]
Therefore, by spectral functional calculus,
\[
\ell_1(A)=P_1.
\]
For
\[
p(t)=\frac{9-t}{8},
\]
the spectral values are
\[
p(1)=1,\qquad p(3)=\frac34,\qquad p(9)=0.
\]
Hence
\[
p(A)=P_1+\frac34P_2.
\]
Using the explicit projectors,
\[
\boxed{ p(A)= \begin{pmatrix}
  7/8&-1/8&0\\
  -1/8&7/8&0\\
  0&0&0
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]


Solution 4 — Principal angles
Choose
\[
Q_U=(e_1\ e_2)
\]
and
\[
Q_W= (\cos\phi\,e_1+\sin\phi\,e_3\ \ e_2).
\]
Then
\[
Q_U^TQ_W= \begin{pmatrix}
  \cos\phi&0\\
  0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its singular values are
\[
1,\qquad\cos\phi.
\]
Thus the principal angles are
\[
\boxed{0,\quad\phi.}
\]
The largest principal angle is \(\phi\).
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\|P_U-P_W\|_2=\sin\phi.}
\]
Changing either orthonormal basis multiplies \(Q_U^TQ_W\) by orthogonal matrices on the left or right, leaving its singular values unchanged.
Thus the principal angles depend only on the subspaces.


Solution 5 — Rayleigh–Ritz
The reduced matrix is
\[
H= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&0\\
  0&9
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Ritz values are
\[
\boxed{\theta_1=2,\qquad\theta_2=9.}
\]
Corresponding Ritz vectors are
\[
u_1=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,1,0)^T, \qquad u_2=e_3.
\]
For the first pair,
\[
r_1=Au_1-2u_1 = \frac1{\sqrt2}(-1,1,0)^T.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\|r_1\|_2=1.}
\]
For the second pair,
\[
r_2=Au_2-9u_2=0.
\]
The spectrum of \(A\) is \(\{1,3,9\}\).
Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{dist}(2,\sigma(A))=1=\|r_1\|.
\]
And
\[
\operatorname{dist}(9,\sigma(A))=0=\|r_2\|.
\]
Both satisfy the residual inclusion bound.


Solution 6 — Quadratic eigenvalue error
For
\[
x=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^T,
\]
the Rayleigh quotient is
\[
\rho_A(x) = \cos^2\theta+4\sin^2\theta.
\]
Since \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\),
\[
\boxed{ \rho_A(x)=1+3\sin^2\theta. }
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\rho_A(x)-1=3\sin^2\theta.}
\]
The residual is
\[
r= 3\sin\theta\cos\theta \begin{pmatrix}
  -\sin\theta\\
  \cos\theta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{ \|r\|_2=3|\sin\theta\cos\theta|. }
\]
Near \(\theta=0\),
\[
\sin\theta\sim\theta,\qquad \cos\theta\sim1.
\]
Thus
\[
\rho_A(x)-1\sim3\theta^2,
\]
while
\[
\|r\|\sim3|\theta|.
\]
The eigenvalue error is second-order in the angular error, while the residual is first-order.


Solution 7 — SVD and pseudoinverse
The matrix
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  3&0\\
  0&1\\
  0&0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
is already in rectangular diagonal form.
We may take
\[
U=I_3,\qquad V=I_2,
\]
and
\[
\Sigma=A.
\]
The singular values are
\[
\sigma_1=3,\qquad\sigma_2=1.
\]
Its pseudoinverse is
\[
\boxed{ A^+= \begin{pmatrix}
  1/3&0&0\\
  0&1&0
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
For \(b=(6,2,5)^T\),
\[
x_{\mathrm{LS}}=A^+b = \boxed{ \begin{pmatrix}
  2\\
  2
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
Then
\[
Ax_{\mathrm{LS}}= \begin{pmatrix}
  6\\
  2\\
  0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{ r=b-Ax_{\mathrm{LS}} = \begin{pmatrix}
  0\\
  0\\
  5
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
The best rank-one approximation is
\[
\boxed{ A_1= \begin{pmatrix}
  3&0\\
  0&0\\
  0&0
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
Its spectral-norm error is
\[
\boxed{\|A-A_1\|_2=\sigma_2=1.}
\]


Solution 8 — Power iteration
Since \(A\) is diagonal,
\[
\boxed{ A^kx_0=(9^k,3^k,1)^T. }
\]
The ratio of the second spectral coefficient to the first is
\[
\frac{3^k}{9^k} = \boxed{\left(\frac13\right)^k}.
\]
The ratio of the third to the first is
\[
\frac1{9^k} = \boxed{\left(\frac19\right)^k}.
\]
Thus the subspace approaches \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\), with asymptotic convergence factor \(1/3\).
If the initial vector has no \(e_1\) component, applying \(A\) cannot create one, because the eigenspaces are invariant.
Therefore power iteration cannot converge to \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\) from an initial vector entirely in \(\operatorname{span}\{e_2,e_3\}\).
If the \(e_2\) component is nonzero, it instead tends toward \(\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}\).


Solution 9 — Chebyshev filter
The unwanted interval is \([3,9]\).
The affine spectral map is
\[
\boxed{s(t)=\frac{t-6}{3}.}
\]
The degree-three Chebyshev polynomial is
\[
T_3(z)=4z^3-3z.
\]
At the desired eigenvalue \(1\),
\[
T_3(s(1)) = T_3(-5/3) = -\frac{365}{27}.
\]
Thus the normalized filter is
\[
\boxed{ p_3(t) = -\frac{27}{365} T_3\left(\frac{t-6}{3}\right). }
\]
We obtain
\[
\boxed{ p_3(1)=1,\qquad p_3(3)=\frac{27}{365},\qquad p_3(9)=-\frac{27}{365}. }
\]
Since \(A\) is diagonal,
\[
\boxed{ p_3(A)(1,1,1)^T = \begin{pmatrix}
  1\\
  27/365\\
  -27/365
\end{pmatrix}. }
\]
The desired spectral component is preserved, while each unwanted component is reduced to about \(7.4\%\) of its original magnitude.


Solution 10 — Residual and angular error
The target projector is
\[
P_U= \begin{pmatrix}
  1&0\\
  0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
(I-P_U)x= \begin{pmatrix}
  0\\
  \sin\theta
\end{pmatrix},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{ \|(I-P_U)x\|=|\sin\theta|. }
\]
The unwanted eigenvalue is \(4\), and the separation from the Rayleigh quotient is
\[
\delta=|4-\rho_A(x)|.
\]
The residual bound gives
\[
|\sin\theta| \le \frac{3|\sin\theta\cos\theta|} {|4-(1+3\sin^2\theta)|}.
\]
For \(0\le\theta<\pi/2\), the denominator is
\[
3\cos^2\theta.
\]
Therefore the right-hand side becomes
\[
\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \tan\theta.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\sin\theta\le\tan\theta.}
\]
The bound is sharp to first order near \(\theta=0\), where \(\sin\theta\approx\tan\theta\).
It becomes less informative as \(\theta\to\pi/2\), because the approximate eigenvalue approaches the unwanted eigenvalue \(4\) and the separation \(\delta\) tends to zero.


Solution 11 — Dirichlet Laplacian
The eigenvalue equation is
\[
-u''=\lambda u.
\]
A nonzero solution satisfying the Dirichlet boundary conditions exists precisely for
\[
\boxed{\lambda_n=n^2\pi^2,\qquad n=1,2,\ldots.}
\]
Corresponding eigenfunctions are
\[
u_n(x)=\sin(n\pi x).
\]
Since
\[
\int_0^1\sin^2(n\pi x)\,dx=\frac12,
\]
the normalized eigenfunctions are
\[
\boxed{ q_n(x)=\sqrt2\sin(n\pi x). }
\]
The Rayleigh quotient is
\[
\boxed{ \rho(u)= \frac{\int_0^1|u'(x)|^2\,dx} {\int_0^1|u(x)|^2\,dx}. }
\]
The min–max principle characterizes the eigenvalues through trial subspaces.
When we restrict the admissible subspaces to a conforming finite-dimensional space \(V_h\subseteq H_0^1(0,1)\), we minimize over fewer possibilities.
Therefore the computed Ritz eigenvalues cannot be smaller than the corresponding exact eigenvalues:
\[
\boxed{\lambda_{k,h}\ge\lambda_k}
\]
for the indices represented by the discrete problem.


Solution 12 — Operator modules
The action of \(\mathbb F[t]\) is defined by
\[
p(t)\cdot v=p(T)v.
\]
A vector subspace \(U\) is a submodule if it is closed under the action of all polynomials.
If \(U\) is a submodule, it is in particular closed under multiplication by \(t\):
\[
t\cdot u=Tu\in U.
\]
Thus \(U\) is \(T\)-invariant.
Conversely, if \(T(U)\subseteq U\), then induction gives
\[
T^k(U)\subseteq U
\]
for all \(k\).
Consequently,
\[
p(T)(U)\subseteq U
\]
for every polynomial \(p\).
Thus \(U\) is a submodule.
For the quotient, define
\[
\overline T(v+U)=Tv+U.
\]
This is well-defined because \(U\) is invariant.
For the Jordan block \(J\) from Exercise 2, \(U=\operatorname{span}\{e_1\}\) is invariant but has no invariant complement.
Therefore,
\[
0\to U\to V\to V/U\to0
\]
splits as vector spaces but not as \(\mathbb F[t]\)-modules.
An operator-compatible direct-sum decomposition is more restrictive than an arbitrary vector-space decomposition.

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.16 Supplementary proof — Why normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable
text:
16.16 Supplementary proof — Why normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable
We proved the spectral theorem for self-adjoint matrices. The more general normal-matrix theorem is worth understanding because it clarifies exactly which hypothesis guarantees an orthonormal eigenbasis.

Step 1: Schur triangularization
Every complex square matrix \(A\) has a Schur decomposition
\[
\boxed{A=QRQ^*,}
\]
where \(Q\) is unitary and \(R\) is upper triangular.
One way to prove this is by induction.
Because the characteristic polynomial has a complex root, \(A\) has an eigenvector \(q_1\).
Normalize it and extend it to an orthonormal basis.
In that basis, the first column of \(A\) has the form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
  \lambda\\
  0\\
  \vdots\\
  0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus the matrix has block upper-triangular form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
  \lambda&*\\
  0&B
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Apply the same argument inductively to \(B\), using a unitary basis change within the orthogonal complement of \(q_1\).
This produces an upper-triangular matrix \(R\).


Step 2: A normal upper-triangular matrix is diagonal
Suppose \(R\) is upper triangular and normal:
\[
R^*R=RR^*.
\]
Normality implies
\[
\|Rx\|=\|R^*x\|
\]
for every \(x\).
Apply this to \(e_1\).
Because \(R\) is upper triangular, its first column has only one potentially nonzero entry:
\[
Re_1= \begin{pmatrix}
  r_{11}\\
  0\\
  \vdots\\
  0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Hence
\[
\|Re_1\|^2=|r_{11}|^2.
\]
But \(R^*e_1\) contains the conjugates of the first-row entries:
\[
R^*e_1= \begin{pmatrix}
  \overline{r_{11}}\\
  \overline{r_{12}}\\
  \vdots\\
  \overline{r_{1n}}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus
\[
\|R^*e_1\|^2 = |r_{11}|^2+ \sum_{j=2}^n|r_{1j}|^2.
\]
Equality of the norms implies
\[
\sum_{j=2}^n|r_{1j}|^2=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
r_{12}=\cdots=r_{1n}=0.
\]
The first row has no off-diagonal entries.
The remaining lower-right block is again upper triangular and normal.
Repeating the argument inductively shows that \(R\) is diagonal.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{A=Q\Lambda Q^*.}
\]
Conversely, if \(A=Q\Lambda Q^*\) for unitary \(Q\) and diagonal \(\Lambda\), then
\[
AA^*=Q\Lambda\Lambda^*Q^*
\]
and
\[
A^*A=Q\Lambda^*\Lambda Q^*.
\]
Because diagonal matrices commute,
\[
AA^*=A^*A.
\]
Thus the equivalence is proved:
\[
\boxed{ A\text{ is normal} \iff A\text{ is unitarily diagonalizable}. }
\]
This theorem shows precisely why nonnormal diagonalizable matrices behave differently from Hermitian matrices: an arbitrary eigenvector basis need not be orthogonal, while a normal matrix always admits an orthonormal one.

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.17 Module D — Final mastery assessment
text:
16.17 Module D — Final mastery assessment
Before proceeding to Module E, the goal is not to memorize every formula. It is to be able to derive the central results, recognize their assumptions, and apply them to unfamiliar examples.

Explain eigenvalues through kernels and distinguish invertibility, diagonalizability, normality, and self-adjointness.
Prove the finite-dimensional self-adjoint spectral theorem and understand the normal spectral theorem.
Construct spectral projectors and derive polynomial functional calculus.
Calculate principal angles and explain the meaning of an invariant-subspace residual.
Prove the min–max principle and derive the Rayleigh–Ritz equations.
Prove eigenvalue residual inclusion and explain residual-to-subspace-error estimates.
Construct the SVD, pseudoinverse, and optimal truncated SVD.
Explain the convergence mechanisms of power iteration and subspace iteration.
Construct and evaluate a Chebyshev filter, and derive its subspace convergence factor.
Connect spectral theory to PDE eigenproblems, compact operators, and the abstract algebra of invariant subspaces.


Recommended consolidation exercise
For the final synthesis, take one Hermitian matrix such as
\[
A= \begin{pmatrix}
  2&1&0\\
  1&2&0\\
  0&0&9
\end{pmatrix}
\]
and reconstruct the following chain without consulting the notes:
\[
\boxed{ \begin{gathered}
  \text{Find eigenvalues and eigenspaces}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Construct the orthogonal spectral projectors}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Express }A\text{ through its projectors}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Construct a polynomial filter }p(A)\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Apply the filter to a trial vector or subspace}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Compute Ritz values and Ritz vectors}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Evaluate residuals and subspace angles}\\
  \downarrow\\
  \text{Explain convergence using spectral separation}.
\end{gathered} }
\]
If you can perform and explain this complete sequence, including why each step is mathematically justified, you have achieved the central objective of Module D.

title: 16  Module D — Spectral Theory
section: 16.18 Transition to Module E — Numerical methods and stability
text:
16.18 Transition to Module E — Numerical methods and stability
Module D has established the exact mathematical structures underlying eigenvalue algorithms.
Module E will investigate what happens when we try to realize those structures computationally.
The focus will shift from the question

Why does the spectral algorithm work in exact arithmetic?

to the more numerical question:

Under what assumptions, and with what accuracy and cost, can we expect it to work in floating-point arithmetic?

The principal subjects will include power and inverse iteration, block subspace iteration, Krylov methods, Rayleigh–Ritz and numerical residuals, Chebyshev recurrence evaluation, conditioning, backward stability, perturbation theory, and precision-dependent convergence.
In the context of hardware-aware scientific computing, a central issue will be the distinction between mathematical convergence mechanisms and implementation-dependent numerical behavior.
For example, an exact-arithmetic Chebyshev filter may reduce unwanted spectral components by a theoretically predictable factor. But an implementation using inexact matrix products and reduced precision also introduces errors that may accumulate, be amplified, or eventually create an accuracy floor.
The study of those interactions is where spectral theory becomes numerical analysis.
The central achievement of Module D is a unified understanding of spectral decomposition, invariant-subspace geometry, variational eigenvalue approximation, and polynomial spectral filtering. Together, these concepts provide the mathematical foundation for studying and analyzing modern numerical eigenvalue algorithms—and, more specifically, Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration.

title: 17  Module E — Numerical Eigenvalue Methods, Conditioning, and Stability
text:
17.1 From a spectral decomposition to a numerical claim
Suppose a program returns a unit vector \(x\) and a number \(\theta\). You can multiply by \(A\), but you do not know any of its eigenvectors. What calculation would justify the statement “this is an accurate approximation to the second eigenvector”? Computing \(\|Ax-\theta x\|\) is a first step. You still need to identify the eigenvalue, establish separation from competing directions, and know how accurately you evaluated the residual itself. Each of the eight sessions develops one part of that argument.
Starting point in Review II. Module A (§4.11) supplied invariant subspaces and direct sums. Module B (§5.7) explained how a functional pulls back through a map. Module C (§§6.7, 6.11) supplied orthogonal projections and the mass-matrix inner product. Module D (§§7.5–7.10) established the spectral theorem, principal angles, Rayleigh–Ritz, and polynomial filtering. Its §7.18 asks what accuracy and cost survive implementation. Here a spectral theorem becomes both a way to design an algorithm and a way to audit its output.
Running example and conventions. Work over a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space, using orthonormal coordinates unless specified. A star denotes conjugate transpose. Write \(\|\cdot\|\) for the Euclidean or induced spectral norm, \(\|\cdot\|_F\) for the Frobenius norm. The Rayleigh quotient is \(\rho_A(x)=x^*Ax/(x^*x)\). Reuse the matrix from §7.5.5,
\[
A_0=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&2&0\\0&0&9\end{pmatrix},
\quad q_1=(1,-1,0)^T/\sqrt2,\quad q_2=(1,1,0)^T/\sqrt2,\quad q_3=e_3 .
\]
The corresponding eigenvalues are \(1,3,9\). These subscripts stay attached to these vectors. For general results we state the ordering separately, since largest magnitude, largest algebraic value and closest to a shift are three different targets.
Read Sessions 1–2 together, derive Sessions 3–4 first for \(A_0\), and work through Session 6 once with scalars before interpreting a matrix experiment. The laboratory is a single MATLAB script collected after the exercises.

title: 17  Module E — Numerical Eigenvalue Methods, Conditioning, and Stability
section: 17.2 Session 1 — Floating-point arithmetic, conditioning, and stability
text:
17.2 Session 1 — Floating-point arithmetic, conditioning, and stability

What one rounding step changes
In binary precision \(p\) a normalized positive number has form \((1.b_2\ldots b_p)_2 2^e\) with a bounded exponent. Adjacent numbers in \([1,2)\) are \(2^{1-p}\) apart. Rounding to nearest therefore gives unit roundoff \(u=2^{-p}\). In binary32, \(p=24\); in binary64, \(p=53\). MATLAB’s spacing at one is \(2u\). The exponent controls range independently of the precision. For a correctly rounded real operation with exact result in the normal range and no overflow,
\[
\operatorname{fl}(a\mathbin{\circ}b)=(a\mathbin{\circ}b)(1+\delta),\quad |\delta|\le u .
\]
Indeed half an ulp in the binade starting at \(2^e\) is \(2^eu\), while the result has magnitude at least \(2^e\). Zero is exact. Near underflow one needs an absolute-error term. A fused multiply-add rounds the combined expression once. Complex arithmetic implemented with real operations has different operation counts.
Hand experiment. With \(p=3\) and ties to even, \(1+1/8\) rounds to \(1\). Thus \((1+1/8)-1\) evaluates to zero while \((1-1)+1/8\) evaluates exactly. The final subtraction in the first expression is itself exact. It exposes the loss in the preceding sum. This is the same difficulty that arises when subtracting two large nearly equal terms in an eigenpair residual.


From dot products to a matrix product
For \(ku<1\) write \(\gamma_k=ku/(1-ku)\). A product of at most \(k\) factors \(1+\delta_j\) differs from one by at most \(\gamma_k\): its upper bound is \((1+u)^k\le 1/(1-ku)\) by binomial expansion and the geometric series, and its lower bound is at least \(1-ku\). Unroll a sequential real dot product. Each exact summand \(a_jx_j\) is multiplied by the rounding factor from its product and factors from subsequent additions, at most \(n\) in total when the first product initializes the sum. Thus
\[
|\operatorname{fl}(a^Tx)-a^Tx|\le\gamma_n\sum_j|a_jx_j|,
\qquad |\operatorname{fl}(Ax)-Ax|\le\gamma_n|A|\,|x|.
\]
Absolute values and the second inequality are entrywise. Equivalently, for this multiply there exists \(\Delta A\) with \(|\Delta A|\le\gamma_n|A|\) giving the computed result exactly as \((A+\Delta A)x\). The perturbation can change with the input and with each multiply. For sparse rows one can replace \(n\) by their maximum number of summed products under the same arithmetic model. Cancellation can make the relative output error large even when the componentwise backward error is small.


Problem sensitivity versus the error of a method
For differentiable \(f\) the local absolute condition number in specified norms is \(\|Df(d)\|\). For \(d,f(d)\ne0\), the relative one is \(\|Df(d)\|\|d\|/\|f(d)\|\). This follows by maximizing the first-order change \(Df(d)h\) over a ball of input perturbations. Specifying which data may change is part of defining the problem.
A forward error measures distance from the exact output. A backward error is the least size of a permitted perturbation for which the computed output is exact. Backward stability means this size is small on the scale of arithmetic error under stated hypotheses. For \(Ax=b\) with nonsingular \(A\), fixed \(A\), and \(r=b-A\hat x\), the exact perturbed right side is \(b-r\). Hence
\[
x-\hat x=A^{-1}r,\qquad
\frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|}\le\kappa_2(A)\frac{\|r\|}{\|b\|},
\quad \kappa_2(A)=\|A\|\|A^{-1}\|=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}.
\]
Here \(\|b\|\le\|A\|\|x\|\) supplies the last factor. For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\), \(b=e_1\) and \(\hat x=(1,1)^T\), the relative residual is \(\varepsilon\) and the relative forward error is one. The SVD from Module D explains this amplification by the long axis of the inverse image ellipsoid. In iterative refinement a more accurate residual helps recover the correction. The eigenvalue analogue requires spectral separation, developed next.
Checkpoint. For \(a=(1,-1)\), \(x=(1,1+\varepsilon)^T\), explain why the dot-product bound divided by \(|a^Tx|\) grows like \(2\gamma_2/|\varepsilon|\). Which two terms cancel?

title: 17  Module E — Numerical Eigenvalue Methods, Conditioning, and Stability
section: 17.3 Session 2 — Eigenpair residuals and perturbations
text:
17.3 Session 2 — Eigenpair residuals and perturbations

A residual as the price of exactness
For a unit vector \(x\), set \(r=Ax-\theta x\). A matrix \(E\) makes \((\theta,x)\) exact for \(A+E\) precisely when \(Ex=-r\). Consequently \(\|E\|\ge\|r\|\), with equality for \(E=-rx^*\). This is an exact, normwise, absolute backward error allowing arbitrary matrix perturbations. For a nonzero unnormalized vector divide the residual norm by \(\|x\|\). Normalizing further by \(\|A\|\) gives a relative perturbation in \(A\) when \(\|A\|>0\).
If \(A=A^*\) and \(\theta=\rho_A(x)\), then \(x^*r=0\). Now \(E=-rx^*-xr^*\) is Hermitian and has the same optimal norm. On the orthonormal pair \(x,r/\|r\|\) its matrix has zero diagonal and off-diagonals \(-\|r\|\), and it vanishes on their orthogonal complement. The case \(r=0\) takes \(E=0\). This construction preserves self-adjointness. Additional requirements such as a fixed sparsity pattern change the backward-error problem.


Locating an eigenvalue and locating a direction
Let \(A=A^*=U\Lambda U^*\), \(x=\sum_i c_i u_i\), \(\|x\|=1\). Pythagoras gives the identity
\[
\|r\|^2=\sum_i|\lambda_i-\theta|^2|c_i|^2 .
\]
Since \(\sum_i|c_i|^2=1\), some eigenvalue lies within \(\|r\|\) of \(\theta\). To identify a target set \(I\), let \(P_I=\sum_{i\in I}u_i u_i^*\) and \(\delta=\min_{i\notin I}|\lambda_i-\theta|>0\). Discarding the target terms gives
\[
\sin\angle(x,\operatorname{ran}P_I)=\|(I-P_I)x\|\le\|r\|/\delta .
\]
Knowing which eigenvalues are excluded is substantive information. An exact eigenvector of the wrong eigenvalue has zero residual. Eigenvectors inside a multiple eigenspace are interchangeable, so a particular basis there cannot be certified from the equation.
For a simple target \(\lambda_j\), expansion of the Rayleigh quotient gives \(\rho_A(x)-\lambda_j=\sum_{i\ne j}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)|c_i|^2\). Its absolute value is bounded by \(\max_i|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|\sin^2\angle(x,u_j)\). Thus the value can settle to many digits while its direction still moves appreciably. For \(x=\cos t\,q_2+\sin t\,q_3\), the value is \(3+6\sin^2 t\) and the residual norm is \(6|\sin t\cos t|\).


Weyl and subspace separation
For two Hermitian matrices \(A\) and \(A+E\), their eigenvalues in increasing order satisfy \(|\lambda_i(A+E)-\lambda_i(A)|\le\|E\|\). Proof. For every unit vector the Rayleigh quotients differ by at most \(\|E\|\). Taking the maximum over vectors in an \(i\)-dimensional subspace and then the minimum over such subspaces preserves both inequalities. Apply Module D’s min–max theorem. This is an absolute bound. Relative sensitivity may be large near zero.
Here is a residual version of the subspace separation argument behind Davis–Kahan. Let \(X^*X=I\), \(H=X^*AX\), and \(R=AX-XH\). Rotate \(X\) by a unitary matrix to diagonalize \(H=\operatorname{diag}(\theta_j)\) in its new basis. If \(U_2\) spans the exact unwanted eigenvectors with diagonal matrix \(\Lambda_2\), then \(S=U_2^*X\) satisfies
\[
\Lambda_2 S-SH=U_2^*R .
\]
If every \(|\lambda_i(\Lambda_2)-\theta_j|\ge\delta>0\), division entry by entry and summation of squares gives \(\|S\|_F\le\|R\|_F/\delta\). The singular values of \(S\) are the sines of the principal angles when the target and trial dimensions agree. This proves a Frobenius sin-theta bound and therefore also bounds the largest sine. Entrywise division alone does not prove the same constant for a spectral-norm right side. For a perturbed invariant subspace of \(A+E\), \(R=-(I-XX^*)EX\); the denominator must still separate the perturbed Ritz spectrum from the unwanted spectrum of \(A\).
Small-gap example. For \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1+g)\) add a real symmetric off-diagonal \(\varepsilon\). The diagonalizing rotation has \(|\tan(2t)|=2|\varepsilon|/g\). Taking \(\varepsilon=g/2\) rotates the axes by \(\pi/8\) even as \(g\to0\). Appending a third eigenvalue \(9\) leaves the first two coordinates as an exact invariant plane. A well-determined plane may contain poorly determined individual directions.


Why nonnormality changes the certificate
If \(A=V\Lambda V^{-1}\) and \(\mu\) is an eigenvalue of \(A+E\), then \(\min_i|\mu-\lambda_i|\le\kappa_2(V)\|E\|\) (Bauer–Fike). For \(\mu\) outside the spectrum, apply \((\mu I-A)^{-1}\) to \(Ex\) for a unit perturbed eigenvector \(x\). The resolvent has norm at most \(\kappa_2(V)/\min_i|\mu-\lambda_i|\), giving the claim. A normal matrix admits unitary \(V\). For a simple eigenvalue, differentiating \(Ax=\lambda x\) and testing with a left eigenvector \(y^*\) gives \(\dot\lambda=y^*\dot A x/(y^*x)\). This is Module B’s dual measurement in action. Nearly orthogonal left and right eigenvectors amplify perturbations.
For the Jordan block \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), adding \(\varepsilon\) in position \((2,1)\) produces eigenvalues \(\pm\sqrt{\varepsilon}\). Even the order of the displacement changes at a defective eigenvalue. More generally the \(\varepsilon\)-pseudospectrum consists of the possible eigenvalues under \(\|E\|\le\varepsilon\). The rank-one construction identifies it exactly with those \(\theta\) admitting a unit vector of residual at most \(\varepsilon\).
Checkpoint. If a normalized Hermitian Ritz vector has residual \(10^{-8}\) and every unwanted eigenvalue is at least \(10^{-3}\) away from its Ritz value, what is certified? Some eigenvalue is within \(10^{-8}\) and the sine to the identified target space is at most \(10^{-5}\).

section: 17.4 Session 3 — Vector iterations as spectral transformations
text:
17.4 Session 3 — Vector iterations as spectral transformations

Power iteration and its rate
Given a unit \(x_0\), form \(y=Ax_k\), \(x_{k+1}=y/\|y\|\) whenever \(y\ne0\). Normalization controls the scale and preserves the line generated by \(A^{k+1}x_0\). For Hermitian \(A\), order \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots\) and write \(x_0=\sum c_i u_i\) with \(c_1\ne0\). Divide the squared norm of the unwanted components by that of the desired component:
\[
\tan^2\angle(x_k,u_1)=
\sum_{i>1}\left|\frac{c_i}{c_1}\right|^2
             \left|\frac{\lambda_i}{\lambda_1}\right|^{2k}.
\]
Consequently the tangent decreases at least as fast as the bound \((|\lambda_2/\lambda_1|)^k\tan\angle(x_0,u_1)\). Equality holds if all active unwanted components have modulus \(|\lambda_2|\). The Rayleigh quotient error is quadratic in the sine by Session 2. A negative dominant eigenvalue reverses sign each iteration. Monitor the line or its residual. A zero starting coefficient stays zero in exact arithmetic. Equal dominant moduli can prevent convergence to a line, as \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) shows.
For \(A_0\), start at \((q_2+q_3)/\sqrt2\). After two multiplications the tangent to \(q_3\) is \(1/9\), and the Rayleigh quotient is \((3+9\cdot81)/82\). Compare the error \(6/82\) with the angle \(\arctan(1/9)\). In an optimization interpretation, \(\rho_A\) on the unit sphere has tangential gradient \(2(Ax-\rho_A(x)x)\) in real coordinates. A stationary point is an eigenvector. Power iteration selects by modulus, so on an indefinite matrix it need not maximize the quotient.


Inverse iteration and Rayleigh quotient iteration
Choose a real shift \(\sigma\) outside the spectrum. Solve \((A-\sigma I)y=x_k\) and normalize \(y\). In the eigenbasis the component multiplier is \(1/(\lambda_i-\sigma)\). For a unique closest eigenvalue \(\lambda_t\), nonzero starting overlap, and second-closest distance \(d_2\), the tangent bound contracts per step by \(|\lambda_t-\sigma|/d_2\). A fixed shift permits reuse of a factorization. For \(A_0\), \(\sigma=2.8\) gives distances \(1.8,0.2,6.2\). The target is \(q_2\) and the worst-case factor is \(1/9\). Near-singularity is the source of selectivity. It also calls for stable shifted solves and residual checks on the original eigenproblem. A solve residual \(s=x_k-(A-\sigma I)\hat y\) changes the inverse application by \(-(A-\sigma I)^{-1}s\).
Rayleigh quotient iteration (RQI) recomputes \(\sigma=\rho_A(x_k)\) each time. Assume \(A\) Hermitian, \(\lambda_t\) simple, gap \(g>0\), and \(x_k\) close enough that \(|\rho_A(x_k)-\lambda_t|<g/2\). Put \(t=\angle(x_k,u_t)\) and \(D=\max_i|\lambda_i-\lambda_t|\). When the shifted solve exists, the same component calculation gives
\[
\tan t_{\mathrm{new}}\le
\frac{|\lambda_t-\rho_A(x_k)|}{\min_{i\ne t}|\lambda_i-\rho_A(x_k)|}\tan t
\le (2D/g)\sin^2 t\,\tan t .
\]
This proves local cubic convergence of the direction. Each changing shift can require a new factorization. Check convergence before solving: at an eigenvector the shifted matrix is singular. At an interior eigenvalue cancellation can also give a singular shift away from an eigenvector. For \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,0,1)\), the equal mixture of the outer directions has quotient zero. A practical safeguard detects a failed solve and selects a perturbed shift. The cubic estimate makes no global claim about which eigenpair a distant start selects.
Checkpoint. Explain why a smaller shift distance helps inverse iteration in exact arithmetic and simultaneously increases the potential amplification of a linear-solve residual.

section: 17.5 Session 4 — Block iteration, principal angles, and extraction
text:
17.5 Session 4 — Block iteration, principal angles, and extraction

Why a basis needs attention
To find a \(p\)-dimensional invariant space, start with \(X_0^*X_0=I_p\), form \(Y=AX_k\), and take \(X_{k+1}\) as the thin \(Q\) in \(Y=QR\). Provided \(Y\) has full column rank, \(R\) is invertible and the range is unchanged by this operation. Independent power iterations tend to align all columns with the strongest direction. A QR step restores a basis with which the weaker directions can still be represented. A unitary change of basis \(X\mapsto XW\) leaves the orthogonal projector \(XX^*\) unchanged.
Write \(A=[U_1,U_2]\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda_1,\Lambda_2)[U_1,U_2]^*\) for Hermitian \(A\), with \(p\) target columns in \(U_1\). Put \(C=U_1^*X_0\), \(D=U_2^*X_0\). Assume \(C\) invertible and every target eigenvalue nonzero. In eigen-coordinates a basis of the iterated space can be written \[
\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda_1^k C\\\Lambda_2^k D\end{pmatrix}
(\Lambda_1^k C)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}I\\Z_k\end{pmatrix},
\qquad Z_k=\Lambda_2^k DC^{-1}\Lambda_1^{-k}.
\] This is the graph of a map from the target to its orthogonal complement. A vector on it has tangent \(\|Z_k v\|/\|v\|\) to the target. Maximization therefore gives \(\tan\theta_{\max}=\|Z_k\|\). In particular \[
\tan\theta_{\max,k}\le
\left(\frac{\max_{\mathrm{out}}|\lambda|}{\min_{\mathrm{in}}|\lambda|}\right)^k\|DC^{-1}\| .
\] Separation is needed across the boundary of the target. Multiplicities wholly inside it cause no difficulty. Taking a block larger than the requested number can move that boundary beyond a cluster; then interpret the bound for the enlarged space and extract the requested Ritz pairs.


Rayleigh–Ritz and finite precision
With orthonormal \(X\), compress to \(H=X^*AX\). Solve \(Hw_j=\theta_jw_j\) with orthonormal \(w_j\), form \(v_j=Xw_j\). Then \(r_j=Av_j-\theta_j v_j\) satisfies \(X^*r_j=0\) by substitution. Conversely this orthogonality for \(v=Xw\) is precisely the projected eigenproblem. Thus the defect annihilates every trial-space test direction (Module B), or equivalently has zero orthogonal projection there (Module C). For nonorthonormal full-rank \(Y\) the corresponding problem is \(Y^*AYw=\theta Y^*Yw\). An ill-conditioned Gram matrix squares the basis condition number. Orthogonalize first.
For \(A_0\), use \(X=[q_2,(q_1+q_3)/\sqrt2]\). The compression is \(\operatorname{diag}(3,5)\), yet \(5\) is not an eigenvalue of \(A_0\). Its residual is \(4(q_3-q_1)/\sqrt2\), perpendicular to both columns. One exact Ritz pair can coexist with a poor second pair. Sorted Ritz values alone do not verify a block.
Householder QR uses unitary reflections \(I-2vv^*/(v^*v)\) to zero entries below a pivot without changing exact lengths. In floating point it is a standard stable choice for a dense block. Gram–Schmidt subtracts projections onto earlier columns. If this leaves a tiny vector, errors made in subtracting large components are magnified upon normalization. A second orthogonalization pass often repairs the defect. If the input block has lost numerical rank, reorthogonalization cannot recover information already lost. Monitor \(\|I-X^*X\|\), the size and conditioning of the small triangular factor, and the direct residual. Computing small angles through \(\arccos(\sigma_{\min}(U_1^*X))\) loses digits near one. Prefer \(\|(I-U_1U_1^*)X\|\) or \(\|U_2^*X\|\) for the largest sine.
Checkpoint. For trial columns \(q_3,(q_2+q_1)/\sqrt2\) and target \(\operatorname{span}(q_3,q_2)\), calculate the tangent after one power step. It is \(1/3\), even though the first column is already exact.

section: 17.6 Session 5 — Krylov spaces and projected eigenproblems
text:
17.6 Session 5 — Krylov spaces and projected eigenproblems

Keeping the history
For \(v\ne0\), \(\mathcal K_m(A,v)=\operatorname{span}(v,Av,\ldots,A^{m-1}v)=\{p(A)v:\deg p<m\}\). Power iteration keeps one polynomial. Krylov projection searches the span of all these candidates. If \(A^m v\) lies in the earlier span then applying \(A\) to any spanning vector stays inside and the space is invariant. Algebraically, \(p\mapsto p(A)v\) maps the polynomial ring onto the cyclic space generated by \(v\). Its kernel is the ideal generated by the least-degree monic polynomial annihilating \(v\). Polynomial division shows that its degree equals the eventual Krylov dimension. This is the first isomorphism theorem of Module A in the language of Module F2.


Arnoldi, Lanczos, and the residual shortcut
Normalize \(v_1=v/\|v\|\). Given \(V_j=[v_1,\ldots,v_j]\), project \(Av_j\) onto the basis, subtract that projection and normalize the remainder: \[
h_{ij}=v_i^*Av_j,\quad w=Av_j-\sum_{i=1}^j h_{ij}v_i,\quad
h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|,\quad v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}.
\] A zero norm gives an invariant space in exact arithmetic. Stacking the identities gives \[
AV_m=V_m H_m+h_{m+1,m}v_{m+1}e_m^*,\qquad H_m=V_m^*AV_m .
\] \(H_m\) is upper Hessenberg because \(Av_j\) lies in the first \(j+1\) basis vectors. For a unit eigenvector \(H_m y=\theta y\), its lifted residual has norm \(|h_{m+1,m}|\,|e_m^*y|\). Only the last coefficient and the last subdiagonal enter.
For Hermitian \(A\), Hermitian symmetry of \(H_m\) forces all entries above its first superdiagonal to vanish as well. Writing its real diagonal as \(\alpha_j\) and nonnegative subdiagonal as \(\beta_j\) gives the Lanczos recurrence \[
\beta_jv_{j+1}=Av_j-\alpha_jv_j-\beta_{j-1}v_{j-1},
\quad \beta_0=0 .
\] In exact arithmetic earlier projections vanish by the Hessenberg identity and symmetry. In finite precision tiny components along converged Ritz directions can grow back, causing duplicate approximate eigenvalues. Full or selective reorthogonalization trades additional work and communication for control of this effect. The direct residual checks both the recurrence shortcut and the projected solve.
Two steps by hand. Start \(A_0\) at \(e_1\). Then \(Ae_1=2e_1+e_2\), so \(\alpha_1=2\), \(\beta_1=1\), \(v_2=e_2\). Next \(Ae_2=e_1+2e_2\), yielding \(\alpha_2=2\), \(\beta_2=0\). The projected problem has eigenvalues \(1,3\). The missing \(9\) cannot be recovered from this start because every polynomial in \(A\) preserves this coordinate plane.
A sparse Arnoldi step needs one matrix application and projections against earlier vectors. For \(m\) steps, storing the full basis costs order \(nm\) and orthogonalization costs order \(nm^2\). Short-recurrence Lanczos can generate coefficients with a few vectors, but recovering Ritz vectors later requires stored or regenerated basis information. Restarting bounds storage by retaining selected approximate spectral information before building a new space. Discarding too much can erase progress near a cluster. Block iteration has fixed width and can exploit matrix–block products. A degree-\(d\) filtered block also belongs to a block Krylov space, but evaluates a prescribed polynomial without storing every power.
Checkpoint. What evidence distinguishes exact invariance from numerical breakdown? A tiny computed \(\beta_j\) is a clue. Directly test \(\|AV_j-V_jH_j\|\) and \(\|V_j^*V_j-I\|\) at the accuracy required by the application.

section: 17.7 Session 6 — Designing and evaluating a Chebyshev filter
text:
17.7 Session 6 — Designing and evaluating a Chebyshev filter

The design problem
Suppose the unwanted eigenvalues of a Hermitian operator lie in \([a,b]\) and all desired eigenvalues lie above \(b\). Let \(c=(a+b)/2\), \(h=(b-a)/2>0\), and \(B=(A-cI)/h\). The unwanted interval maps to \([-1,1]\). A filter should be bounded there and large at every target. The same map works for a target below \(a\) using the parity of the polynomial. An interior band generally needs a different filter design: two exterior tails cannot both be mapped to this single unwanted interval by one affine map without also including the interior target.
Define \(T_j(\cos t)=\cos(jt)\). The addition formula gives \(T_0=1\), \(T_1=z\), \(T_{j+1}=2zT_j-T_{j-1}\). Thus \(|T_j|\le1\) on \([-1,1]\), and \(T_j(-z)=(-1)^jT_j(z)\). For \(z>1\) substitute \(z=\cosh s\) into the same recurrence to obtain \(T_j(z)=\cosh(js)\), \(s=\operatorname{arcosh}z\). Growth is exponential for fixed exterior \(z\). It slows as the target approaches the cutoff. Taking higher powers \(z^j\) also amplifies exterior components, but misses the extremal property below.
Normalized minimax theorem. Fix \(z_*>1\), \(d\ge1\). Among real polynomials \(p\) of degree at most \(d\) satisfying \(p(z_*)=1\), the least possible maximum of \(|p|\) on \([-1,1]\) is \(1/T_d(z_*)\). The candidate is \(p=T_d/T_d(z_*)\). To prove optimality, suppose a competitor has strictly smaller maximum. The difference \(T_d-T_d(z_*)p\) alternates in sign at \(\cos(j\pi/d)\) for \(j=0,\ldots,d\). It has \(d\) distinct interior zeros and another zero at \(z_*\). A nonzero polynomial of degree at most \(d\) cannot have \(d+1\) roots. This optimality concerns uniform suppression of an interval with a specified exterior normalization. It does not optimize wall time or rounding errors.


Subspace convergence and degree choice
The spectral theorem gives \(T_d(B)u_i=T_d((\lambda_i-c)/h)u_i\). Apply the graph proof from Session 4 with each eigenvalue replaced by its filter value. For full initial target overlap, \[
\tan\theta_{\max,k}\le \rho_d^k\tan\theta_{\max,0},\qquad
\rho_d=\frac{\max_{\mathrm{out}}|T_d((\lambda-c)/h)|}
{\min_{\mathrm{in}}|T_d((\lambda-c)/h)|}.
\] If the nearest target maps to \(z_*>1\) and all unwanted eigenvalues lie in the design interval, \(\rho_d\le\operatorname{sech}(d\,\operatorname{arcosh}z_*)\). For a desired one-block contraction \(\tau<1\) choose \(d\ge\operatorname{arcosh}(1/\tau)/\operatorname{arcosh}z_*\). Round upward. This counts polynomial degree, hence block products, per application. It is a sufficient interval estimate. The finite set of actual unwanted eigenvalues can give a smaller ratio.
Running matrix. Seek \(q_3\) of \(A_0\). For \([1,3]\), \(B=A_0-2I\) has eigenvalues \(-1,1,7\). A degree-two filter has values \(1,1,97\). Starting at \((q_2+q_3)/\sqrt2\), two ordinary power steps leave tangent \(1/9\). One degree-two filter also takes two products and leaves tangent \(1/97\). Both calculations start with the same angle and cost the same number of applications. Differences in QR, memory access and coefficient operations enter an actual timing comparison.


Evaluating a polynomial without forming powers
Use \(Y_0=X\), \(Y_1=BX\), \(Y_{j+1}=2BY_j-Y_{j-1}\). Induction gives \(Y_j=T_j(B)X\). Only successive blocks are needed. The product \(BY=(AY-cY)/h\) can be implemented as an operator action. Forming \(B\) once can change cancellation, rounding and memory requirements. An exact-arithmetic scalar normalization common to the entire block leaves the resulting space unchanged.
To control range, choose an exterior reference \(z_s>1\), typically near the largest mapped target, and set \(W_j=Y_j/T_j(z_s)\). Define \(s_j=T_{j-1}(z_s)/T_j(z_s)\). Then \[
s_1=1/z_s,\quad s_{j+1}=1/(2z_s-s_j),\quad
W_0=X,\quad W_1=s_1BX,\quad
W_{j+1}=2s_{j+1}BW_j-s_js_{j+1}W_{j-1}.
\] This follows by dividing the recurrence by \(T_{j+1}(z_s)\). It avoids computing the huge normalization factor explicitly. Common scaling controls overflow but leaves the ratio between the strongest and weakest wanted components intact. Large degree can make the filtered block nearly rank deficient before QR. Compare singular values of the small \(R\) factor, shorten the polynomial or orthogonalize between complete shorter filters. Inserting arbitrary independent normalizations into an unmodified three-term recurrence changes the polynomial.


What a local error becomes
For the unscaled recurrence define a local additive defect \(F_j\) in each computed step, incorporating whatever product and update errors occurred: \[
\widehat Y_0=X,\quad \widehat Y_1=BX+F_1,\quad
\widehat Y_j=2B\widehat Y_{j-1}-\widehat Y_{j-2}+F_j,\quad j\ge2 .
\] Let \(U_0(z)=1\), \(U_1(z)=2z\), \(U_{k+1}=2zU_k-U_{k-1}\) be the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind (here \(U_k\) is a polynomial). Subtract the exact recurrence. Induction, using \(U_0=1\) for the newest defect, gives the exact error representation \[
\widehat Y_d-Y_d=\sum_{j=1}^d U_{d-j}(B)F_j .
\] This identity assumes a fixed exact \(B\) and exact initial block. Errors in storing or applying \(B\) can be included in \(F_j\). It does not presume independent random signs. Projection onto any eigendirection reduces the propagation to scalar weights. For \(z=\cos t\), \(U_k(z)=\sin((k+1)t)/\sin t\), bounded by \(k+1\) including the limiting endpoints (expand the sine quotient as a sum of unit complex exponentials). Consequently for the unwanted spectral projector \(P_2\), \[
\|P_2(\widehat Y_d-Y_d)\|\le
\sum_{j=1}^d(d-j+1)\|P_2 F_j\|.
\] For \(z=\cosh s>1\), the corresponding weight is \(\sinh((k+1)s)/\sinh s\). An early error in a desired component can grow very large in absolute norm. Whether it rotates the range is a separate question. For instance, at \(d=3\) a defect in the first product contributes \((4B^2-I)F_1\), while a defect in the last update contributes \(F_3\) directly.


Turning application error into angle error
In the target/complement coordinates write the input block as \(\binom{C}{D}\), and write one computed filter output as \(\binom{P_1 C+G_1}{P_2' D+G_2}\), where \(P_1,P_2'\) are diagonal target and unwanted filter values, and \(G_i\) are the total filter errors in those coordinates. Put \(\alpha=\min|\operatorname{diag}P_1|\), \(\beta=\max|\operatorname{diag}P_2'|\). Right-multiplying by \(C^{-1}\) shows that the graph of the output has tangent bounded by \[
t_{\mathrm{new}}\le
\frac{\beta t+\|G_2 C^{-1}\|}{\alpha-\|G_1 C^{-1}\|},
\qquad t=\|DC^{-1}\|.
\] Indeed the smallest singular value of the top block after multiplication is at least the denominator, which must be positive. The unwanted numerator is bounded by the triangle inequality. This inequality explains why a global absolute error bound alone is a poor predictor of angle accuracy. Unwanted leakage adds a new direction and poor target overlap can amplify it.
If the resulting step bounds yield uniform constants \(t_{k+1}\le q t_k+\eta\) with \(0\le q<1\), summing a geometric progression gives \(t_k\le q^kt_0+\eta(1-q^k)/(1-q)\). The second term predicts a possible stagnation scale. It is an upper envelope, never a proof that every run stagnates there. Errors can cancel or decrease as the residual shrinks. A verified residual and a gap estimate are needed to diagnose a real run.


Bounds that miss part of the spectrum
If an unwanted eigenvalue falls just outside the designed interval, its multiplier becomes \(\cosh(d\,\operatorname{arcosh}|z|)\) in magnitude. Recompute the actual ratio \(\rho_d\): convergence can slow and an unwanted direction can even dominate. Conversely an overly wide interval can bring the nearest target closer to \(1\), requiring higher degree. Obtain bounds from analysis of the operator, enclosing intervals such as Gershgorin bounds, or preliminary iterations with explicit margins. An interior Ritz estimate of an extreme eigenvalue alone is generally not an outer enclosure, as min–max already shows.
Checkpoint. With \([a,b]=[1,5]\) and target \(8\), \(z_*=2.5\). Show \(T_3(2.5)=55\). If an unwanted \(6\) was missed, its mapped value is \(1.5\), giving \(T_3(1.5)=9\). The ratio estimate changes from \(1/55\) to \(9/55\) when this is the only missed eigenvalue.

section: 17.8 Session 7 — Mixed precision and hardware-aware computation
text:
17.8 Session 7 — Mixed precision and hardware-aware computation

An error budget by operation








Operation
Where accuracy enters
Measurement or design choice




Store and apply \(A\)
Quantization perturbs the operator before accumulation begins
Retain a reference action for verification


Evaluate the filter
Every recurrence defect is propagated by a different polynomial
Select degree, scaling, product and update precisions separately


QR
Small singular directions of the input may be obscured
Check orthogonality and inspect the triangular factor


Rayleigh–Ritz
Projection errors perturb a small Hermitian problem
Form and solve the compression accurately, check its symmetry


Stop and report
Cancellation in \(AX-X\Theta\) may hide the true residual
Reapply the original operator in a specified verification precision



If storage gives \(\widetilde A=A+E_s\) and arithmetic returns \(\widetilde A X+F\), the product error relative to the original data is \(E_s X+F\). Higher-precision accumulation can reduce \(F\) but does not remove \(E_sX\). If \(X\) itself is quantized, expand \((A+E_s)(X+E_x)\) to see the additional terms \(AE_x+E_sE_x\). In a distributed computation rounding communicated entries contributes to \(E_x\), possibly only on boundary data. A uniform normwise model may overestimate that effect. Floating-point format, product precision, accumulation precision and communication format must be specified separately.
Verification bound. If the computed verification residual is \(\hat r=r+e\) with \(\|e\|\le\epsilon_v\), then \(\|r\|\le\|\hat r\|+\epsilon_v\). A matvec bound from Session 1 plus bounds for the scale and subtraction can supply \(\epsilon_v\) under a known arithmetic model. A double-precision direct residual is a practical independent diagnostic when the filter ran in single. Calling it a rigorous enclosure additionally requires controlling its own evaluation and norm rounding. Increasing the verification precision can reveal an existing error without changing the iterate.
A scalar identity behind residual-based methods. For a polynomial \(p\) and approximate eigenpair \((x,\theta)\), the factor theorem gives \(p(z)-p(\theta)=(z-\theta)s_\theta(z)\). Therefore \[
p(A)x=p(\theta)x+s_\theta(A)r,\qquad r=Ax-\theta x .
\] For \(p(z)=2z^2-1\), \(s_\theta(z)=2(z+\theta)\). Near convergence the argument of the operator in the correction is small. If a product error is proportional to the norm of its input, the error in applying an operator to a small residual may shrink with convergence. An accurately evaluated residual and a controlled correction recurrence are essential. When the input residual is already corrupted at the scale of \(u\|A\|\), the argument loses force. This identity provides a way into the seminar paper’s residual-based recurrence. The ordinary recurrence in the lab is its comparison case. For the actual algorithm and its numerical evidence see Kodali, Ramakrishnan and Motamarri, Residual-based Chebyshev filtered subspace iteration.


Cost of reaching an accuracy target
A dense matrix–block product with an \(n\times p\) real block costs approximately \(2n^2p\) scalar floating-point operations. A sparse product costs approximately \(2\,\mathrm{nnz}(A)p\). A thin dense QR costs order \(np^2\) and the compressed eigensolve costs order \(p^3\). A degree-\(d\) filter takes \(d\) matrix–block products before extraction. These counts give no sustained bandwidth, occupancy or collective latency. For an illustrative machine model with peak rate \(F\) and bandwidth \(B_w\), moving \(S\) bytes and doing \(W\) operations requires at least \(\max(W/F,S/B_w)\) time for the modeled resources. Sparse indices, cache reuse, conversions, synchronization and contention affect actual time. A block may reuse matrix entries across columns. Distributed inner products require reductions, whereas stencil products often require neighbor exchanges.
For a fair comparison specify a target cluster, a common residual tolerance on the original operator, an orthogonality threshold, starting block and stopping rule. Time setup, transfers, filtering, QR, extraction and verification; include all repetitions needed to reach tolerance. Record failures to meet tolerance. A low-precision run with faster individual products can take longer to deliver an acceptable subspace, or never meet the criterion. Timing the dense teaching example says little about a sparse device implementation.
Checkpoint. A single-precision filter and double-precision QR produce \(\|I-X^*X\|\approx10^{-15}\) but a verified residual of \(10^{-6}\). These diagnostics can coexist: one measures internal geometry of the basis, the other tests its relation to \(A\).

section: 17.9 Session 8 — A controlled experiment from prediction to verification
text:
17.9 Session 8 — A controlled experiment from prediction to verification

Construct a problem with known answers
Take \(n=32\) and the orthonormal discrete cosine basis \(U\). Its zeroth column is constant \(1/\sqrt n\), and for row \(i=0,\ldots,n-1\) and column \(j=1,\ldots,n-1\) its entry is \(\sqrt{2/n}\cos(\pi(i+1/2)j/n)\). Set \(A=U\Lambda U^T\) with 29 equally spaced unwanted eigenvalues from \(1\) to \(5\) and targets \(8,9,10\). The dense rotation is deliberate: rounding a diagonal example can preserve exact zeros and hide leakage between directions. The exact mathematical construction and its stored floating-point realization differ slightly.
For each target eigenvector take its equal mixture with a different unwanted eigenvector. Pair \(8\) with \(5\), \(9\) with \(1\), and \(10\) with the second-smallest eigenvalue. These three vectors are orthonormal. Each angle is initially \(\pi/4\). For the pair determining the worst angle the power multiplier ratio is \(5/8\) and the degree-three Chebyshev ratio is \(1/55\). All other ratios are smaller. The graph estimate is attained, so the predicted largest tangents are exactly \((5/8)^k\) and \(55^{-k}\) in mathematical arithmetic. Convert a tangent \(t\) to a sine by \(t/\sqrt{1+t^2}\) before comparing with the lab’s sine diagnostic.
Each outer step applies the chosen operator, orthogonalizes, solves the projected eigenproblem, and checks the residuals in the original coordinates. The lab retains the QR basis for the next step; rotating it to the Ritz basis gives the same next range in exact arithmetic. It records the largest column residual, largest sine, maximum sorted Ritz-value error and orthogonality defect. Only the synthetic example supplies the exact target basis and exact target values. In applications, identification and separation must come from other information.


A measured history
The numbers below were obtained by independently executing the real-valued case study in NumPy with the same cosine construction, polynomial and precision split used in the MATLAB script. Both variants use binary64 QR, extraction and verification. The binary32 variant stores the mapped matrix in single and performs the filter recurrence in single. Last digits and stagnation levels depend on implementation.

Largest sine, single filter

Max residual, single filter

At step one the largest angle belongs to the \(8,5\) pair, while the largest residual can belong to a different pair: a residual weights the angle by the local eigenvalue separation. At step eight the double run meets an absolute residual tolerance of \(10^{-12}\); the displayed single run does not. The experiment combines storage and arithmetic errors. To isolate storage, round \(B\) to binary32 once and convert it back to binary64 for all products. To probe communication errors separately, an experiment needs an explicit communication pattern and quantization model.


Transfer to a variational PDE problem
In §6.11, \(Kx=\lambda Mx\) came from testing \(-u''=\lambda u\) with finite-element basis functions. Assume \(K=K^*\), \(M=M^*>0\) and \(M=LL^*\). Set \(y=L^*x\) and \(C=L^{-1}KL^{-*}\). Then \(Cy=\lambda y\) is Hermitian, \(\|y\|^2=x^*Mx\), and \[
Cy-\theta y=L^{-1}(Kx-\theta Mx).
\] For an \(M\)-normalized approximate eigenvector, \(\|Kx-\theta Mx\|_{M^{-1}}\) is precisely the Euclidean residual norm of the transformed problem. Solve triangular systems to apply the transformations. An \(M\)-orthonormal trial basis \(X\) gives the small matrix \(X^*KX\) and the Ritz residual satisfies \(X^*(KX-MXH)=0\). These are the Galerkin test equations again. A verified algebraic residual certifies the discrete eigenproblem. Errors due to the mesh and the choice of trial functions require an additional approximation argument.
Checkpoint. Why can a change of finite-element basis alter the Euclidean norm of a residual without changing the mathematical approximation? The residual represents a functional; its coordinates and the mass Gram matrix transform together. The dual norm accounts for both changes.
